Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure
articles.description: OpenAI introduces its National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint to protect local resources, create jobs, and guide responsible AI infrastructure development.
articles.content: New commitments to the communities where we build and policy proposals to help more Americans share in the benefits. The promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures. It can help someone learn a new skill, build a business, or solve a problem that was previously out of reach. Building more computing infrastructure capacity in the United States can help lower the cost of delivering AI, put these tools in more people’s hands, and ensure America stays at the forefront of the technology. The communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too. Residents should be able to influence how a campus is developed, hold developers accountable for covering the cost of powering it, and share in the jobs and business opportunities it creates. How we build these campuses is one of the first tests of whether the benefits of AI will be broadly shared. Today we’re publishing our National Community Compact(opens in a new window) and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint(opens in a new window). The compact sets out what communities can expect from OpenAI at future campuses that we own and operate. The blueprint proposes policies to help ensure that compute campus development gives communities a meaningful voice, protects families from new costs, and broadly shares the economic gains of AI. This builds on work we began in January, when we announced our Stargate Community commitments to pay our own way on energy and develop plans shaped by local priorities. We followed with specific commitments in Georgia and Ohio, covering energy costs, water use, local investment and accountability. Throughout that work, we’ve listened to residents, local leaders, schools and businesses about what matters to their communities. Today’s announcement is the next step in that ongoing effort. Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We’ll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we’re doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments: Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We’ll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we’ll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled. Protect local resources and report on our impact. We’ll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We’ll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information. Create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We’ll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We’ll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select. Those priorities will differ from place to place. In Effingham County, Georgia, residents helped shape a $4.8 million grant to provide free school meals for all 14,000 students in the county. In Pike County, Ohio, families identified childcare as a priority, leading to a joint $6 million commitment from OpenAI and SB Energy. Families should be able to count on basic protections whoever builds a campus in their community. Voluntary commitments from companies are an important starting point, but our blueprint goes further—asking federal, state, and local policymakers to establish clear rules for how the industry builds. New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies. Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared. That starts with who pays for power. State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and protect other customers if a project falls through. Utilities should also make it easier for campuses to connect if they can safely cut demand when power is scarce. At our planned Effingham County campus, for example, our agreement with Georgia Power allows the utility to reduce the power it delivers to us by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand. Congress can help meet growing demand by speeding up transmission upgrades and restoring and expanding tax incentives for clean electricity. Communities also need a way to hold developers accountable. The blueprint calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise, and hiring, and for narrow limits on when developers can require public officials to sign NDAs. When states or local governments offer tax incentives, the terms should be public, with measurable commitments and a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short. Finally, the blueprint proposes practical ways to keep more of the work local to ensure compute campuses support local workers and local businesses. Developers can share purchasing plans early enough for local suppliers to compete for contracts. Employers, building trades unions, and community colleges can use hiring forecasts to train residents for jobs they know will be available, from electrical work during construction to maintaining power and cooling systems for years afterward. The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

Two new candidate vaccines to join Ebola trial as treatment research advances
articles.content: Expert groups convened by the World Health Organization (WHO) have recommended adding two new Ebola vaccine candidates to the ongoing Tumaini clinical trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The recommendation marks the first time vaccines specifically designed to protect against Bundibugyo virus, the virus responsible for the current outbreak, will be evaluated during an outbreak of the disease. The two vaccine candidates are ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna’s mRNA-1469. WHO’s independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccines Prioritization recommended both for further clinical evaluation this week, based on available preclinical and early clinical evidence. The companies were informed on Monday. The vaccine candidates will enter the trial following national approvals. “The fact that these vaccines are ready to enter clinical trials is a testament to the power of science and partnership,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “I thank the scientists, health workers and partners in the DRC and around the world who have brought us to this point, and especially the people taking part in the trial. Their participation will generate vital evidence that could help save lives. Vaccines alone will not end this outbreak, but they could become a powerful new tool for bringing it under control.” The Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale, the DRC's national public health and biomedical research institute is leading the Tumani vaccines trial, with the University of Antwerp, Belgium, in close collaboration with WHO, Epicentre, Médecins Sans Frontières, the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Antwerp, and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the Ministry of Health of the DRC and the Institut National de Santé Publique. The rapid development of candidate vaccines is made possible by investments by the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations. Tumaini is designed to test multiple vaccine candidates within a single trial, using a ring-vaccination approach that enrolls contacts of people with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. It builds on an approach pioneered by WHO and partners during the West Africa Ebola outbreak a decade ago, when a landmark trial in Guinea established the efficacy of Ervebo against Ebola virus, also known as Zaire ebolavirus. Ervebo is the first vaccine being evaluated in a Tumaini trial to now assess efficacy against Bundibugyo virus. Four vaccination rings are already in place, with several more being prepared. The rings include contacts of people who became ill or died from Ebola. Research into potential treatments is also advancing. The WHO-sponsored PARTNERS trial, launched in July, is evaluating whether the monoclonal antibody MBP134, the antiviral remdesivir, or a combination of both can improve survival among patients with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. In addition, maftivimab will soon be added to the trial to assess its use as a potential treatment. A complementary post-exposure prophylaxis study with obeldevisir is underway. WHO is supporting research during the Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak through its R&D Blueprint and Health Emergencies Programme, including developing research protocols, providing strategic and technical advice, coordinating among partners, and providing operational support to embed rigorous and ethical studies within the response. Initial findings from the treatment trials are expected in the coming months, with results from the vaccine trial expected in early 2027. Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations’ agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations – leading the world’s response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care. Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. “Together for health. Stand with science”, the theme of World Health Day 2026, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide.

articles.title: Married couple, school employee oust incumbents on Clintondale school board
articles.content: A married couple who have opted to send their children to a neighboring school district are among three challengers elected to the Clintondale school board. David and Samantha Hilliard, who have enrolled their boys in Chippewa Valley Schools, won the seats along with Dorothy Wilkins, a longtime school employee. Board president Jared Maynard and trustee Diane Zontini were removed by voters in Tuesday’s midterms elections. The Hilliards join siblings Lisa and Kurt Wilson, Lisa Valerio-Nowc, Ava Mcdowell, and Barry Powers on the seven-member Clintondale Board of Education. They follow Jon and Cassie Gruenberg, who formerly served on the Eastpointe school board. Cassie resigned before her term expired and Jon, a longtime board member, lost his re-election bid in Tuesday’s election. Samantha Hilliard said both she and her husband would like to see increased decorum at the school board level, along with more accountability and transparency to the 1,677-student district in south Clinton Township. “I am humbled by the response and grateful for the support we’ve received,” she said the day after the election. “We hope to increase community engagement, which in turn will bring in more students to Clintondale and improve the quality our schools.” The couple, who work in the mortgage industry, said they decided to enroll their sons, ages 11 and 6, in Chippewa Valley Schools for various reasons, including reviews of the two districts along with personal knowledge. “Our son was going to Rainbow Elementary and after seeing what was going on in Clintondale, such as the ongoing teacher contract issue, we decided to make a change,” Samantha Hilliard said. “Plus, I’ve been involved as a volunteer at Chippewa Valley, so I saw a difference there.” As for critics who raise the issue over which district their children attend, Samantha Hilliard said she understands their concern. “I would say we are the perfect people to make a change. I would love to send my children to our neighborhood school. It’s not the teachers, it’s not the students, it’s a systematic issue at Clintondale that we’re going to have to turn around,” she said. David Hilliard said their goals are to set an agenda of “students first” and pave a new future for the district so that more people will enroll their children at Clintondale. He said studies show Clintondale’s elementary schools are highly rated, but it’s at the middle and high school levels where students run into difficulty. Hilliard, 42, also said the decorum should extend to school board members who have been known to argue with each other, and the length of board meetings, which routinely can stretch on past two hours. “I think there is a lack of control when you allow someone to behaves that way during a public meeting or behind closed doors,” he said, noting that the board needs set boundaries and get back to talking about improving the educational climate for students. David Hilliard is also a member of the Clinton Township Conservation & Beautification Committee and the Historical Commission. Maynard, a staunch Republican, said the new board members will be sworn in during the January meeting. “I wish all the success to our new superintendent and incoming board,” he said. “Over the last four years there has been great work done and there is a great foundation laid for the future success. I will continue to advocate for all the children in the district.”

articles.title: Michigan Democrats prepare for a second trifecta in state government
articles.description: Michigan Democrats won the governor’s race, control of the state House of Representatives, and an expanded majority in the state Senate during this week’s election.
articles.content: The Michigan Capitol building in Lansing.(Emma Winowiecki / Michigan Radio)Huge election night wins for Michigan Democrats are bringing the party back in full control of the Michigan Legislature and governor’s office.The party grew its state Senate majority by at least two seats. It flipped at least eight Republican-held state House of Representatives seats to take back the chamber, according to the Associated Press.State Rep. Alabas Farhat (D-Dearborn) said voters want to see action.“We now have a mandate to deliver for the working families and have to do it aggressively and have got to be serious here, be bold in how we deliver,” Farhat said on election night.Democrats last held a trifecta during the 2023-24 legislative term. Before that, it had been nearly 40 years.Democratic lawmakers passed many marquee laws during their first year in complete power, like gun safety policies, clean energy standards, and repealing anti-union legislation. But many felt like they left too much on the table during a slow 2024.Republicans retook the House of Representatives that year.When asked what lessons to take from that last trifecta, House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) said each Legislature is different.“We have a healthy number of returning members and we have a decent number of new members bringing new fresh energy and new blood to the table here. So, I look forward to packing that all together and making sure that we are an extremely productive Legislature meeting the needs of this moment,” Puri said after claiming victory at the election night watch party.Unlike the last trifecta, Democrats will have more than a one-vote majority in the upcoming session. The extra wiggle room could help them tackle more ambitious policies. Especially with Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson incoming.Current Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) will serve as her lieutenant governor next term. Before that happened, Brinks declined to say which policies were still on the table during the remainder of the year.“We’ll see what’s possible. Like with any legislature, you can only do what’s possible with the people that you have at the moment in history that you find yourself,” Brinks said Wednesday.The House and Senate Democratic Caucuses could take another step toward making their next leadership picks official Thursday.Puri is expected to continue leading House Democrats. The Senate will likely choose Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) as its next leader.

articles.title: Hines rides Blue Wave to defeat Bouchard for Michigan’s 10th District congressional seat
articles.content: Democrat Christina Hines defeated Republican Michael Bouchard for the 10th District congressional seat to represent over three-quarters of Macomb County residents. Hines, 36, of Warren, defeated Bouchard Jr., 32, of Rochester Hills, 188,078 to 162,347 in Macomb and Oakland counties to capture the seat and become the first Democratic Macomb County resident to represent the county since David Bonior in 2002, according to unofficial election results. Hines collected 60.2% of the vote in Macomb County and 51.7% of the tally in Oakland County, results say. Macomb comprises about 89% of the district. Hines’ rode a blue wave to victory as Democrats took control of both the U.S. House and Senate, in an overwhelming rebuke of Republican President Donald Trump and his policies. Dems swept Michigan’s top races: Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers for U.S. Senate, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson beat GOP U.S. Rep. John James for governor, Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit defeated Doug Loyd for Attorney General and Lt. Governor Garlin Gilchrist beat Macomb County Clerk Anthony Clerk for Secretary of State. The 10th District is composed of Macomb County south of Hall Road (M-59), Shelby Township, Utica, about one-fourth of Macomb Township, and Rochester and Rochester Hills. James, a Shelby Township resident, will give up the seat in January after two terms in Washington, D.C. Hines is a former assistant prosecutor in Washtenaw County who promised to provide a check on the president and bring down rising costs, protect Social Security and Medicare, remove corporate money from politics and provide amnesty of law-abiding immigrants, among other things. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel credited Hines with being “able to win in one of the nation’s most competitive districts.” “The people of Michigan’s 10th District know there is nobody better to put in charge than a mother — especially one who is also a prosecutor,” Hertel said in a written statement. “Christina is simply continuing her life of public service under a new title in Washington. As a Congresswoman, she will continue to advocate for the most vulnerable among us. With her grit and dedication, I know she will be successful. Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said in a writte statement: “As an accomplished prosecutor and Macomb County native, Christina has always served her neighbors while being guided by Michigan values. In the House of Representatives, she will put in the work to lower costs, protect healthcare, stand up for workers, bring down the cost of housing and childcare, invest in public education, and look out for the people of Michigan.” During the campaign, former Arizona congresswoman Gabby Giffords visited and campaigned for Hines in Mount Clemens. Giffords, who was shot in January 2011 while attending a gathering for constituents,founded GIFFORDS PAC, the national gun violence prevention organization. “We were proud to stand with her, and I am thrilled that voters across the 10th District made their voices heard and decided to send a strong gun safety champion to Washington,” Giffords said Wednesday in a press release. “I spent a lot of time with Christina and I know she has the courage to stand up to the gun lobby and keep guns out of the wrong hands. GIFFORDS was proud to be an early supporter of her campaign and, as a career prosecutor who worked tirelessly to keep families safe, we look forward to working with her in Congress to enact commonsense gun safety reforms that will save lives.” During the campaign, Hines and her supporters attacked Bouchard, the son of Oakland County Sheriff MIke Bouchard, for his support of Trump and his policies, including the war in Iran. “He stands with Trump and he supports sending billions overseas and forcing taxpayers here to foot the bill,” she told The Macomb Daily. “We need members of Congress who are capable of holding people of their own party accountable, and my opponent is clearly incapable of doing that. We’re spending billions of dollars on another war that families cannot afford, gas prices are through the roof, diesel has hit record high and increasing the cost of all of our goods.” Robert Johnson, who voted Tuesday at the Boy and Girls Club in Eastpointe, said he cast his ballot for Hines and other Democrats in opposition to Trump and his policies. “Under the current administration, I don’t agree with the direction that we’re headed in,” Johnson said. “I’m against wars, and gas prices are high. I figure we can get balance back in making these decisions.” Bouchard, an Army captain and veteran, campaigned on his background and traditional conservative values. Hines, who headed the sexual-assault unit in Washtenaw, overcame several attack ads by Bouchard and his supporters. One ad that seemed to resonate featured a woman who said she was rape victim and claimed that Hines bungled the case. Hines responded with an ad that disputed the allegation and indicated a judge approved dismissal of the case. Macomb County Sheriff’s Anthony Wickersham said voters shouldn’t believe the “lies” by Bouchard and his supporters. On Tuesday, Ebony Samual, 49, of Eastpointe, said after casting a ballot she discounted the criticism, noting Hines’ 10-year career in Washtenaw County. “She also prosecuted a lot of people,” Samuel said. Samuel said also convincing her was the fact that Hines supporters “knocked on my door” four times during the campaign. “She earned my vote,” Samuel said. Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer praised Hines five days befoe the election in an Instagram video with Hines. “Christina Hines knows a little something about solving problems even when things get chaotic,” Whitmer said. “That’s the kind of get-stuff-done leadership we need in Congress right now. Less chaos and more solutions to lower costs for Michigan families.”

Following midterm landslide, Democrats pressed by supporters to deliver on promises
articles.description: WASHINGTON — As the monumental midterm victories set in, Democrats began to talk strategy Wednesday on how to deliver what voters want: lower prices, attainable health care and an end to a stagnant and expensive conflict in the Middle East. Starting in January, the party will control both chambers of Congress, giving them the upper hand over much […]
articles.content: Supporters of Rep.-elect Zach Dembo, a Kentucky Democrat who flipped a Republican seat, cheer during Dembo’s victory speech in Lexington on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Brian Simms for Kentucky Lantern)WASHINGTON — As the monumental midterm victories set in, Democrats began to talk strategy Wednesday on how to deliver what voters want: lower prices, attainable health care and an end to a stagnant and expensive conflict in the Middle East. Starting in January, the party will control both chambers of Congress, giving them the upper hand over much of President Donald Trump’s agenda, including his judicial nominees, and the power to investigate the first two years of Trump’s second term, including his business ventures, war decisions and mass deportation campaign. Democrats had gained 237 seats — well past the 218 needed — in the U.S. House as of Wednesday afternoon, according to The Associated Press, which also showed Democrats flipped 29 GOP House seats. The party trounced conventional expectations in the Senate by flipping seven seats, giving Democrats and independents who caucus with them a total of 54 in the upper chamber, according to the AP, as of 4 p.m. Eastern. Climbing inflation and record fuel prices followed Republicans on the campaign trail, fueling the groundswell for Democrats. Voters blamed Trump for higher prices in stores and at the pump as his war in Iran entered its ninth month, and as sweeping tariffs remained on imports. Shawn Fain, leader of the United Auto Workers union, said “it’s not a massive win for anybody until these people go to work and deliver results.” The union, which endorsed Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in early June, has roughly 1 million active and retired members — 350,000 of them in Michigan alone, according to Fain. El-Sayed won the Senate race in Michigan on Wednesday. “I believe this election is a mandate for change, but it is up to the Democratic Party now to deliver. And if they don’t deliver, we’ll be the first ones to call them out on it,” Fain said. ‘Legislative razor wire’ Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said voters delivered “a generational remake of the Senate map that has huge consequences for history.” The New York Democrat, who is poised to lead the upper chamber once again, told reporters Wednesday morning that Senate Democrats have three priorities: lower the cost of living, “clean up” corruption in government and “check on Trump’s chaos at home and abroad,” including the war with Iran. “Whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court, and entangle him in legislative razor wire,” Schumer said. Giving brief answers to a barrage of questions, Schumer hinted that Democrats could end the war in Iran with the “power of the purse” and sidestepped a question about “nuking” the filibuster. “I’ll have more to say in the coming days about how Democrats pulled off this victory, how our majority plans to deliver for the American people,“ Schumer said. When asked if Senate Democrats will work with Trump, Schumer said, “We are going to work hard to drive costs down with the president or without him. Period.” ‘A dramatic change in direction’ House Democratic leaders celebrated the blue tsunami across the country while vowing to fight for an “affordable America” in the next Congress. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said “the American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction, and that’s exactly what House Democrats will deliver beginning on Day One,” during a press conference Wednesday afternoon. Jeffries got a step closer to becoming the next speaker of the House following Democrats’ dramatic win Tuesday night. If elected by a majority of House members, Jeffries would make history as the first Black person to hold the gavel. Jeffries was joined by Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene of Washington state, House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, and the chair and vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus, Reps. Pete Aguilar and Ted Lieu, respectively, both from California. Meanwhile, the GOP’s mid-decade redistricting blitz to shore up several seats flopped Tuesday night following Democratic victories in several districts Republicans redrew. DelBene, who leads the Democratic Party’s campaign apparatus for House races, said “every single redistricted Frontliner will return to Congress,” using the committee’s term for its most endangered incumbents. “Simply put, their gerrymandering scheme absolutely backfired, and it should send a strong message to any Republican thinking of pursuing any more gerrymanders next year,” she said. Agenda items on tap As Democrats plan to center their agenda on affordability, Lieu spelled out some of the party’s legislative priorities in the new Congress. For starters, Lieu said Democrats would pass a bill to reverse the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law’s sweeping Medicaid cuts, which axe roughly $1 trillion in Medicaid spending over 10 years. He also said they would pass legislation to “restore” the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits, which expired in December 2025 and were used by individuals who buy their own health insurance through the Affordable Care Act Marketplace. “We will pass a bill to stop the stupid Trump tariffs jacking up prices on Americans, and we will pass a bill to stop the Iran war,” the California Democrat added. Congressional Progressive Caucus Members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus touted victories in the wave election. Rep. Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat who chairs the caucus, said the group’s roughly 100 members will work with Jeffries on “a mandate for dramatic change” but warned that he and colleagues want significant transformation. “Last night was not a sign that all of Democrats’ problems are solved,” Casar said on a virtual call with reporters. “The election is not an endorsement of returning to the status quo or tinkering around the edges. This is a message that people in this country are mad as hell, and are giving Democrats a shot to show them we can do something about it.” Democrat Will Lawrence, who defeated incumbent GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, said Congress needs “to set our foreign policy straight.” “A huge cause for regret among Trump voters in this district is because he said he wasn’t going to start any new wars, and look at what he got us into now in Iran. So we have a mandate to pass a war powers resolution to restrain further hostilities in Iran,” Lawrence said. Lawrence co-founded the Sunrise Movement, a climate-focused political action group, and received backing from congressional progressives. Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said despite the momentous wins, the Democratic Party is still “not particularly popular.” “I think we’ve got a shot to show that we can deliver on the kind of bold populist change that people ran on and won on,” Jayapal said. “And I think that is going to be our task going forward for the next two years.”

articles.description: East Lansing Police Department is asking for tips and video after two shootings this weekend left five people injured. Police said Wednesday evening in a news release that the two […]
articles.content: East Lansing Police Department is asking for tips and video after two shootings this weekend left five people injured. Police said Wednesday evening in a news release that the two shootings appear to be unconnected and none of the victims were Michigan State University students. The statement said police recovered seven guns from the two shooting locations. Investigators believe that several gunmen in each shooting left the area immediately after firing. Witnesses and victims provided the descriptions of the shooters, according to police. https://lansingcitypulse.com/five-people-shot-overnight-in-east-lansing-as-city-calls-for-help-with-multiple-shootings-dui-and-medical-cases/ Police on Wednesday released descriptions of three people in the first shooting, around M.A.C. Avenue and Linden Avenue around 12:26 a.m. on Nov. 1. Black male, early 20s, five feet seven inches, skinny build with dreads, wearing a black track suit with a grey skull mask Light-skinned Black male wearing a gray hoodie and pants Unknown male wearing a “Michael Myers” mask and jumpsuit costume The victims are a 20-year-old male from Lansing, a 19-year-old male from Illinois and a 23-year-old male from Lansing. The second shooting happened around Frye Avenue and Stoddard Street and happened around 1:40 a.m. on Nov. 1. Police described people wanted for that shooting as: Light-skinned Black male, early 20s, five feet six inches, brown shoulder-length dreadlocks wearing a white shirt and shorts Black male, 20s, wearing a black hoodie, black ski mask and darkish jeans Light-skinned Black male 20s with dreads The victims in the second shooting are a 19-year-old male from Detroit and an 18-year-old male from Detroit. ELPD will be using all available resources, including local and federal partners and seeking prosecution against the individuals involved in each shooting. At present, no charges have been filed. There is no one in custody. Video tips (e.g., Ring, Tesla, cell phone or any other videos) may be submitted to ELPD Detective Jordyn Willis at jwillis@cityofeastlansing.com or call (517) 319-6842. Any other tips related to these crimes may be submitted to ELPD Detective Katey Harrison at kharris@cityofeastlansing.com or call (517) 319-6851. ELPD is also working with Crimestoppers of Mid-Michigan to allow witnesses to share tips anonymously. If you have information to share, call the tip line at (517) 483-7867 (STOP) or report it at https://www.p3tips.com/tipform.aspx?ID=903. Police released these images of guns related to the shootings.

articles.title: Zohran Mamdani wins dismissal of pied-à-terre tax challenge
articles.content: Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations New York City has won a legal battle over its new tax on luxury second homes, potentially clearing a hurdle for Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plans to collect hundreds of millions of dollars in new tax revenue. On Wednesday, a state appeals court reversed a lower court's ruling that had given property owners temporary relief from the new surcharge and dismissed their lawsuit against the tax. The new pied-à-terre tax is intended to raise revenue from certain high-value properties used as second homes. While Mamdani has said the tax would help fulfill a campaign promise to tax the rich, its rollout has faced significant political and legal hurdles. The tax has been subject to three separate legal challenges, including claims that the city's rollout would cause “mass confusion” for property owners and that the surcharge unfairly discriminates against wealthy residents. In September, a Staten Island judge ordered the city to redo notices it had mailed to property owners who might be subject to the surcharge. Wednesday's ruling marked a victory for the Mamdani administration against the lawsuit, filed by property owners who argued that the new pied-à-terre tax hadn't been properly rolled out. The appeals court found that the property owners lacked standing to sue because they hadn't shown they suffered a concrete injury from the city's actions. The judges said receiving a tax notice or appearing on a public list of properties potentially subject to the surcharge was not enough to establish such harm. The court did not determine whether the city had followed every procedure correctly, and the decision does not resolve separate legal challenges to the tax. In a statement Wednesday, Mamdani celebrated the decision, saying the appeals court had rejected an attempt by wealthy property owners to avoid paying their fair share. “The pied-a-terre surcharge asks those who can afford luxury second homes to contribute toward the safer streets, cleaner parks and essential public services that every New Yorker deserves,” Mamdani said. He added that the city would continue defending the tax against ongoing legal challenges. But Mamdani's claim that the tax will bring in $500 million a year remains in question. The city's Department of Finance has already granted more than 8,800 exemption requests. Earlier this year, city Comptroller Mark Levine estimated that the tax could generate up to $380 million from roughly 11,200 properties. This story has been updated with new information. Giulia Heyward is a breaking news reporter on the Day-Of desk. She previously worked at NPR, as a breaking news reporter, and the New York Times, as a reporting fellow on the national desk. articles.title: Democrats won Congress. Now they have to figure out how to deal with Trump.
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Democratic leaders in Congress have just a couple months to decide how they want to balance investigations into President Donald Trump and his administration with securing his signature on major bills to address the cost of living, a top concern for voters. While Democrats gained control of the House and Senate in this year’s midterm […]
articles.content: U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters on Nov. 4, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Tom Brenner/Getty Images)WASHINGTON — Democratic leaders in Congress have just a couple months to decide how they want to balance investigations into President Donald Trump and his administration with securing his signature on major bills to address the cost of living, a top concern for voters. While Democrats gained control of the House and Senate in this year’s midterm elections, the party won’t hold veto-proof margins when the new session of Congress begins in early January. That will require congressional leaders and the president to find compromise on legislation. Failure to do so would block any bills that could improve the lives of Americans from becoming law and potentially lead to more shutdowns, since Congress must fund the government every year. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who will very likely become speaker in January, and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, will set the tone for that relationship, though committee chairs will play a significant role as well. Trump said during an impromptu press conference Wednesday in the construction zone for his White House ballroom that he will “get along, probably, with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive. But I have the power of the veto.” Trump said he wasn’t concerned about Democrats potentially trying to impeach him for a third time. “I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that,” he said. ‘Trump’s supplicant Senate’ Schumer said earlier in the morning his top priorities will be to address the rising cost of living, to “clean up corruption in government” and act as a check on “Trump’s chaos at home and abroad.” “This war must end,” he said. “And make no mistake, whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court and entangle him in legislative razor wire. The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over.” Trump said during his press conference that the war in Iran will continue until “whenever” he wants to end it. Schumer said he’d share more details in the weeks ahead about what the Democratic majority will do come January, but added he hadn’t yet spoken to the president about how the two separate but equal branches of government might work together. Democrats, he said, will use must-pass government funding bills to place guardrails on the administration and the war in Iran, though he didn’t say how he’d get the president to sign those bills. “We are going to end the war,” he said. “We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war and the founding fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people.” Schumer sidestepped a question about whether he would try to eliminate the legislative filibuster, which has forced bipartisanship in that chamber for decades. The rule requires at least 60 senators vote to advance a bill before it can move onto final passage. “The first thing we’re going to do is reduce people’s costs and work the legislative process so it does,” he said in response to the reporter’s question. Schumer also declined to say directly whether Democrats will seek to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a process that would start in the House. “Everyone will make their own interpretation of what it meant in terms of Hegseth,” he said, responding to a question about the election results. Schumer intends to seek the role of majority leader, according to his office. No Democrats have announced they plan to challenge him, making the race unopposed. Medicaid cuts targeted Jeffries said during an afternoon press conference that Democrats “are ready, willing and able to find bipartisan common ground with the other side of the aisle as long as we can bring about meaningful change on the issues that matter. And that begins with decisively addressing the affordability crisis.” But he also made clear House Democrats’ to-do list will begin with reversing changes and cuts to Medicaid, the state-federal health program for lower-income people, that Republicans included in their “big, beautiful” bill, as well as restoring the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that lapsed at the end of last year. Jeffries did seem to brush aside the possibility of impeaching Trump or Hegseth, responding to questions by asking if Hegseth was actually still around. “I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment,” he said. “We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability because the House is a separate and co-equal branch of government.” House Democrats are likely to reverse Republicans’ “hands off” approach to artificial intelligence and data centers with their majority. California Democratic Rep. Ted Lieu said during the same press conference that it was a “bad decision” for Republicans to “let the AI industry run wild.” “Two things will change next term,” he said. “We will hold public hearings on AI. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails on AI, and specifically data centers. You see huge pushback from the American people for the out-of-control AI industry.” Republican leadership battle ahead Republican leaders will play a role in brokering deals with Democrats, though Senate GOP lawmakers will have more influence than their House counterparts. House Democrats will be able to pass most legislation with a simple majority vote. But in the Senate, Democratic leaders will still need to garner some level of bipartisan support to advance bills unless they eliminate the procedural step that requires at least 60 senators to vote to move toward final passage. Senate Republican Leader John Thune, R-S.D., plans to run for another term heading up his party in that chamber, though this time as minority leader, according to a spokesperson. Thune, first elected to the Senate in 2004, rose through the ranks of Senate GOP leadership before taking over as majority leader this Congress. That gives him two years of experience negotiating floor schedules and amendment debate with Schumer. In the House, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., plans to step down from leadership rather than try to stay in the top spot, which will be minority leader for the GOP next year, according to a spokesperson. Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise, currently the majority leader, and Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, chairman of the Judiciary Committee, are both running for that role. An individual familiar with Scalise’s plans told States Newsroom his “number one goal will be to lead the conference back into the majority. He is a proven and tested leader who is ready on day one. He’s spent his career unifying Republicans, and he is prepared for the big legislative and oversight battles ahead. The conference knows him, how he fights, and that he’s a trusted leader.” Jordan wrote in a letter to his fellow House Republicans that the party “must learn” from the results of this year’s election as it looks forward. “I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats’ playbook. I know what it will take to lead our Conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the Democrats’ tactics,” he wrote.” We need a Leadership team that is active and engaged, forward-thinking and straight-shooting.” Scalise has been a member of the House since May 2008 and a member of House GOP leadership since 2013, first as whip then as leader. Jordan was first sworn in as a member in January 2007. He became chairman of the Judiciary Committee four years ago. Trump said he planned to “stay out” of that race and that he didn’t ask Johnson to step aside as the leader of House Republicans. Those elections are expected in mid-November. Whoever House Republicans elect will set the tone for when to negotiate legislation with Democrats and when to try to block bills from passing that chamber.

Chamber director elected as Romeo president
articles.content: A local chamber of commerce official defeated two current Romeo officials on Tuesday in a competitive race to serve as president of the village. Kelley Stephens out-tallied village Clerk Jamie Lucero and village Council Trustee Justin Parker for the 4-year term by collecting 595 votes, or 37.7%, compared to 536 votes, 34%, for Parker, and 439 votes, 27.8%, for Lucero. There were eight write-ins. Stephens, who has been executive director of the Northern Macomb Regional Chamber of Commerce for 17 years, wrote Wednesday on Facebook: “I woke up this morning feeling incredibly grateful, humbled, and excited about what lies ahead.” “Thank you for placing your trust and confidence in me to serve as your next Village President,” she wrote. “It is an honor that I do not take lightly. “My commitment to Romeo remains the same: to listen, to be accessible, to make thoughtful decisions, and to always keep the best interests of our Village at heart. “The campaign may be over, but the real work is just beginning. And I couldn’t be more excited to get started!” Stephens vowed during the campaign to increase interaction with other units of government, including Macomb County, try to attract businesses to the Powell Road corridor, keep the downtown business district vibrant and start a regular newsletter. Stephens moved from Shelby Township to Romeo with her husband in about 1980 and has worked for the chamber for a total of 23 years. She also has served on the Downtown Development Authority. The couple has owned multiple businesses. The president position was made full-time eight years ago. The current president, Meagan Poznanski, opted to run for clerk and lost by a nearly 2-to-1 margin to Lisa Hall, who received 977 votes while Poznanski drew 500 votes. Hall has worked for multiple municipalities, including Washington Township. She served as the part-time DDA director and has a bachelor’s and master’s degree in public administration. Treasurer Caroline Miller faced no opposition. Incumbent council Trustees Zach Fowler, Matt Edwards and Shelley Rosso retained their positions, thwarting efforts by challengers Leo Hudson and Charles Bennett. Challenger Sharon Smith defeated incumbent Trustee Zachary Throne, who was appointed last April, for a partial term of two years. In another pair of contested races, Lenox Township voters elected two Republican trustee candidates over two Democrats as part of the township increasing its board from five to seven members. Thomas Clifford, 71, and Ron Zemens, 72, were chosen over Ed Pate, 66, and Cory Ferriby, 38. Clifford received 2,538 votes and Zemens received 2,398 votes while Pate drew 1,985 tallies and Ferribly drew 1,956 votes. Clifford previously served on the township board and serves on the township Board of Review. He was an electrician for the county Roads Department. Zemens served on the township Board of Review and has been a business owner for over 35 years. Both new trustees said they oppose a data center coming to the township, which has been the subject of discussion for a center to possibly locate in the southeastern corner.

articles.title: Scarlett Johansson Breaks Silence on ‘The Batman Part II’ Role: “It Was Very Hard to Figure Out”
articles.description: The actress' character in Matt Reeves' sequel to DC Studios' 2022 film has yet to be revealed.
articles.content: The actress' character in Matt Reeves' sequel to DC Studios' 2022 film has yet to be revealed. Scarlett Johansson is opening up about her mysterious role in The Batman Part II, revealing that the part gave her “a lot of existential angst.” In an interview with Entertainment Tonight, published Wednesday, the actress was asked about her upcoming projects, The Exorcist: Martyrs and The Batman Part II, and which role pushed her furthest out of her comfort zone. “Probably the role in The Batman,” she responded. “It gave me a lot of existential angst for some reason.” Johansson went on to explain that the role was particularly difficult to figure out, though she wasn’t sure exactly why. Related Stories Lifestyle Skyler Gisondo on His Style Evolution, Landing His First Fashion Campaign With Bonobos and Playing Ariana Grande's Fiancé in 'Focker-in-Law' TV Earl Barret, 'Too Close for Comfort' Writer and Producer, Dies at 94 “It was very hard to figure out. I don’t know why, whether it was just the role or was just where I’m in my life, or what’s going on, but it was just hard to crack it. And that’s all I can say about it. It was a tough role in a lot of ways,” she added. Director Matt Reeves confirmed in May that Johansson would be joining the sequel to his 2022 film, which stars Robert Pattinson as Bruce Wayne/Batman. However, details about the character she will portray have yet to be revealed. In addition to Johansson, new additions to the sequel’s cast include Sebastian Stan, Charles Dance as well as Brian Tyree Henry and Sebastian Koch. (See the full cast here.) Production on The Batman Part II briefly paused in October after Reeves stepped away to attend to a family matter, according to DC Studios. Later that month, Steven Soderbergh (Ocean’s Eleven, Traffic) stepped in, with the studio’s support, to help Reeves complete the final stretch of principal photography. The Batman Part II is currently scheduled to hit theaters Feb. 18, 2028. articles.title: Midterm winners include several who made history
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Winners of more than a dozen congressional and gubernatorial races have broken longstanding barriers of race, gender and sexuality. The results set records for the most Black governors and most women governors, and the first Black woman governor, Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms. Democrats, who flipped the U.S. House and Senate, had more historic firsts, though […]
articles.content: Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat who is now senator-elect for Michigan, speaks to Democratic supporters at a unity rally held at Renaissance High School in Detroit on Aug. 7, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)WASHINGTON — Winners of more than a dozen congressional and gubernatorial races have broken longstanding barriers of race, gender and sexuality. The results set records for the most Black governors and most women governors, and the first Black woman governor, Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms. Democrats, who flipped the U.S. House and Senate, had more historic firsts, though Rep. Byron Donalds will become the first elected Black Republican governor in the country after winning his race in Florida. Nevada and Wisconsin also elected their first Black governors. Seventeen women will serve as governor in 2027, breaking the previous record of 14 in 2025, according to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. That includes Democrat Deb Haaland, a member of the Pueblo of Laguna who made history in 2021 as the first Native American to serve as a Cabinet secretary. Haaland won her race in New Mexico, making her the first Indigenous woman to be elected governor in the U.S. And three Democratic senators-elect will make history once they are sworn in for the 120th Congress in January. In New Hampshire, Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas will be the first openly gay elected senator. Michigan elected the first Muslim senator, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, and Minnesota voters made Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan the first Native American woman senator, who could be joined by Alaska Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, an Alaska Native whose Senate race was too close to call Wednesday. Another tight Senate race is in Mississippi, where Democratic candidate Scott Colom could become the first Black senator from the state since the Reconstruction era if he defeats GOP incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Race-based caucuses expand Tuesday’s historic wins also means growth for certain caucuses aligned with Democrats. The Congressional Hispanic Caucus will grow to more than 50 members from 44. Six incoming members of the all-Democratic caucus flipped Republican-held seats in Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada and Texas. The Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus will gain at least four new members, growing to the largest size in its history at 22 members, Rep. Grace Meng, chair of the caucus said in a statement. A House race in Arizona that has not been called would give the caucus 23 members if Democratic candidate Amish Shah wins. “Last night’s election was a resounding repudiation of President Trump and his failed policies that put the safety, security, and civil rights of Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians, and Pacific Islanders at risk,” Meng said. Record-setting women Following Tuesday’s election, Democrats will control 28 governorships compared to 20 for Republicans, with two results still unknown. Several will be their states’ first elected women governors. “This was an impressive result for women in American politics, with women setting records and breaking significant barriers around the nation,” the Center for American Women and Politics Director Debbie Walsh said in a statement. “I’m particularly encouraged to see an increase in the number of women governors.” In Minnesota, Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar will become the state’s first woman governor. As part of a Democratic sweep of Texas, the Lone Star State elected its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, who ousted Republican Gov. Greg Abbott seeking his fourth term. And in Ohio, Dr. Amy Acton will become the Buckeye State’s first woman and first Jewish governor. Acton, who served as Ohio’s health director, defeated her Republican challenger Vivek Ramaswamy, who in the closing weeks of the campaign stood by a political ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother calling her daughter a liar. Acton was removed from her mother’s custody after her stepfather was indicted for sexually abusing her as a child. Black governors Five Black governors won their races on Election Day, setting a record for the most Black governors in office at once. Bottoms, Georgia’s first Democratic governor since 1998, will be the first Black person and first woman governor of Georgia. In Wisconsin, voters elected their first Black governor, David Crowley, a former county executive who billed himself as a centrist Democrat. And in Nevada, Aaron Ford, a Democrat and the state’s attorney general, ousted Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore easily won his reelection bid.

articles.title: Trans sports bans get voter approval in 4 states
articles.description: Voters in four states — Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington — are on track to pass or have passed measures to restrict transgender athletes’ participation in sports, a key policy focus of the Trump administration. Colorado, Nebraska and Washington’s measures were ballot initiatives, while Arizona reached the ballot by way of the legislature. Although there […]
articles.content: Ahnaleigh Wilson, 17, of Eastmont High School, center, and Frances Staudt, 17, of Tumwater High School, right, speak with the media about Initiative 638 at Let’s Go Washington’s election night watch party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Redmond, Wash. (Photo by Ryan Berry/Washington State Standard)Voters in four states — Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington — are on track to pass or have passed measures to restrict transgender athletes’ participation in sports, a key policy focus of the Trump administration. Colorado, Nebraska and Washington’s measures were ballot initiatives, while Arizona reached the ballot by way of the legislature. Although there were sweeping Democratic wins in Republican strongholds Tuesday, GOP-backed proposals are winning over voters in various parts of the country. Arizona’s initiative, which was garnering approximately 59% support late Wednesday, expands existing restrictions on transgender athletes to include private athletic associations and prohibits schools and athletic organizations from allowing individuals to use bathrooms, locker rooms and other private spaces designated for a sex different from the one recorded on their original birth certificate. Colorado’s Proposition 134 was passing with 52% of the vote. The measure would require school athletic teams from elementary school through college to be designated for male, female or coeducational participation and require students to compete according to their biological sex. Nebraska’s measure is an amendment to the state constitution, which now prohibits students of the male sex from participating on teams designated for girls’ and women’s teams. Washington’s initiative will prohibit transgender girls from competing in girls’ K-12 sports and require healthcare documentation verifying sex eligibility for students seeking to participate on female teams. The state interscholastic athletics association reported knowing of only about 10 transgender athletes participating statewide each year. According to Ballotpedia, 29 states had laws, regulations or interscholastic rules limiting or banning participation on female school sports teams to students of the female sex. articles.title: As voters task Dems with delivering affordability, Hines keeps her family close to heart
articles.description: After Election Day delivered major gains for Democrats across the country, party leadership and their newly-elected members are pledging to deliver on the mandate that Republicans promised voters in 2024: lowering costs and delivering economic relief. Among those candidates is U.S. Rep.-elect Christina Hines (D-Warren), who flipped Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, currently held by U.S. […]
articles.content: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines take questions from the press following a campaign launch in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo Kyle Davidson/Advance)After Election Day delivered major gains for Democrats across the country, party leadership and their newly-elected members are pledging to deliver on the mandate that Republicans promised voters in 2024: lowering costs and delivering economic relief. Among those candidates is U.S. Rep.-elect Christina Hines (D-Warren), who flipped Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, currently held by U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), who opted against seeking reelection to run for governor, which was unsuccessful, as he lost to Democrat Jocelyn Benson. Made up of Rochester and Rochester Hills in eastern Oakland County, and the southern portion of Macomb County, which has long been defined by the blue-collar workers who call it their home, Michigan’s 10th District was a major target for Democrats and Republicans. While Hines and her Republican opponent, Michael Bouchard Jr., each campaigned on lowering costs, voters elected Hines, a former prosecutor, to succeed James in Congress. Speaking with Michigan Advance Wednesday, Hines said her district’s residents were concerned about how expensive life can be while heading into the polls. Christina Hines, the Democratic nominee for the 10th Congressional District, addresses supporters and Democrats at a rally featuring former President Barack Obama at Cass Technical High School on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) “Whether it’s healthcare, gas, groceries, whatever it is, people need some relief and they need some change,” Hines said. “And so I think that that’s what they were voting for certainly here in our district.” As Democrats pledge to deliver the relief Americans are seeking, Hines said her perspective as a working mother of three is more in line with the residents of her district than members of Congress. “I talk about how there’s more millionaires in Congress than there are moms, and that is so different, right?” Hines said. “Like many people in Congress don’t have to think about, ‘Oh my gosh, it just took me $90 to fill up my minivan, and how is that going to impact my grocery budget?’” For that reason, Hines said she will always be focused on lowering costs, noting that if more members of Congress had the experience of an ordinary working life, it would be a very different place. When asked if there was one central issue she would address in her first term if given the opportunity to deliver a solution, Hines pointed to healthcare. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “I’m hearing just heartbreaking stories from people all over this district that cannot afford the care that they need,” Hines said, noting that her mother was chronically ill when she was growing up, and that she had been on Medicaid before. “Every single American should have access to quality, affordable healthcare and I will genuinely work with anyone and create any type of plan and review any type of plan to make that happen,” Hines said. In addition to the key issues around affordability, Hines said she would also like to take a look at regulations around big tech and AI. In addition to her perspective as a parent, she also pointed to her experience as a former child abuse prosecutor, where she’d seen the ways social media can harm children’s mental health. “So far we’ve had a Congress that has really failed to put any guardrails up to keep our community safe,” Hines said, noting her excitement to begin working putting those regulations in place. “We’ve got a lot of younger people, a lot of parents that are coming in,” Hines said in reference to her fellow newly-elected members of Congress. “I bet that we can find some really great bipartisan approaches here to protect families.”

articles.title: Nintendo's biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business
articles.description: And what that could mean for physical Switch game costs.
articles.content: For years, the AI industry's insatiable demand for memory and storage has had plenty of knock-on effects on the price and availability of PC components like RAM, SSDs, and GPUs. Now those shortages are also squeezing the supply of ROM chips that power physical Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 game cartridges. Chip manufacturer Macronix announced in its third-quarter earnings report that the company's production of ROM chips "has reached its end" and that it will begin "gradually decoupling from the game industry," as reported by Taiwanese news site BigGo Finance. That could be an issue for Nintendo, which analyst David Gibson notes uses Macronix as its "main memory chip maker" for physical game cartridges. That ROM production—which has shrunk 39 percent in the last year and now represents just 5 percent of Macronix's business—is being crowded out by production of more lucrative, in-demand chips like NOR- and NAND-based memory and eMMCs, the company said. With Macronix's production capacity stuck at 25,000 12-inch wafers a month—and $1.2 billion in planned new capacity taking a year or more to spin up—less profitable ROM chips are taking up wafer space that can earn more through other types of chips.Read full article Comments

articles.title: AI PACs spent millions trying to shape Congress — here’s how they fared
articles.description: AI industry PACs spent millions influencing the 2026 midterms, with mixed results. Political groups are already looking toward the next election cycle.
articles.content: Political groups both supporting and opposing the AI industry spent millions of dollars trying to influence Tuesday’s midterm elections and shape the future of AI regulation. That spending produced mixed results, with some of the most heavily backed candidates losing their races. On the industry side, two AI-focused political action committees (PACs) that raised and spent money to influence the elections — American Mission and Building the Future — collectively spent $4.8 million to back South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham, who lost. American Mission is the Republican spending arm of Leading the Future (LTF), a broader political group backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and the VC firm Andreessen Horowitz. American Mission also spent more than $500,000 apiece supporting Republican House candidates Aaron Flint in Montana and Laurie Buckhout in North Carolina, both of whom lost. LTF’s Democratic spending arm, Think Big, had better luck backing Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz, who won reelection. Groups advocating for stronger AI safeguards also saw mixed results. Public First, which is backed by Anthropic, supported several Republicans who lost through its affiliated PAC but had more success backing Democratic candidates. It also contributed $3 million to a PAC supporting California state Sen. Scott Wiener, who was leading his race at the time of publication. Meanwhile, Guardrails Alliance, a group that has sought to make taking money from AI companies a political liability, spent more than $1 million apiece opposing two candidates who lost: California Rep. Jimmy Gomez and Montana’s Aaron Flint. It also spent $300,000 supporting Angela Gonzales-Torres, who defeated Gomez. It’s difficult to separate the impact of AI-related spending from the broader Democratic wave that swept Tuesday’s elections. Elon Musk, who reportedly poured half a billion dollars into supporting Republicans in the midterms, also saw many of his candidates lose. Indeed, LTF also backed some candidates it believed were likely to win, only to see them lose to the Dems. For LTF, though, the general election wasn’t the main focus. The group told TechCrunch ahead of Election Day that it thinks primaries (the contests that choose each party’s nominee) are a more effective use of its money, because spending there can build name recognition and help candidates set up AI policy agendas. LTF spent $27.38 million in the primaries, including $8 million alone on opposing New York Assembly member Alex Bores, who lost his bid for Congress back in June. When deciding whether it’s worth jumping into a general election race, LTF assesses how competitive the race is, whether it thinks spending could make a difference, and whether it should keep its powder dry for future elections. Charlie Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, had a different theory for why LTF spent comparatively little in the general election. “They don’t want their money to become an issue in these elections,” he said. He pointed to the Michigan Senate primary election, in which a pro-Israel lobbying group called AIPAC spent close to $30 million backing Democratic candidate Haley Stevens against Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens conceded the primary to El-Sayed, who went on to win the Senate seat. “AIPAC became the story in that race,” Blaettler said. “We know people hate AI billionaires. They hate the people running these companies. They’re very distrustful and disgusted by the political spending and lobbying that the tech industry does. If they spend in a competitive race, they would just become an enormous liability for their candidates.” The main fight among AI-related PACs, whether they are pro-industry or pro-regulation, is whether Congress should establish a national AI framework that overrides state laws, or whether states will maintain their own ability to impose safeguards. Neither side seems poised to back down. LTF, which favors a single national AI framework, told TechCrunch it plans to keep spending in the 2028 elections, while Guardrails Alliance says it wants to keep opposing candidates backed by the AI industry. Blaettler said that while LTF’s ads rarely touch on AI, instead focusing on popular issues for each candidate, Guardrail Alliance’s ads are specifically about who is taking money from the AI industry. “Our goal is to make AI money politically toxic,” Blaettler said. articles.title: El-Sayed tells AP Michigan rejected ‘hateful, spiteful campaign’ after months of Republican attacks
articles.description: El-Sayed tells AP Michigan rejected ‘hateful, spiteful campaign’ after months of Republican attacks AP News Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate Win Is Big to Muslim Americans, but Not Because of Faith The New York Times El-Sayed: Michigan rejected ‘hateful, spiteful campaign’ The Hill El-Sayed’s first step to ‘transform’ politics: Erasing money’s influence The Washington Post El-Sayed Calls Out JD Vance in Victory Speech WSJ
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed told The Associated Press on Wednesday that Michigan voters had rejected “a hateful, spiteful campaign” after months of Republican attacks on his Muslim identity in one of the nation’s most closely watched Senate races. El-Sayed said he was “running on adrenaline and caffeine” after his race with Republican Mike Rogers was called early Wednesday, giving Democrats another significant victory in a premier swing state as they won a substantial majority in the Senate in Tuesday’s midterms. Throughout the cycle, Republicans sought to demonize El-Sayed, who was born in the U.S. after his parents immigrated from Egypt. President Donald Trump repeatedly called him a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists.” “Michigan proved just how big we are. Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face,” El-Sayed said. “Michiganders rejected that. Every single county, every single one, pushed against that.” In an AP interview, Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed says while becoming the nation’s first Muslim senator is something his young daughters will read about in history books, that wasn’t his main objective. In a sign of how combative the race had become, Rogers and El-Sayed had not spoken as of Wednesday afternoon, even after Rogers issued a statement conceding the race. In 2024, Rogers called then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin to concede on Wednesday morning, before the AP had even called the race. El-Sayed, who will become the nation’s first Muslim senator, told the AP by phone that the morning was “a moment of reflection,” including about what his victory would mean to his two young daughters. His 3-year-old, he said, has no idea what happened, while his 8-year-old understands but sees it as normal. “Now, this is something they read about in the history books,” he said. With approximately 97% of the vote in, El-Sayed held a 7 percentage point lead over Rogers. Every county in the state shifted toward Democrats compared with 2024, according to AP voting data. U.S. Senate vote margin compared to 2024 presidential vote margin The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of more than 4,500 voters in Michigan, showed that Michigan Senate voters were roughly split on whether El-Sayed’s views were “too extreme,” with about half saying they were. El-Sayed rose from a double-digit defeat eight years ago in the state’s Democratic gubernatorial election to an upset victory of an establishment-backed candidate in the primary after being outspent by tens of millions. He said his campaign proved that “old-fashioned politics can work if you’re willing to do the work.” El-Sayed quickly pivoted, though, toward the future, saying his victory is “not the success” and that “the success is what you’re able to do with the seat.” He would not commit to supporting Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer for another term, saying he did not yet know who else might run. Schumer is expected to retain the leadership position. “I do believe we need new leadership and I think people are hungry for it,” El-Sayed added. Associated Press reporter Linley Sanders contributed.
