articles.title: Detroit, meet your new representatives in Lansing and Washington D.C.
articles.description: Detroiters on Tuesday overwhelmingly elected Democrats to represent them at the national and state levels. Here's what you need to know:
articles.content: Detroiters on Tuesday overwhelmingly elected Democrats to represent them at the national and state levels. Here’s what you need to know: District 13 U.S. Rep. Donavan McKinney (D) With the election of lifelong Detroiter Donavan McKinney, Detroit residents now have Black representation in the U.S. House for the first time since 2023. According to the City of Detroit’s unofficial election results, McKinney beat out Republican candidate T.P. Nykoriak with 113,713 votes, or about 92% of the vote. He will assume the office — which is currently occupied by Shri Thanedar, who McKinney beat in the primary — on Jan. 3, 2027. The 34-year-old University of Michigan alumnus has been serving in Michigan’s 11th House District since 2025. His term ends on Jan. 1, 2027. McKinney is a democratic socialist candidate who ran on progressive priorities like affordable and guaranteed housing, criminal justice reform, reproductive freedom, getting “big money out of politics,” and more. As the District 13 Rep, McKinney will be serving the second-poorest congressional district in the country, according to US census data. That data estimates District 13’s poverty rate to be over 27%. McKinney was raised in poverty on the northeast side of Detroit by his mother and grandmother. According to his campaign website, McKinney is husband to wife, Shaunté, and a father of two. McKinney has already been receiving praise for his win by groups like progressive nonprofit Indivisible Guide and labor union UAW International Union on social media. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel released a statement Tuesday congratulating McKinney, saying his leadership will be “key” to following through on priorities like “wealthy pay their fair share, expanding access to healthcare and housing, and making sure every Michigander has a fair shot, no matter their zip code.” “As a labor organizer and state representative, Donavan has the values and experience we need to fight and deliver for Detroiters in the halls of Congress,” the statement reads. BridgeDetroit could not reach McKinney for comment Wednesday afternoon. District 12 U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D) Detroiter Rashida Tlaib has secured her reelection and will return to Washington D.C. for her fifth term serving Michigan’s 12th congressional district in the U.S. House of Representatives in 2027. Voters cast 77,084 ballots for the incumbent, giving her a landslide victory over Republican candidate James D. Hooper with nearly 93% of the vote. The Wayne State alumna and fellow democratic socialist has been serving as in the U.S House of Representatives since 2018. Tlaib has consistently aligned herself with other progressive congresswomen, as well as championed progressive issues and legislation like the Unhoused Persons Bill of Rights and banning federal funding for surveillance tech. She currently serves on committees and caucuses for justice and accountability issues, like the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, as well as the Get the Lead Out Caucus. Tlaib is an attorney and has previously served at the state level, becoming the first Muslim woman state legislator in 2008. Who’s showing up for Detroiters in Lansing Four new state senators will begin representing Detroiters in Lansing come Jan. 2027. After winning his first campaign for office, attorney and organizer Justin Onwenu will represent District 1 after winning 93.42% of the vote, or 48,577 votes. Appointed by former Mayor Mike Duggan in 2024 as the City of Detroit’s first Director of Small Business Affairs, Onwenu now serves as director of small business affairs under Mayor Mary Sheffield. He released a statement across social media Wednesday celebrating his win, thanking his opposition and reaffirming his commitment to Detroit and Downriver. “Across backgrounds, Michiganders are united in our desire for a state government laser-focused on lowering the cost of living, investing in our neighborhoods, protecting our rights from attacks by the Trump administration, and delivering the most ethical and effective state government in the country,” the multi-part statement read. “I will fight every day to make Michigan’s government work as hard and be as good as our people. We can do it and we’ll do it together.” District 2 will be represented by Uncommitted movement co-founder Abbas Alawieh, who won 86.62% of the vote with 3,061 votes. According to reporting from WDET, Alawieh’s voting group “mobilized more than 100,000 Michigan voters in the 2024 Democratic primary.” He has been a staff member in multiple political offices. Alawieh’s campaign profile acknowledged his win in a short post on social media last Tuesday night, thanking Senate District 2. “This win and this seat are yours,” part of the the post’s text portion read. “It will be my honor to serve you, your loved ones, and all our neighbors as your State Senator.” Author and consultant John Conyers III — son of Detroit civil rights icon and longest-serving Black congressman, John Conyers Jr. — will be representing District 3. Voters cast 68,097 ballots, or 93.07% of the vote, for Conyers. Conyers’ campaign and personal/professional account shared a post announcing his win on Wednesday. “The real work starts NOW,” part of the written portion of the post reads. “Let’s maintain this momentum and continue to come together to make our cities and state better.” Incumbent Mary Cavanagh will continue representing District 6, having secured her second-term win with over 96% of the vote, or 73,771 votes. Cavanagh — who is the daughter of former state politician Phil Cavanagh and granddaughter of former Detroit mayor Jerome Cavanagh — assumed office in 2023. Before her state Senate tenure, Cavanagh was elected to represent Michigan’s 10th district in the state House of Representatives in 2020. Detroiters have also voted to send 12 Democrats to the state House of Representatives. Longtime politician and incumbent Tyrone Carter will be representing Michigan’s 1st District, having won with 91.26% of the vote, or 14,528 votes. He has been serving in the Michigan House of Representatives since assuming office in 2019. Carter is the husband of District 6 Detroit police commissioner Lisa Carter. Carter acknowledged his win and thanked his supporters during a short Facebook live on Wednesday afternoon. “Thank you all to the people in District 1 for supporting me and sending me back for a fifth term,” he said. Incumbent Alabas Farhat kept his seat representing Michigan’s 3rd Dstrict with 88.95% of the vote, or 2,350 votes. Farhat assumed office in 2023, andwas reelected in 2024. Farhat was removed as Minority Vice Chair on the House Appropriations Committee by the Republican speaker. He also came under fire for supporting a Republican-backed anti-transgender bill last September. Former educator Regina Ross will be representing Michigan’s 4th District, having won 95.79% of the vote, or 27,130 votes. Michigan’s 5th District will be represented by Candace Calloway, who won with 96.77% of the vote, or 23,503 votes. A Detroit construction worker, AmeriCorp alumni and DPSCD academic interventionist, Calloway is also the daughter of District 2 City Councilmember Angela Whitfield-Calloway. Incumbent Tonya Myers Phillips secured a second term in the 7th District seat with 95.51% of the vote, or 15,842 votes. Environmental justice advocate and Democratic socialist candidate Chris Gilmer-Hill won the 8th District seat 94.53% of the vote, or 22,792 votes. Former Detroit police commissioner Willie Burton won the 9th District with 91.77% of the vote, or 28,785 votes. Incumbent Veronica Paiz will continue representing the 10th District, having won with 91.81% of the vote, or 10,568 votes. Paiz was previously elected as the 11th district representative in 2022 and served on the Harper Woods City council before that since 2015. Detroiter Kimberly Fisher will be representing the 11th District after winning 95.72% of the vote, or 15,173 votes. As of Wednesday evening, a pop-up on her website has acknowledged her win, thanking District 11 and saying the victory “belongs to every neighbor who believed.” Incumbent Kimberly L. Edwards secured another term serving in the 12th District with 96.16% of the vote, or 6,609 votes. Edwards has been in office since 2023. District 16 incumbent Stephanie A. Young will return to Lansing, having secured her seat with 95.76% of the vote, or 14,806 votes. Young previously served as a representative for the 8th District from 2021 to 2023, before assuming the 16th District office. A post on her professional Facebook page acknowledged her win and thanked voters and election officials Wednesday afternoon. “You’ve given us our marching orders and we’re ready to rise to the challenge as unified leaders to make Michigan brighter for you and your family,” part of the written portion of the post read. 17th District incumbent Laurie Pohutsky secured her fifth term in the state House of Representatives with 94.19% of the vote, or 10,983 votes. Pohutsky was appointed speaker pro tempore of the Michigan House and served in that position from 2023 to 2025. She was elected as the 19th District representative in 2018 and stayed in that seat before being elected to serve the 17th District in 2022. Pohustky’s personal/professional Facebook page acknowledged her win and thanked voters on Wednesday. “From the bottom of my heart, I’d like to thank the people of District 17 for once again giving me the opportunity to be their voice in Lansing,” the written portion of the post read. “It’s an honor to serve you and I’m so grateful for your support.”

articles.title: Voters reject most big tax overhauls, with a few notable exceptions
articles.description: Despite the blue wave that swept the nation on Tuesday, voters were more cautious about making sweeping changes to their taxes. Most states with tax policy on the ballot saw voters reject large-scale change, though some passed smaller changes or reined in officials’ ability to make changes. “Even though there are big political shifts on […]
articles.content: Voters fill out ballots for the midterm election at the Millwood Field House on Tuesday in Oklahoma City. Oklahoma voters rejected measure that would have capped annual increases in property taxes, one of a number of tax-related measures that were on the ballot in multiple states. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)Despite the blue wave that swept the nation on Tuesday, voters were more cautious about making sweeping changes to their taxes. Most states with tax policy on the ballot saw voters reject large-scale change, though some passed smaller changes or reined in officials’ ability to make changes. “Even though there are big political shifts on the federal level, people are generally feeling the same about taxes as they always have,” said Janelle Fritts, senior policy analyst at the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan analysis and research organization. One of the biggest examples: California’s much-discussed billionaire wealth tax looked likely to fail, with a ‘no’ vote of more than 55% by Wednesday morning. Proposition 40 is a measure no other state has tried: a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth to raise tens of billions to close budget holes in the state’s Medicaid, food assistance, education and other programs. Opposition, led by California billionaires including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, raised more than $379 million to defeat the measure, outspending its supporters more than 250-1, The Washington Post reported. But the campaign spending alone may not have fully accounted for its failure, Fritts said. “The specific proposal had a lot of really strange structural issues,” she said, noting that it would have retroactively applied to any California resident who was a billionaire as of Jan. 1, 2026, and that it taxed everything a billionaire owned — from cars and yachts to art and collectibles — some of which could be difficult to place a value on. “When people started understanding what was really in the bill, I think that was a deterrent,” she said. She expects it could influence similar efforts in other states to tax the wealthy. Proponents of California’s billionaire wealth tax have already promised to try again. Washington state voters appeared to be choosing to keep the state’s new millionaire tax, as a ballot initiative to repeal it was failing 58% to 42% by Wednesday morning. Earlier this year, Washington’s Democratic-led state legislature created a 9.9% tax on annual incomes above $1 million. The repeal measure, which failed to garner support in the state’s population centers, was a political victory for its champion, Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson, according to the Washington State Standard. “Washingtonians understood one thing,” Ferguson told a gathering hosted by a campaign opposing the measure, the Washington State Standard reported. “We’re not going to give tax breaks to millionaires when we can use those dollars to make life more affordable for working families all across the state.” In Colorado, a sweeping income tax change remained too close to call Wednesday, though ‘yes’ votes had a slight lead. Amendment 87, if it passes, would hike taxes on the state’s highest-income households, and cut taxes for nearly everyone else by replacing the state’s flat 4.4% tax. A ballot measure that would block Amendment 87 appeared short of the majority needed to pass, while a legislatively-referred measure to raise the revenue the state is allowed to keep appeared likely to pass. Property tax wins, losses Voters in Florida showed an appetite for change, overwhelmingly approving a constitutional amendment that will make one of the most significant alterations to their property taxes in decades. Amendment 3 will gradually reduce Floridians’ property taxes — aside from those that benefit public schools — by increasing the state’s homestead exemption. That will let homeowners cut their property tax bills by exempting a bigger share of their home’s value from taxation. The state GOP endorsed the amendment, but other groups — including law enforcement, child welfare advocates and municipal government officials — say it would blow a massive hole in local governments’ budgets. Florida’s state and local coffers could take a hit of up to $12 billion each year beginning in 2031, according to state projections. “It will be a pretty big challenge for local governments,” Fritts said. “They’re going to have to shift a lot of things around. “Not a lot of other states were willing to take as big a swing on property taxes as Florida,” she said. Oklahoma voters rejected a measure that would have capped annual increases in property taxes. The state legislature proposed the initiative to address rising costs, but critics said it would hurt funding for public schools and other services. The state estimated local governments would have lost nearly $46 million in property tax revenue in the first year, had it passed. Oklahoma House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, a Republican, said Tuesday night that the vote showed that Oklahomans “don’t want to see changes to property taxes, and so moving forward, we’ll take that into consideration,” the Oklahoma Voice reported. In Wyoming, voters defeated a property tax cut initiative that would have exempted half of a primary residence’s assessed value from being taxed. Had it passed, Proposition 1 could have decreased the state’s annual property tax revenues up to $124.8 million, WyoFile reported. The initiative was opposed by a variety of groups including state hospital and education associations, as well as some Republican and Democratic officials. Reining in government power In North Carolina, voters approved both tax-related constitutional amendments. The most controversial, which passed with 60% of the vote, will cap how much cities and other local governments can grow their revenue. It was a priority for Republican leadership focused on addressing constituent complaints over rising prices. But critics say the new limits could torpedo local budgets, forcing local governments to cut services including public safety, libraries, parks and education, NC Newsline reported. North Carolinians also approved a new maximum state income tax rate of 3.5% in a Republican-backed constitutional amendment that caps the rate for personal and corporate income taxes. Critics have said it will cement tax cuts that mainly benefit the wealthy and corporations. An Iowa constitutional amendment to make it harder for state legislators to tinker with taxes looked as though it would pass. The GOP-backed measure would require a two-thirds supermajority of state lawmakers to raise personal or corporate income taxes. The Iowa Capital Dispatch reported that Republican supporters argued the restriction was needed to preserve tax policies including 2025’s 3.8% flat-rate income tax. But critics said it would lock in unsustainable tax cuts that mostly benefit Iowa’s wealthier households and could push the state to raise other taxes when it needs revenue, such as sales tax increases that have a bigger impact on low- and middle-income families. In Massachusetts, a ballot measure that would change how the state’s tax revenue limit is calculated was still too close to call as of Wednesday morning. Current state law caps how much tax revenue the state can keep each year, and any extra beyond the cap is refunded to taxpayers as credits. But if voters approve the ballot measure, taxpayers would be more likely to get money back in a given year. Proponents say it would slow down state spending, while opponents have said it leaves less money available for public services. Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org. This story was originally produced by Stateline, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Michigan Advance, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

articles.title: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
articles.description: Researchers say group may have been Kremlin-sponsored in search of diplomatic targets.
articles.content: Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday. The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data. Wielding DarkSword One of the impersonated sites was america250.org, belonging to a non-partisan group of lawmakers, business executives, and at least one former member of the Trump administration. The attackers registered america250[.]holiday and used it as a reverse proxy to america250.org. The imposter website delivered content from the real one that added malicious JavaScript into it.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Lawrence says Democrats must deliver bold change after election victories
articles.description: After declaring victory in a hard-fought battle for Michigan’s most competitive swing district, U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence reconvened with his supporters and members of the media to celebrate his victory and reaffirm his commitment to promises he made along the campaign trail. Standing outside his campaign office in Lansing, Lawrence offered his thanks to family […]
articles.content: Congressman-elect William Lawrence outlines his priorities for serving in the U.S. House while speaking with reporters outside his campaign HQ in Lansing, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)After declaring victory in a hard-fought battle for Michigan’s most competitive swing district, U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence reconvened with his supporters and members of the media to celebrate his victory and reaffirm his commitment to promises he made along the campaign trail. Standing outside his campaign office in Lansing, Lawrence offered his thanks to family members, staff, campaign supporters and U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) who currently represents the district. “I was thankful to get a phone call from him last night and have a conversation with him where he congratulated and conceded the race, and I expressed my readiness to work with him on the transition and I thanked him directly for his service,” Lawrence said. The Associated Press called the race for Lawrence at 2:05 p.m. on Wednesday, with unofficial results showing Lawrence with 51% of the vote and Barrett with 47.7%. The soon-to-be freshman representative reiterated his belief that “Washington’s priorities are all upside down,” and emphasized that there is much to be done over the next decade to deliver economic security, restore law and order, address worsening climate change and bring peace to the global stage. “We’re not going to get it all done over the next few years, but I’m excited to get to work with some very specific priorities,” Lawrence said, pointing to constituent services, ending foreign wars and accountability for big tech as his main concerns. U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Lansing) speaks with reporters the morning after the election, Nov. 4, 2026 (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance) Shortly after speaking with reporters, Lawrence joined members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus’s Political Action Committee on a press call where they laid out their goals for the remaining two years of President Donald Trump’s administration. Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), the caucus chair, said Tuesday’s election delivered big wins for progressives, with the caucus set to grow its ranks by 25 members. He noted that even candidates who did not campaign as progressives campaigned on issues that progressives have championed for decades, including opposition to big money in politics, ending foreign wars, standing up to political corruption and delivering healthcare reforms. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE However, Casar emphasized that Democrats cannot remain idle in the next two years. “Last night was not a sign that all of Democrats’ problems are solved,” Casar said. “The election is not an endorsement of returning to the status quo or tinkering around the edges. This is a message that people in this country are mad as hell, and are giving Democrats a shot to show them we can do something about it. And so it’s our turn to take them up on that opportunity.” Maxwell Frost, the co-chair of the caucus’s political action committee underscored Casar’s point, noting that “especially over the last decade, voters will give you power and take it away just as quickly as they gave it to you.” Heading into the 120th Congress, Casar emphasized that the Congressional Progressive Caucus and its more than 100 members would be a crucial governing partner in Congress, noting that they hold a productive relationship with U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who will likely be elected the next Speaker of the House. Congressman-elect William Lawrence “Leader Jeffries has said this election is a mandate for bold change, and the progressive caucus is ready to be the energy behind delivering these results,” Casar said. In addition to delivering economic security and anticorruption measures, Lawrence said House Democrats will also need to set its foreign policy straight. “People in my district are tired of these endless wars,” Lawrence said. “We’ve seen one war after another. We’re throwing good money after bad – trillions each year – and we are not any safer or more secure or more prosperous than when these forever wars began. People across the political spectrum are ready for a change.” Casar also stressed that Democrats’ newly won majority in Congress is not for one day, or 100 days but 100 weeks. “Every single week, we should now be sending a bill to Donald Trump’s desk that is overwhelmingly popular with the American people, that cracks down on corporate greed, that cracks down on price gouging, that cracks down on big money in politics,” Casar said. “We won such a big victory last night that we’re not going to settle for one progressive bill on the first day.”

articles.title: Uranium cubes reveal why the German nuclear project failed
articles.description: "Our calculations suggest Heisenberg significantly underestimated the materials required."
articles.content: During World War II, physicists on the Manhattan Project worried that the Nazi German nuclear program might achieve the first nuclear bomb before the US and its allies. That's not what transpired, but historians have debated just how close the Germans came to achieving criticality in their last attempt at building a reactor: the B8 pile. Werner Heisenberg, who led that effort, claimed that they were close and had only needed a little more uranium. But according to a paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences Nexus, that was not the case: The project simply didn't have sufficient uranium and heavy water to build a working bomb, given the design they were using. This particular research started in 2013, when University of Maryland physicist Timothy Koeth—a co-author on the new paper—received the gift of a mysterious heavy metal cube from a friend. He instantly recognized it as one of the uranium cubes used by German scientists in their unsuccessful attempt to build a working nuclear reactor. Only 14 such cubes are known to exist today. In 2019, we reported on Koeth’s quest to track down the cube’s origins, as well as several other similar cubes that had somehow found their way across the Atlantic. At the time, Koeth and his partner in the quest, then-graduate student Miriam “Mimi” Hiebert, had tracked down 10 such cubes around the US. For instance, the Smithsonian Institute had a German uranium cube in storage. They tracked a third cube to Harvard University, where it was regularly passed around to students in introductory physics classes as a curiosity.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Bridge Listens Issues Watch recap: Behind the Democrat rout in Michigan
articles.description: Bridge Capitol and data reporters discussed Tuesday’s midterm election, which saw Democrats sweep the ticket and regain control of the congressional delegation and state Legislature.
articles.content: Bridge Michigan’s virtual discussions continued Wednesday with a deep dive into the results of Tuesday’s midterm election Reporters analyzed candidates’ paths to victory, which issues drove voters’ decisions and what comes next Catch a replay of the conversation below The blue wave that hit the United States this week swept through Michigan as well, allowing Democrats to keep control of the state’s highest offices, regain control of the Legislature and congressional delegation. So, what happened and why? And where does Michigan go from here? Capitol reporters Lauren Gibbons, Simon D. Schuster and Jordyn Hermani and data and accountability reporter Matt Mencarini analyzed the results of the election and took reader questions in a special virtual event Wednesday moderated by Bridge Michigan Executive Editor for Impact Joel Kurth. The hour-long discussion touched on candidates’ paths to victory, the issues foremost on voters’ minds, the role President Donald Trump’s policies played in the outcome and a lot more. Missed the discussion? Watch here: The discussion was part of Bridge Listens, our yearlong effort to listen to readers’ top concerns during the 2026 campaign season. Related: How Abdul El-Sayed, Jocelyn Benson won Michigan: Big turnout, Democratic shifts Democrats take full control of Legislature, Michigan government. What to expect Michigan Dems flip three US House seats as Huizenga, Barrett fall Michigan election results: Governor, Senate, US House, proposals, more All year, Bridge hosted virtual discussions about what matters to readers, culminating in last month’s Bridge Issues Summit at Marygrove Conservancy in Detroit. Other virtual discussions have focused on the state of democracy,, the economy, the environment, healthcare and K-12 schools. articles.content: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed will be the first Muslim to sit in the U.S. Senate. Getting there meant a campaign in which his faith was the argument against him — from his opponent, from members of Congress and from a president on a stage. Independent journalist Ali Harb spent the race in Michigan. He tells host Robyn Vincent what that kind of politics leaves behind after the counting stops. Make America Great Again, or MAGA, hats are pictured during an election night event for Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Detroit. Michigan just elected Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to be its next U.S. senator, defeating Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed is the first Muslim elected to the office. In his victory speech, he returned to a theme he ran on. “I love America,” El-Sayed said. “But I love America enough to ask her to be America for all her kids. See, America is not just a flag, not just our red, white and blue. It’s not just the patriotic songs that we sing or a landmass we call home. America is about these truths that we hold. That all people are created equal and the inalienable rights we still struggle to guarantee.” On Oct. 25 in Port Huron, the president of the United States stood on a stage and warned the crowd about him. “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator. And that’s a fact. Not gonna let that happen,” President Donald Trump said. Trump said El-Sayed would be the only senator who would have to walk through a metal detector before he was allowed into the Senate. He said a Democratic win would “invite hordes of jihadists to our shores.” PolitiFact rated the Muslim Brotherhood claim “Pants on Fire.” That was the closing argument. El-Sayed won anyway. Those attacks landed in a country where views of Islam have hardened sharply since 2002. In January, 51% of U.S. adults told Pew Research Center that Islam encourages violence more than other religions do. In March 2002, 25% said so. Ali Harb is an independent journalist based in Washington, D.C. He covers American foreign policy, elections and Arab American communities, and he spent this campaign in Michigan. He joined host Robyn Vincent to discuss the anti-Muslim rhetoric that ran through Michigan’s U.S. Senate race and what it leaves behind. Hear the full conversation using the media player above. articles.title: In blue wave, Democrats flipped legislatures, won trifectas and toppled GOP supermajorities
articles.description: Democrats seized more power over state governments than the party has had in years after the party swept races up and down the ballot in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Republicans have held a majority of state legislatures and governorships since 2010. But that reign appears over as Democrats swept a majority of governorships and state legislative […]
articles.content: Indiana state Reps. Ed DeLaney, Cherrish Pryor, Phil GiaQuinta, Carey Hamilton, Vanessa Summers and Greg Porter declare that Indiana Democrats broke the House GOP’s supermajority on Tuesday night. Democrats flipped several legislative chambers and broke Republican supermajorities across the country. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Democrats seized more power over state governments than the party has had in years after the party swept races up and down the ballot in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Republicans have held a majority of state legislatures and governorships since 2010. But that reign appears over as Democrats swept a majority of governorships and state legislative chambers. Tracking from the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee on Wednesday showed the party had flipped 12 chambers so far, winning the most chambers since 2008 and putting Democrats in control of more than half the nation’s state legislative chambers. “With this sweep, Democrats have achieved their best performance since the Watergate scandal,” the committee, which works to elect Democrats at the state level, said in a news release Wednesday. Unofficial results show Democrats will control the Arizona legislature for the first time in 60 years. Building off a historic sweep of statewide races, Democrats are poised to take control of the Texas House for the first time in over 20 years. In North Carolina, Democrats flipped several House seats held by influential, veteran Republicans to give the party control of the lower chamber for the first time since 2010. “We have the power to make this state better,” state Rep. Robert Reives, who was introduced as the next House speaker, said Tuesday night. Many legislative races had yet to be called by midday Wednesday. But the National Conference of State Legislatures said current results showed Democrats would secure new trifectas – control of both chambers and the governor’s office – in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Democrats also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas. Additionally, Democratic wins crushed GOP supermajorities in several states. In Florida, the loss of the Republican supermajority takes away the party’s power to override rules regarding procedure and debate and override the governor’s veto. Democratic gains also ended supermajorities in the Indiana state House, the Kansas House, both of Missouri’s legislative chambers, the Ohio House, and the South Carolina House. In a statement on Wednesday, the Republican State Leadership Committee, which works to elect Republicans at the state level, cited an “historically difficult political environment” facing the party. “Democrats made state legislative races a national priority, pouring unprecedented resources into these contests because they understand the power state legislatures hold in shaping policy and building the pipeline for the next generation of leaders,” President Edith Jorge-Tuñón said in the statement. “In many key battleground states, the national political environment and the impact of top-of-the-ticket races significantly affected our candidates’ ability to defy historical trends.” Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org. articles.title: Stateside: Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026
articles.description: Last night, Democrats across the nation swept midterm elections and regained control of the U.S. House and Senate. In Michigan, voters chose U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in a historic victory, Democrats swept all the statewide races, and regained control of both branches of the state Legislature. Today on the show, we look at some topline takeaways from the results.

articles.title: Mamdani reacts to blue wave election results across the country
articles.content: NEW YORK (WABC) -- New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday called the election "a referendum on politics at large across this country." Mamdani said too many politicians have been telling working people that their needs are unrealistic while doing whatever the wealthiest people in the country ask of them. "Our job is not to better manage a decline. It is to inspire our country to heights we've never been to before, where the working people who built this country are at the center of our politics," he said. "The fact that states like South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa are even in question speaks to the fact that this entire country is ready for a politics that means something in people's lives," Mamdani said. "The American people want change they can feel in their wallets." Mamdani also praised the victory of Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who will become the first Muslim elected to serve in the U.S. Senate. "To see that victory after everything he had to reckon with during the campaign, whether it was the extraordinary amount of money spent to oppose him or the racism and slander he faced on a daily basis, is incredibly exciting," he said. "As he said last night, the good guys won." National leadership could feature several prominent New Yorkers in the coming term. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries would become the first Black speaker of the House if elected by his colleagues, while Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer is poised to serve as majority leader. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, remains in the White House. "Having leaders in Washington who are from our city and of our city is incredibly important because the struggles of New Yorkers are not intellectual concerns to them. They're challenges they hear about from constituents every single day," Mamdani said. When asked how the election results would benefit New Yorkers facing economic challenges, Mamdani said Democratic control of Congress could shift the focus from protecting existing benefits to advancing affordability measures. "It means that we can go from being on the defensive to the offensive. The defensive means trying to prevent as many New Yorkers as possible from losing their SNAP benefits or losing their health insurance. That's a reflection of policies that republicans have refused for the last few years. The offensive is delivering to make life more affordable for them," Mamdani said. Despite significant policy differences with Trump, Mamdani said there are still opportunities to work together. "One of those very limited areas of agreement is the welfare of the city as a whole," he said. The mayor also noted that six members of the Democratic Socialists of America were elected to the House of Representatives, including two from New York City. He said he had called both members-elect to congratulate them. ----------* Get Eyewitness News Delivered * Download our connected TV app * More local news* Send us a news tip* Download the abc7NY app for breaking news alerts on the go

articles.title: Voters back tougher crime penalties, reject marijuana rollbacks
articles.description: Millions of voters in 11 states approved tougher criminal penalties and more bail restrictions in Tuesday’s midterm elections, while rejecting efforts to roll back marijuana legalization and expand cooperation with federal immigration authorities. The results reflected a mixed approach to criminal justice policy, with voters supporting harsher penalties for certain drug and human trafficking offenses […]
articles.content: Sheriff’s deputies walk past voting booths at San Francisco City Hall on Nov. 3, 2026. Voters across 11 states weighed in on criminal justice and drug policies Tuesday, approving tougher bail restrictions and criminal penalties while rejecting efforts to roll back marijuana legalization. (Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images)Millions of voters in 11 states approved tougher criminal penalties and more bail restrictions in Tuesday’s midterm elections, while rejecting efforts to roll back marijuana legalization and expand cooperation with federal immigration authorities. The results reflected a mixed approach to criminal justice policy, with voters supporting harsher penalties for certain drug and human trafficking offenses and greater authority for judges to deny bail, even as they resisted other changes to state laws. The measures were among 15 criminal justice and drug policy proposals on ballots in nine states, covering issues ranging from pretrial detention and crime victims’ rights to immigration enforcement and traffic cameras. Voters expand bail restrictions Voters in Indiana, Louisiana and Tennessee approved constitutional amendments expanding restrictions on bail. In Indiana, 59% of voters supported a measure allowing judges to deny bail when evidence of guilt is strong and a defendant poses a substantial risk to another person or the community. Louisiana voters approved a measure prohibiting post-conviction bail, which is sometimes referred to as an appeal bond, for people convicted of aggravated offenses against minors. Post-conviction bail allows a person who has been found guilty of a crime to remain free or be released from custody while they wait to be formally sentenced or while they appeal their conviction. In Tennessee, voters expanded the list of offenses for which judges can deny bail, including charges of terrorism, second-degree murder and aggravated rape of a child. Tennessee voters also approved a constitutional amendment expanding crime victims’ rights, including the right to receive notice of criminal proceedings, to attend hearings and to be heard during decisions involving defendants’ release, sentencing and parole. Those outcomes continue a recent trend of voters supporting greater restrictions on pretrial release. In May, Alabama voters approved a similar constitutional amendment allowing judges to deny bail for defendants charged with certain violent offenses. Tougher penalties gain support Colorado voters approved two measures increasing criminal penalties for fentanyl offenses and child sex trafficking. Proposition 132 increases penalties for certain fentanyl offenses, requires court-ordered treatment for some possession convictions and changes how drug possession is considered under the state’s habitual criminal law. Proposition 133 requires life imprisonment without parole or release for people convicted of human trafficking of a child for sexual servitude. But Colorado voters rejected Amendment 81, which would have required state and local law enforcement to notify federal immigration authorities after charging certain people who are unlawfully present in the country or whose immigration status could not be determined. In Arizona, voters supported measures designating drug cartels as terrorist organizations under state law and restricting the use of photo traffic enforcement systems, such as stop sign and speed cameras. Missouri voters narrowly approved a constitutional amendment establishing elected county sheriffs as the chief law enforcement officers in most counties and limiting the circumstances under which they can be removed from office. Voting rights and pardons In Virginia, 55% of voters approved a constitutional amendment automatically restoring voting rights to people with felony convictions after they complete their sentences, replacing a system that required a gubernatorial pardon or a successful petition for restoration. Kentuckians overwhelmingly approved a constitutional amendment that will prohibit the governor from issuing pardons or commuting sentences during a period beginning 60 days before a gubernatorial election until five weeks after it. Marijuana rollback efforts fail While voters supported tougher criminal penalties, proposals affecting marijuana legalization were defeated. In Massachusetts, voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have repealed much of the state’s law allowing licensed recreational marijuana sales. The outcome preserves a legal market approved by voters in 2016. The proposal would have eliminated licensed recreational sales while continuing to allow adults to possess limited amounts of marijuana. In Idaho, voters rejected a constitutional amendment that would have given state lawmakers exclusive authority to legalize marijuana, narcotics and other psychoactive substances. The measure would not itself have legalized or prohibited marijuana. Instead, it would have prevented citizens from using the state’s ballot initiative process to legalize those substances. Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org. articles.title: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters
articles.description: AMD's gaming revenue fell 40 percent in an otherwise record $13.4 billion quarter.
articles.content: AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company's gaming segment cratered. AMD CFO Jean Hu said, "We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. The middle point of our guidance represents approximately 66% year-over-year revenue growth, primarily driven by the acceleration of our Data Center segment." AMD says its Q4 revenue projections are up another 27 percent from this quarter's results. As reported by Tom's Hardware, Intel's Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion. That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel's revenue for the first time in history. The data center segment of AMD's business was up 97 percent year over year, with a record $8.5 billion. AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs. Sales of AMD Ryzen mobile chips led growth in the Client business, which includes desktop Ryzen processors and posted $2.95 billion in revenue, up 7 percent year over year.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Jocelyn Benson says Democrats have ‘mandate.’ How she plans to lead Michigan
articles.description: Jocelyn Benson and Democrats will have full control of all branches of government starting Jan. 1. Expect her to try to score early victories and face economic realities.
articles.content: After a commanding victory, Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson called the results a ‘mandate’ to follow through on lowering costs, improving the state Benson will enjoy Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, though observers warn a friendly Legislature doesn’t equate to rubber stamps Tops on Benson’s list: Transparency, lowering bills, improving schools Following a wave election that will bring them control of state government in 2027, Democrats now have to meet the realities of government and the execution of an ambitious policy agenda laid out on the campaign trail. On Wednesday, Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson called the election “a clear mandate to work for (Michiganders), to lower costs, to grow our economy, to improve our public schools, and get things done.” She should have the backing to enact her agenda, after Democrats flipped 11 seats in the state House and three in the Senate to achieve broader majorities than what Democrats clinched in 2023 and 2024. They will control the House 63-47 and Senate 23-15 at the start of the new legislative session in 2027. But political observers cautioned winners not to misread the results of an election that many see as a rebuke of Republican President Donald Trump. Related: Now, the hard part: Jocelyn Benson has big plans. Michigan has big problems How Abdul El-Sayed, Jocelyn Benson won Michigan: Big turnout, Democratic shifts Democrats take full control of Legislature, Michigan government. What to expect Benson and others shouldn’t think voters “have fallen back in love with Democrats,” said Brandon Dillon, a lobbyist and former chair of the Michigan Democratic Party. Even so, voters “certainly sent a message” they need a break from Trump’s agenda and relief from rising costs, Dillon said. Democrats will also face realities that could limit their ambitions — in particular policy changes from the One Big Beautiful Bill that could leave lawmakers with a substantial budget deficit in the new year. “To the extent that the policy agenda depends on money, the fiscal picture is not real bright right now,” said Bob Schneider, research associate at the nonpartisan Citizens Research Council. Donate ‘Quick relief’ on costs of living As she prepares to succeed term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer on Jan. 1, Benson said she’s working to identify “where we can deliver quick relief in the early days of our new term, beginning with the bills families feel every month.” “Voters in Michigan spoke loud and clear — they want leaders who will work together to lower their costs and grow our economy,” she said. “I know that the costs hitting people’s pocketbooks hurt monthly. We cannot wait to get things done.” Benson was light on specifics, but she suggested part of that strategy could involve working Trump on tariff solutions or aggressively recruiting employers with well-paying job opportunities for Michigan residents. At a debate less than a month ago, Benson was adamant: “I will call Canada and negotiate a contract between Michigan and Canada to eliminate the tariffs and the costs in Michigan.” After the election, Benson was more measured, offering to work with Trump. “If we can work together to protect the people of Michigan from the harm that these tariffs have caused, I would love to and I’m open to that,” Benson said. Options are limited for state leaders facing economic headwinds, as many of the causes are systemic or decided at the federal level. And the state’s financial situation remains an open question. Changes to payments for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Medicaid could represent “either a mildly tough challenge or or maybe a really tough challenge,” said Schneider, the policy analyst. Revenue estimates officials will finalize in January could mean “we’re $700 million in the hole before we even start thinking about new stuff” or perhaps the state’s budget remains balanced after a recent surge in revenue brought on in part by tariff refunds, Schneider said. Winnie Brinks, Benson’s running mate and current Senate Majority Leader, demurred when asked Wednesday about what she believes Democrats can achieve. “The world changed a lot yesterday, so that may have an impact on what is possible,” said Brinks, who will become president of the Senate as lieutenant governor. “So I’m not going to get ahead of myself on that.” Gas tax future, new revenue options? Michigan has the sixth-highest gas tax in the nation, at 52.4 cents a gallon, and officeholders nationwide have mentioned they may consider a tax holiday as gas remains well over $4 a gallon. During the campaign, Benson initially had concerns about a state gas tax holiday, though she said during an October debate that she was open to the idea. On Wednesday, Benson said reducing gas taxes remains an option in the short term. But she said the state should overhaul how road repairs are funded. “We need to think about how to restructure our budget process so that we are identifying new sources of revenue that can help pay our bills in the state, but also streamlining how things are spent so that we’re reducing costs as well,” she said. According to the Department of Treasury, 98% of all funds generated at the pump now go back to state and local road agencies for construction, maintenance and upkeep. Commitment to transparency Michigan has long been considered one of the worst states in the nation for government transparency. As of Tuesday, Michigan is projected to be the only state that fully exempts the governor’s office and Legislature from public records laws. Massachusetts voters approved a ballot question this week expanding the state’s public records law to include those officeholders. The Freedom of Information Act applies to state departments, schools and local government agencies across Michigan, but critics argue the process is riddled with loopholes and often results in high costs and long delays. On Wednesday, Benson reiterated her promise to voluntarily make the governor’s office open to FOIA “on Day 1.” “We’ve got plenty of examples in other states to craft our policies by, and we’ll release those specific policies in the weeks ahead,” she said. “But they will begin with my administration on Jan. 1.” Managing a trifecta Benson may have the backing of Democrats in the Legislature, but observers say that doesn’t guarantee smooth sailing. Democrats’ broad gains — the largest shift in power in the state House since 1964 — also means the caucus will have a broader coalition, with both moderates and Democratic socialists among the new members. That can cause friction with other members who have their own policy priorities. Dillion, the former Democratic Party chair, predicted “this Legislature is going to be a little bit more assertive, I would think, and not necessarily give as much deference to the governor.” “In order to get things done here, you’re going to have to have strong relationships, personal relationships with the leadership in the legislature and other members,” Dillon added. “It’ll be a give and take.” Benson said voters “want leaders who will work together.” Tom Leonard, a former Republican House speaker who ran for governor this year, predicted Benson “is going to want to be very hands on” and more involved in policymaking than Whitmer has been in the final two years of her term. A broad majority can actually offer additional difficulties, Leonard explained, as members may feel more freedom to diverge on their priorities or hold out for an ask in exchange for their support. “It’s the most rewarding part of the job, but it can also be the most taxing,” Leonard said, who considers Benson a friend.

articles.title: Democratic newcomer upsets incumbent Republican for state House seat
OpenAI is already trying to shape the 2028 election
articles.description: OpenAI’s Chris Lehane wants AI to define the 2028 election, proposing a new social contract that could benefit Americans while also advancing the AI giant’s own business interests.
articles.content: OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane thinks the 2028 presidential election could be a defining moment for AI. And he wants politicians to start developing policies that address Americans’ concerns about the technology, rather than simply paying lip service to anti-AI sentiment and the backlash against data centers. In a new essay, Lehane compares AI’s potential to reshape the economy to President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, the 1930s set of federal programs and reforms enacted after industrialization and the Great Depression shattered the old economic order. He observes that Americans today feel similarly anxious about losing control over their economic futures and urges politicians to find a “compelling third path” that allows people to share in AI’s benefits. He lays out five policy priorities, spanning worker protections and education to AI safety and data center development. The essay comes on the heels of a stunning Democratic victory in the midterm elections, in which Democrats flipped control of Congress amid widespread voter frustration over the cost of living. Kate Brennan, who leads AI and corporate power policy at the AI Now Institute, told TechCrunch that Lehane’s rhetoric marks a notable shift from OpenAI’s policy agenda last year, which focused on accelerating AI development, reducing regulatory barriers, and expanding infrastructure. Unsurprisingly, many of Lehane’s proposals would encourage wider AI adoption and support the infrastructure expansion companies like OpenAI need to grow. The original New Deal established protections for workers and placed constraints on corporate power. It’s less clear how Lehane’s vision would hold AI companies accountable for the economic disruption their technology could create. “Invoking a New Deal metaphor is to invoke state capacity to actually benefit the public,” Brennan said. “This is written by a private company that is trying to advocate for policies for its own benefit. It is ahistorical at best and harmful at worst.” While AI wasn’t a dominant issue in the midterms, opposition to data centers emerged as a major bipartisan concern in several races in the midterms. And Lehane may be right that AI will become a bigger part of the conversation over the next two years. Affordability is already shaping up as a key issue for the 2028 election as Americans grapple with inflation, tariffs, and the rising cost of living. AI could become an increasingly large part of that conversation as voters stress about data centers hiking up electricity bills, AI replacing their jobs, and technology’s economic gains flowing only to a handful of wealthy companies. Lehane acknowledges many of these concerns, but he offers few concrete proposals to prevent AI’s gains from becoming concentrated. Instead, he largely pitches AI as a path to greater prosperity for Americans willing to embrace it. Take his proposals for the tax code. He suggests incentives for workers to learn AI skills, easier capital access for entrepreneurs, and new approaches to employee ownership and profit-sharing. Those are not the same as binding requirements that would ensure workers share in AI-generated wealth or that companies pay the costs of displacing workers. “I was struck by how much of this policy is for a future…that is already predicated on mass AI adoption and AI benefiting society, which we have yet to see,” Brennan said. “All of it is predicated on benefiting from AI’s upside.” Brennan said it would make more sense to see things like a revised corporate tax rate or tax incentives for hiring human beings rather than automating jobs, as well as ways to keep companies from amassing outsize market power. Lehane’s emphasis on expanding AI’s economic opportunities, rather than limiting potential harms, extends to data centers. He notes concerns about data centers while emphasizing the construction jobs and local tax revenue they could generate. He then warns that politicians who support a data center moratorium could jeopardize America’s lead over China, going so far as to compare that stance to the 2002 vote to authorize the Iraq war. Lehane also makes child safety and education central to his proposed agenda, stressing the importance of age-appropriate protections and safeguards around AI companions for minors. He also warns against keeping AI out of classrooms, arguing that doing so could lead to inequality between wealthy students and “children in rural communities.” But the argument takes for granted that AI improves learning, a claim that remains unproven and one critics say deserves more examination than more funding or individualized attention from human teachers. Lehane also calls for enforceable AI safety standards, independent evaluations, public oversight, and the ability to restrict AI systems or use a kill switch to shut them down — though recent studies show that OpenAI and other AI labs haven’t published comprehensive plans for what they would do if a model escaped human control. Brennan called these stances “disingenuous,” pointing to OpenAI’s history of opposing legislation designed to impose such measures. In 2024, for example, OpenAI opposed California’s AI safety bill, SB 1047, which would have mandated catastrophic risk evaluations and shutdown capabilities. Last year, OpenAI also sought to limit state regulation, arguing that states could undermine American innovation. The company has more recently shifted some of those positions, backing several state safety laws and saying it would be open to independent evaluators embedded in the company. Lehane also argues that people should maintain control over consequential decisions made using AI, rather than handing off judgment entirely to machines. But that raises the question of what human control really looks like in a society where humans are increasingly being required to use AI in education, work, healthcare, and government. Throughout his essay, Lehane frames AI as a technology that could give Americans back their sense of agency and economic opportunity. But he ties average Americans’ “middle class” success to participation in an economy increasingly shaped by companies like OpenAI. Whether his policies will meaningfully redistribute power or subtly entrench it is less clear. TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI for more specifics on Lehane’s proposals and the company’s stances, but it did not respond by the time of publication. articles.title: Analyzing East Lansing’s Election: Turnout Was High; Student Votes Helped Sink a Proposal to Move Council Elections
articles.description: More than 17,600 East Lansing residents cast a ballot in Tuesday's election.
articles.content: East Lansing voters were part of a national environment that broke heavily in favor of Democrats at Tuesday’s election, as Democrats flipped the U.S. House and Senate and seized control of both chambers in the Michigan legislature. A closer look at the local results shows a high turnout in East Lansing and precincts on Michigan State University’s campus swung a vote against a proposal to switch City Council elections from odd- to even-numbered years. There were more than 17,600 votes cast in East Lansing precincts, according to unofficial results from the Ingham and Clinton County clerks’ offices. This is an increase from the roughly 14,000 votes cast in the 2022 midterm election. East Lansing voters continued their decadeslong support for Democrats, with gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson, U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence each winning at least 68% of the vote in all 14 city precincts. In some precincts, Democrats received more than 90% of the vote. All three Democrats won their races, according to the Associated Press. Democrats up and down East Lansing ballots won their races, including Rashida Harrison in Michigan’s 28th Senate District and incumbent State House Democrats Rep. Julie Brixie and Rep. Penelope Tsernoglou, who were reelected as Democrats gained control of both chambers of the Michigan legislature. Megan Kathleen Cavanagh and Noah Hood, incumbent Michigan Supreme Court Justices who were backed by the Ingham County Democratic party and East Lansing voters, retained their seats. Campus votes are instrumental in keeping City Council elections in odd-numbered years. A proposal to amend the City Charter to switch City Council elections from odd- to even-numbered years was narrowly defeated, with 6,819 voters in favor and 7,197 against. Had the proposal passed, it would have aligned City Council elections with federal and state general elections, substantially increasing turnout, especially among Michigan State University students. Precincts on MSU’s campus were critical in the vote against the charter amendment, as most off-campus East Lansing voters supported the amendment. The proposal was rejected by a margin of 378 votes and in the four campus precincts, 619 more voters opposed changing the election years than supported. Sarah Reckhow, who helped organize the campaign in favor of the amendment, said she believes an explanatory caption the City Council added to the ballot question swayed the student vote. The caption the council added is the first paragraph in the ballot text. The full text reads as follows: “A citizen-initiated proposal to amend the City Charter to move all City elections to even years, which, if passed, would extend the terms of current officeholders by one year. Note that even if approved, the City Council must take action to finalize the move of City elections to even years. “Shall the East Lansing City Charter be amended to require the City Council to move all elections held under the City Charter from odd-numbered years to even-numbered years?” Reckhow, an MSU political science professor, said the caption may have led some voters to view the proposal primarily as a means to extend City Council members’ terms by a year, rather than as a change to the timing of local elections. She said some voters may have opposed the amendment because they did not want current council members to remain in office for another year. “A lot of students don’t necessarily have a great impression of the East Lansing City Council,” Reckhow said in a call with East Lansing Info Wednesday. “A response to that can be ‘Wait, they’re going to be in office another year.’” The caption was controversial when the City Council added it. Adam DeLay, a former City Council candidate who campaigned for the amendment, accused the council of trying to “poison pill” the vote at a meeting in August. At that meeting, Councilmember Mark Meadows argued the initial language left out important information by not stating that members’ terms would be extended. Additionally, restrictions on campaigning in MSU dorms made it hard for proponents for the amendment to reach student voters, Reckhow said. Despite the proposal failing, Reckhow said the campaign in favor spoke with many residents about why it’s important to participate in local elections and the role members of the City Council play. She said she hopes this helps to increase turnout at the 2027 City Council election. Elsewhere on the ballot, four other city charter amendments were strongly supported by voters. A proposal to create a committee that analyzes local access to healthcare and provide recommendations to local, state and federal officials was favored by more than 70% of East Lansing voters. A proposal to create a healthcare committee in Lansing was passed by voters as well. Three other charter amendments that originated from a city committee that recommended changes to the charter were approved by voters with strong margins. These amendments largely allow more flexibility for city officials to delegate certain tasks. The election was marked by high turnout. Leading up to Tuesday’s election, City Clerk Emily Gordon told ELi she was preparing for a “presidential level” turnout. The preparation turned out to be worthwhile. While the midterm election didn’t quite reach 2024 presidential turnout, where nearly 19,000 votes were cast, more than 17,600 East Lansing voters turned in their ballots. High turnout in East Lansing was widely reported after the 2022 midterm election, when students waited in line for hours to register and vote. Still, there was a roughly 25% increase in turnout for this year’s midterm election in East Lansing compared to four years ago. While there were no lines similar to the polls at Brody Hall in 2022, which wrapped around halls throughout the building, there were a few voting locations that saw significant waits. During major elections, many MSU students still need to register to vote or update their registration on Election Day. These voters are funneled to a couple of locations called Election Day Vote Centers because registration is not done at regular polling places. This year’s Election Day Vote Centers were located at City Hall and WKAR’s Studio A in MSU’s Communications Arts and Sciences building. Students who had finished voting at City Hall a little after 5 p.m. estimated they waited in line for about 40 minutes. At about 6 p.m., students at the Communication Arts and Sciences building told ELi it took about an hour to cast a ballot. There was also a long line at the MSU Union, as students in line at about 7 p.m. said they had waited for more than an hour to vote. ELi did not observe any similar long wait times at other regular polling places. We’re still waiting to hear who won a seat on the school board. There were only three on-ballot candidates in a race for four seats on the East Lansing Board of Education. The on-ballot candidates – Abbie Tykocki, Tali Faris-Hylen and Delia Fernandez-Jones – each easily claimed a seat. The winner among three write-in candidates seeking the final seat is unclear. Scott Farver, Timothy Schmitt and Abigail Wright-Geddes each ran as official write-in candidates, and results show that hundreds of write-in votes were cast in the election. However, the results on the county clerk’s website do not distinguish who these write-in votes are for. ELi reached out to Clerk Gordon asking if a fourth school board trustee has been elected. She responded in an email Wednesday afternoon, writing that more will be known about this race starting Thursday. Do you have a question that you would like ELi to investigate? Just click here! articles.title: Benson promises bipartisan approach as she prepares to take office with Democratic trifecta
articles.description: At her first press conference as Governor-elect, Jocelyn Benson repeatedly emphasized the importance of working with legislators across the aisle to deliver on her campaign promises of lowering costs and increasing wages — even as she will be governing alongside a large Democratic trifecta in the Legislature. Benson won the governor’s race Tuesday as Democrats made […]
articles.content: Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson spoke to reporters the morning after winning the gubernatorial election, telling reporters that her agenda for the first 100 days would be rolled out soon. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)At her first press conference as Governor-elect, Jocelyn Benson repeatedly emphasized the importance of working with legislators across the aisle to deliver on her campaign promises of lowering costs and increasing wages — even as she will be governing alongside a large Democratic trifecta in the Legislature. Benson won the governor’s race Tuesday as Democrats made gains across the country, including in Michigan, where they flipped a number of seats in both the state House and Senate, retaining their majority in the latter and regaining it in the former. “Voters in Michigan spoke loud and clear. They want leaders who will work together to lower their costs and grow our economy,” Benson said, noting that specific plans for her first hundred days in office would be announced soon. “That is my focus, and as well as improving our public schools. And so you can expect to see some specific things that we’re going to start working on that we’ll be able to announce more in the weeks ahead. That hopefully will enable us to hit the ground running.” Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson and her lieutenant, Winnie Brinks, spoke to reporters the morning after winning the gubernatorial election. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance) Benson referenced a few specific policies that she intends to put in place, all of which align with past campaign statements on the issues, including voluntarily making the governor’s office subject to public records requests and evaluating different ways to reduce the gas tax. But despite entering the position on Jan. 1, 2027 with her party in control of both legislative chambers, as well as both the attorney general’s office and that of secretary of state, Benson repeatedly emphasized the need to work across the aisle. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “We do have a historic trifecta that we’re excited about because I’m going to Lansing not to play political games but to get things done. And I believe with this trifecta, you will see a number of leaders committed to that,” Benson said. “But in addition to that, every voice will have a place around our table.” She said that the results of Tuesday’s election in Michigan showed that the people had an appetite for elected leadership who “will work for the citizens and not Donald Trump.” “Michiganders have given us a clear mandate to work for them, to lower costs, to grow our economy, to improve our public schools, and get things done,” she said. “And we will meet that mandate working hand in hand with our legislative leaders and everyone in the Legislature on both sides of the aisle, frankly, from day one.” Lt. Governor-elect Winnie Brinks, the outgoing Senate Majority Leader, agreed, citing her own time as a legislator. “I know how this works,” she said. “Real progress doesn’t come from one office or one party alone. It comes when people sit down at the same table and focus on what works for the families that we serve. I’m ready to partner with anyone in either party, in either chamber, to get things done for Michigan and turn Governor-elect Benson’s agenda into real results for people.” Lieutenant Governor-elect Winnie Brinks spoke to reporters the morning after Democrats won the gubernatorial election. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance) Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel, speaking to reporters after Benson and Brinks’ press conference, said that he had been told that the Democratic majorities in the Legislature were the largest since 1978. “We had just great candidates that worked across the state and did that work on the ground,” he said. “Lots of exciting things in the Legislature, and it gives us that opportunity to have a majority that can get big things done for people and make Michigan a place where people can afford to raise a family again, which I think is the most important thing.” Hertel was less gracious to the Republicans as they face losses in the midterms, though he did note his own experience working across the aisle when he was a state legislator. “I do believe in being a gracious winner,” Hertel said. “But on the opposite side of that, Mike Rogers ran what I think is one of the most racist, Islamophobic, terrible campaigns that I’ve ever seen. It should be offensive to anybody that that was even possible. That was a campaign out of some past time in America where I think we were a much more hateful place, and so, I do find a little joy, I will say, in rejecting that.” Benson noted that U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Twp.), her Republican opponent in the governor’s race, had called her earlier that day to concede the race. In a video posted to social media, James also said that he had called her to congratulate her on a win. “The constituents that I have had the privilege of representing, thank you,” he said. “I’ve always said that when service calls, we have an obligation to answer, and sometimes it calls us home. So, I look forward to getting back to my first and most important titles, that being husband and dad. But regardless, I’m never going to relent in working with anyone and everyone for a greater, more prosperous, and a more free Michigan.”
