articles.title: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”
articles.description: Tech industry in denial as US overwhelmingly votes to restrict AI, data centers.
articles.content: Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide. One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects. In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US.Read full article Comments

articles.title: MLW's Court Bauer touts company's 'huge' 2026
Now, the hard part: Jocelyn Benson has big plans. Michigan has big problems
articles.description: From low reading scores and sagging wages and an aging population, Michigan faces a host of challenges identified by readers through Bridge Listens. What to expect from the governor-elect.
articles.content: Democrat Jocelyn Benson will lead a state facing several challenges Residents are worried about healthcare and housing costs to energy and democracy Benson will have allies with a Democratic controlled Legislature, but are her plans realistic? Minutes after becoming governor-elect early Wednesday, Jocelyn Benson said “now the work begins.” She isn’t kidding. Michigan faces myriad challenges, from lower-than-average wages and rising healthcare costs to sagging reading scores, an influx of data centers and concerns about government transparency. Those were among the top concerns identified in Bridge Listens, a yearlong effort that involved more than 6,400 residents who identified and ranked the state’s top challenges. Throughout Benson’s campaign for governor, she answered questions about how she would solve the issues vexing the state.Here’s what to know. Michigan residents are frustrated by higher prices. Many told Bridge they voted for candidates they thought would rein costs in. (Bridge photos by Janelle James, Kelly House and Kathy Kieliszewski) Affordability The issue Michiganders face rising costs on groceries and gas and a lack of affordable housing. Related: How Abdul El-Sayed, Jocelyn Benson won Michigan: Big turnout, Democratic shifts Democrats take full control of Legislature, Michigan government. What to expect Jocelyn Benson beats John James in Michigan governor’s race Manufacturing remains Michigan’s most important economic sector — but continues to shed jobs. The state’s median household income of almost $73,000 is about 10% less than the national rate, while the unemployment rate is higher and the workforce is older. Dan Gilmartin, executive director and CEO of the Michigan Municipal League, said at the Bridge Michigan Issues Summit last month there’s been lots of talk, but “we don’t act” like there’s an ongoing housing crisis.Donate “Cost of materials, cost that goes into it, all the way through financing, all the way through availability, and really a comprehensive way of dealing with that is the only way we really make a dent in this,” Gilmartin said. Benson’s plans Benson wants to create a healthcare affordability board, change how the state sets energy rates, pass a $5,000 caregiver tax credit and expand a cash to moms program. She aims for “holding accountable investors who buy up properties and drive up rents solely to make a profit.” She has also called to “expand and modernize the Michigan Homestead Property Tax Credit to reflect today’s housing costs and inflation.” That would include raising the income eligibility limit for the program, she said, “so more working families, seniors, and fixed-income homeowners” can qualify. Reality check Some of Benson’s proposals would be costly, and with Michigan facing tight budgets in recent years, Benson has not described how she would get the money to pay for the policies. The $5,000 tax credit alone would have cost the state $37 million when term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer proposed it in the 2024-2025 budget. Benson should have an easier time with Democrats winning control of the state Legislature. Reforming the Homestead Property Tax Credit , for instance, has had bipartisan support. More Fact guide: Michigan affordability, economy How governor candidates will address economy In their words: candidates on economy Michigan rural communities ‘overlooked’ in economic development Panel: No silver bullet for housing, but Michigan policymakers have to act Michigan advocates say students need more skills to be ready for life after high school whether that’s college, the trades or joining the workforce. (Owin Widdis for Bridge Michigan) Schools The issue Michigan third-grade reading scores at a new low, more than a fourth of students are chronically absent and only a fourth of high school juniors are “college ready,” according to the SAT. On spring 2024 tests, Michigan ranks 44th for fourth grade reading. Michigan is expanding options for dual enrollment and career technical education but many worry that not enough students are earning a college degree. Benson’s plans She wants to raise the minimum teacher salary to $60,000 a year, change the state’s high school graduation standards and provide schools more funding. She wants to raise more money for special education and ensure the state School Aid Fund only goes toward PreK-12 schools, not colleges and universities. It’s unclear whether she will opt Michigan into the Education Freedom Tax Credit program. The effort would pay for students to attend private schools but public school students can also use scholarships for some activities. Proponents say it’s a way to help students and families while critics say it’s a voucher in disguise and will divert money from public schools. Reality check Money is always an issue. Public opinion polling shows people think teachers should start at $54,600 and average pay should be $71,445. Jason Burns, a research specialist at the Education Policy Innovation Collaborative, who studies teacher compensation, previously told Bridge it would take about $350 million to $400 million to raise teacher pay in line with public opinion. It’s unclear where Benson would get the money to protect School Aid funding from higher education. The current state budget includes a record $1.7 billion of these funds for colleges and universities. More: Fact guide: Michigan schools are struggling. What to know How Michigan’s next governor will try to fix schools School challenges particularly profound Up North What’s behind Michigan’s poor reading scores To fix Michigan schools, experts urge better reading skills, less politics Jocelyn Benson is advocating for an independent prescription drug board. (Rod Sanford for Bridge Michigan) Healthcare The issue Michiganders face rising healthcare costs including higher premiums, while an estimated 690,000 in Michigan face medical debt, according to KFF, a California-based research nonprofit focused on health care. According to newly released data, premium rates will jump an average of 14.2% for about 400,000 people who purchase their own health plans. Another 400,000 receiving coverage through small group plans — covering small businesses with fewer than 51 employees — are seeing rates rise 9.6% on average. Michigan faces a shortage of physicians, first responders and mental health professionals. Rural communities especially struggle to find enough workers. A growing number of Americans are uninsured, having lost coverage under commercial insurance and Medicaid. Some fear things are about to get much worse, as sweeping changes in Medicaid that start in January force thousands of Michiganders to lose coverage and the health care industry millions of dollars. Benson’s plans Benson said she would create an independent prescription drug affordability board to “hold pharmaceutical companies accountable for price gouging and identify ways to reduce the overall cost of care. Benson said she will protect Medicaid but did not specify how and wants to expand access to health services. “Our programs will include partnering with local health care providers to invest in mobile health centers to bring low or no-cost preventative services directly to rural and underserved areas hit hardest by hospital closures and federal funding cuts,” Benson said. She also touts a medical debt forgiveness expansion, incentives for doctors to service in rural areas and increased price transparency in healthcare. Reality check Many of Michigan’s biggest healthcare issues stem from federal policies outside Benson’s control. Michigan faces an expected $2 billion shortfall, in large part, because of sweeping changes requiring people to work 80 hours a month or prove that they cannot. This plan starts Jan. 1. Creating a prescription drug board is a priority of legislative Democrats but it’s unclear how much say the board could have on drug costs — and some studies have questioned their effectiveness in the 11 states with them. Lawmakers tried this before with Democratic majorities in both chambers and failed to pass the proposal. The state already offers mobile health sites. More Fact guide: Health care costs climbing, challenges loom. What to know How next governor would address health care Medical debt soars as hospitals expand Panel: Michigan healthcare costs are rising, complicated, but still fixable (Bridge Michigan file photo) Environment and data centers The issue The tax breaks lawmakers passed in Decemeber 2024 exempt qualifying hyperscale data centers from the state’s 6% sales and use tax through 2050. Since then, at least 18 hyperscale proposals have been put on the table. Michigan residents continue to push back on data centers, with one poll after another indicating high disapproval. Dozens of communities have passed moratoriums, while others have mounted recall efforts targeting local elected officials for not opposing the projects. At the state level, pressure is mounting for legislative leaders to reverse course on some of the state’s data center efforts.Proposals have ranged from limiting companies’ energy and water use, rolling back tax breaks or creating a statewide moratorium on data center projects. Michigan passed a law in 2023 requiring the state’s regulated utilities to achieve 100% clean energy by 2040. But rising energy demand from data centers only makes it more difficult and offers questions about how local communities want to meet that demand. Benson’s plans Benson has called for a moratorium on new data centers until guardrails are in place. She has not been specific on what those guardrails are. “No data centers will be built in Michigan unless there are rules in place that make them negotiate with communities in the open,” she said in a September social media post. “We will ban them from getting tax breaks and using up our water, and we will require them to pay for the power they use.”Benson supports the clean energy law but has said she wants local communities to weigh in. Reality check Governors have limited ability to set environmental policies without cooperation from the Legislature. While Benson will benefit from Democratic leadership in the House and Senate, chamber leaders have yet to outline priorities. Michigan is desperate for economic development and a single hyperscale data center can bring in tens of millions annually in local taxes as well as jobs and spinoff investment. Businesses are highly interested in them and would likely lobby against new restrictions. Democrats also led the Legislature when tax breaks for data centers initially passed with, so removing those tax breaks would require asking some of the prior proponents who are still in office to make an about-face. More: Fact guide: Michigan environment, energy and data centers How governor candidates will address environment, energy Michigan loves a river story; happy ending isn’t guaranteed How many tax breaks are enough for data centers? Federal policies shield conditions of Michigan dams Experts predict more Michigan data center regulations amid public pushback Michigan residents say they are concerned about democracy and government transparency. (Brayan Gutierrez for Bridge Michigan) Democracy The issue Michiganders said they are concerned about the rising political tensions, election security and government transparency. Michigan voters overwhelmingly supported a ballot proposal to limit corporate spending in politics Tuesday night but a free market think tank has already filed a lawsuit challenging the measure. Michigan had been one of two states that exempted the state legislature and governor’s office from having to provide records to the public. But voters in Massachusetts week voted in support of opening records up to the public. Benson’s plans Benson said she would voluntarily open her office to the Freedom of Information Act on her first day in office. Her predecessor, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, made the same vow 2018 but never f

articles.title: Hackers stole DreamHost customer files and inboxes during months-long attack
articles.description: The web host said hackers exploited a vulnerability to access customer emails and files during a "deliberate attack."
articles.content: Web host DreamHost has confirmed that hackers stole customer emails and credentials during a months-long cyberattack on its systems. DreamHost disclosed the breach last Thursday after it sparked an outage that spanned several days, during which it reset some customer passwords. In a data breach notice filed with California’s attorney general, the web host said the attack began in August and allowed hackers to obtain session tokens, which keep users logged in after entering their passwords. If stolen, hackers can break into a system as if they were that user. The company said hackers exploited an unspecified vulnerability in DreamHost’s file manager, which customers use to store their files. When reached by TechCrunch, a DreamHost spokesperson declined to say why the company did not detect the cyberattack until last week, citing an ongoing investigation. The spokesperson did not say what the vulnerability is. The company said it was unrelated to the vulnerabilities recently discovered in the PHP web software. DreamHost’s spokesperson said that the number of affected customers is “well under 10%” but would not provide a more accurate figure. The web host touts some 400,000 paying customers across its network. articles.content: Following his public disputes with California authorities during the COVID-19 pandemic, Elon Musk personally moved to Texas, outside of Austin, in 2020. Over the next six years, he doubled down on the Lone Star State. In 2021, Musk increasingly focused the Starship program in South Texas, urging SpaceX employees to move there and work on the company's future. In March of that year, he began using the name Starbase to describe the production and launch facilities near the Rio Grande River. In 2023, he built a massive factory east of Austin to manufacture customer terminals and other electronics for the Starlink program. In July 2024, he announced that SpaceX would relocate its corporate headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas. articles.title: Appeals court hands Mamdani legal win on NYC luxury second-home tax
articles.content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani scored a legal victory Wednesday after a state appeals court reversed a lower court ruling that had ordered his administration to redo the rollout of a tax on high-end second homes. The four-judge panel unanimously dismissed the homeowners' lawsuit, finding that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing. The decision overturned a September ruling by a Staten Island judge who had ordered the city to restart the tax's implementation. The ruling allows Mamdani's administration to continue implementing the surcharge — also known as a pied-à-terre tax — a key part of his agenda to raise taxes on wealthy New Yorkers and help close the city's budget gap. The tax still faces separate legal challenges. NYC JUDGE ORDERS MAMDANI TO REDO SECOND-HOME TAX ROLLOUT The surcharge, approved by the New York state Legislature in May, applies to qualifying second homes valued at $5 million or more for one- to three-family properties and $1 million or more for condos and co-ops. The city's Department of Finance sent initial determination notices to approximately 17,000 property owners in July. A Staten Island judge ruled Sept. 29 that the city had mishandled the rollout and ordered officials to restart the process. The city appealed while continuing to implement the tax. The appellate judges found that receiving an initial tax notice or appearing on the city's property valuation list did not establish sufficient harm to bring the lawsuit. The court also rejected the homeowners' arguments that the process caused concrete injuries through privacy concerns or the costs of seeking exemptions. MAMDANI’S LUXURY-HOME TAX ROLLOUT DERAILED FOR NOW AS JUDGE DELIVERS WIN TO NYC HOMEOWNERS OVER MASSIVE LIST Mamdani welcomed the ruling, accusing wealthy property owners of trying to avoid paying additional taxes. "From day one, those with the most have attempted to use every legal avenue available to shield their wealth and avoid contributing more to our city," Mamdani said. Randy Mastro, an attorney representing the homeowners, criticized the court for dismissing the lawsuit without addressing the merits of their challenge. "It’s a shame that, after the City admittedly botched the rollout of this surcharge, the court today took the procedural offramp of standing to avoid addressing the merits of this case," Mastro said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "What the City has done here is unconscionable — trying to ensnare thousands of people who don’t owe this surcharge into having to prove they live in their own homes or else have to pay it. "But now, this lawless and chaotic data collection scheme will go unremedied." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Mastro said the surcharge faces another legal test next month over its constitutionality. Mamdani said his administration would continue defending the law against separate challenges in Suffolk County.

articles.title: Idaho voters reject abortion ballot measure as Missouri, Nevada and Virginia back access
articles.description: Nationwide results for abortion ballot initiatives on Tuesday night largely favored protecting access to abortion and other reproductive care, with the exception of Idaho, where a measure that would have restored access to abortion was soundly defeated. Idaho’s outcome stood in stark contrast to the other three ballot questions, with 56% voting against the approval […]
articles.content: A “Stop Prop 1” sign leans up against the wall during an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Boise, Idaho. Voters soundly defeated a measure that would have restored access to abortion in the state, a sharp contrast with outcomes in three other states that expanded or enshrined abortion rights. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Nationwide results for abortion ballot initiatives on Tuesday night largely favored protecting access to abortion and other reproductive care, with the exception of Idaho, where a measure that would have restored access to abortion was soundly defeated. Idaho’s outcome stood in stark contrast to the other three ballot questions, with 56% voting against the approval of Proposition 1 and 44% voting in favor, nearly the inverse of Missouri’s outcome, where 55% of voters struck down an amendment that would have reinstated the ban that was overturned through a ballot initiative in 2024. Other abortion-related measures were on the ballot in Nevada and Virginia, two states where abortion is already accessible until 24 weeks and 26 weeks of pregnancy, respectively. Voters in both of those states passed constitutional amendments ensuring the right to abortion. The outcome in Idaho ensures the state’s abortion ban remains intact. The ban prohibits abortion at any stage of pregnancy with exceptions only for rape and incest in the first trimester and to save a pregnant patient’s life. Blaine Conzatti, president of the Idaho Family Policy Center, the organization that helped craft the ban and campaigned against the initiative, said in a statement that “abortion advocates fundamentally misunderstood Idaho.” “As we proved last night, a broad majority of Idaho voters support our pro-life laws,” Conzatti said. “This is what happens when Christians speak out and get engaged — we win.” Melanie Folwell, executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families and lead organizer of the initiative, said in a statement that more than $1.3 million in donations from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and the Catholic Diocese of Boise fueled a disinformation campaign about what the law would do. “We’re encouraging Idahoans to reach out to their lawmakers, particularly those politicians who encouraged voters to reject Prop 1 and wait for a legislative fix, and demand needed exceptions in the coming session,” Folwell said. A federal appeals court ruled on Oct. 30 that Idaho’s law does not include exceptions for a pregnant person whose physical or mental health is in jeopardy by continuing the pregnancy, a situation that Idaho doctors have repeatedly said puts them in a position to feel compelled to wait until a patient’s life is in danger before acting. A peer-reviewed study published in 2025 in JAMA showed 114 OB-GYNs left Idaho or stopped practicing obstetrics between August 2022 and December 2024, the first two years after the ban took effect. That number represents 43% of the 268 physicians practicing obstetrics statewide. Several of those who left have said publicly that the ban made it more difficult to do their jobs without fear of criminal prosecution. Providers found guilty of violating the ban face up to five years in prison, the revocation of their medical license and up to $20,000 in civil penalties. Many doctors who have continued to practice obstetrics and gynecology in Idaho say the loss of those providers has increased their workload to a stressful and at times dangerous degree. In the months leading up to the vote, Idaho women shared their stories of needing to seek care in other states, including Utah, because of fatal fetal anomalies, along with others who said their care during a miscarriage was delayed, causing dangerous infections. With the failure of the ballot measure, pregnant patients who need an abortion will continue to need to seek care in other states. Dr. Caitlin Gustafson, a physician in rural Idaho and board president of the Idaho Coalition for Safe Healthcare, told Stateline she was deeply saddened by the results, but said the fight is “far from over” because she knows every community across Idaho is affected by the law. “The work ahead is to make sure that other aspects of reproductive healthcare can stay in place, that we can proactively protect IVF, contraception, and timely miscarriage care,” Gustafson said. “Because that was part of this effort too. We must protect all areas of reproductive freedom and privacy. I remain committed to fight for women, families, and my medical colleagues who provide safe healthcare across Idaho.” Missouri defeats amendment despite heavy lawmaker involvement The Fairness Project, a national nonprofit organization that supports ballot initiatives on economic and social issues, funded efforts to defeat Amendment 3 in Missouri, where the legislature attempted to undo an initiative passed by voters in 2024. “Missouri is a shining example of politicians trying to take people’s rights away and voters taking them right back,” said Hannah Ledford, executive director of the Fairness Project, in an interview Wednesday. “It is so cool.” Ledford said the outcome in Idaho compared with Missouri wasn’t surprising, in part because Missouri’s measure was a defensive move against the legislature attempting to take a right away, while Idaho’s initiative was proactive and would grant rights. “The proactive question is just inherently more difficult than convincing voters to vote ‘no,’” Ledford said. According to the Missouri Independent, the Amendment 3 effort had significant and organized support from Republican lawmakers this time around, along with Gov. Mike Kehoe’s office and many of the state’s largest churches. It also would have added a constitutional amendment prohibiting gender-affirming care for minors, which is already state law. National anti-abortion leaders had pointed to Missouri’s amendment as a possible model for reinstating abortion bans in other states by pairing abortion restrictions with a ban on gender-affirming care. “When Missouri wins, every other state will learn that these bad amendments can be reversed and undone. But if it loses, no other state will likely try this again for a long time, perhaps for a generation,” said David Bereit, executive director of the Virginia-based Life Leadership Conference, during a virtual fundraising event in October. Virginia, Nevada enshrine constitutional right to an abortion Nevada voters easily passed the second round of the measure amending the constitution to include a right to abortion up to fetal viability, generally considered to be about 22 to 24 weeks of pregnancy. After that point, exceptions could be made to preserve a pregnant person’s life or health. About 63% of voters approved the measure. State law requires that constitutional amendments be passed by voters twice to take effect — it passed with 64% approval in 2024. In Virginia, voters approved the amendment that protects the freedom to make decisions about prenatal and postpartum care, birth control, childbirth, abortion, miscarriage management and fertility care. It also protects doctors, nurses and patients from being punished for those decisions and allows exceptions during later pregnancy for abortion if the pregnant patient’s health is at risk or the fetus cannot survive. The measure garnered 62% approval from Virginia voters. “Never again will our reproductive rights be a political football in Virginia,” said Han Jones, campaign manager for Virginians For Reproductive Freedom, on Tuesday, according to Virginia Mercury. “It takes multi-year concerted work, but as you can see in Virginia, it’s paying off.” Missouri Independent reporter Anna Spoerre and Virginia Mercury reporter Charlotte Rene Woods contributed to this report. Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org. articles.title: Highland Park mayor to request recount after community leader wins
articles.description: Shamayim 'Mama Shu' Harris garnered 50% of the votes to narrowly defeat incumbent Highland Park Mayor Glenda McDonald, according to unofficial results.
articles.content: Detroit Free Press is a partner and shares a reporter with BridgeDetroit. Stories shared are not under a paywall. Detroit Free Press Highland Park’s current mayor says she will request a recount after losing Tuesday’s election to a longtime community leader. Shamayim Harris, known as “Mama Shu,” won the mayoral race in the 2.9-square-mile city, according to unofficial race results. Harris narrowly beat incumbent Glenda McDonald by a margin of just 27 votes. Harris received 50% of the votes, whereas McDonald garnered 49%. Harris, founder of the nonprofit Avalon Village, campaigned on her role as a city leader and her experience as a school administrator, mother, minister and community builder. “Highland Park has always had what it needs: its people. For nearly two decades at Avalon Village, we’ve transformed blight to beauty. I didn’t want to leave Highland Park and move to a beautiful place; I wanted to make where I live beautiful. Now we get to do that work for the whole city and I am truly honored and overjoyed to get started. I ran on results you can see, and I will regularly report to residents on what we’re getting done,” Harris, 61, said in a statement after the election. Harris said she intends to launch a task force to tackle vacant land and illegal dumping, focus on community-centered public safety and bring investment and small businesses to Highland Park, a city with a population of nearly 9,000. She also campaigned on job training, entrepreneurship and getting citywide communications out to residents. “As I’ve said throughout the campaign – our administration will focus on citizens first,” Harris, who received an outpouring of support on social media, said Wednesday, Nov. 4. Highland Park Incumbent Mayor Glenda McDonald Credit: Courtesy photo McDonald, reached by phone Wednesday afternoon, said she had no comments other than that she’ll be asking for a recount. “If it’s still the same, I will be conceding the race and wishing Mama Shu well,” she said. In a statement, Harris spokesperson Amber Ogden said Harris respects the election process and fully supports her opponent’s right to request a recount. “She remains focused on serving our community and looks forward to working together for the future of Highland Park once the final results are official,” Ogden told the Free Press. Avalon Village — which focuses on transforming vacant and blighted land in Highland Park — came about after Harris’ 2-year-old son, Jakobi RA Harris, was killed in a 2007 hit and run. Then, in 2021, her other son, Chinyelu Humphrey, was fatally shot. She has said that she feels as though her sons are still with her, speaking to her over her shoulder, influencing her actions. Their memory inspired her to turn “blight to beauty” on Avalon Street, between Woodward and Second Avenue. The village has more than 40 parcels of land and 5 houses, including a Homework House for afterschool learning, a marketplace for women entrepreneurs and a healing space. Harris, recognized as one of CNN’s Top 10 Heroes in 2023 and among USA Today’s 2024 Women of the Year, was born in Highland Park and grew up in Detroit. She moved back to Highland Park in 2003. Harris turned over leadership of Avalon Village to her daughters, Aziza Brent and Kafi Humphrey. McDonald led the August primary election with 49.6% of the votes. She served on Highland Park’s City Council for a full and partial term before becoming mayor in 2023. Reach reporter Nushrat Rahman at nrahman@freepress.com.

articles.content: AT&T’s smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home. The company says its Connected Life system is the “first” home security product to integrate with Google Home Premium, enabling a bunch of Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events, search your video history, and more. With the update, Gemini for Home can provide detailed descriptions about events captured by your security cameras, such as who delivered a package and how many items they dropped off. You can also search recorded video footage using natural language questions, like “What dug up the yard last night?” or “Who let the dogs out?”, as well as review daily summaries of activity in and outside your home. These features are only available with AT&T’s professional $29.99 / month Connected Life monitoring plan. AT&T is also adding the ability to automatically arm or disarm your home based on your proximity to your home. AT&T launched its Connected Life system last December in partnership with Google and Abode. It’s now taking advantage of Google’s Gemini-powered Home APIs, which allow smart home brands and developers to build AI-powered features into their devices. ADT has also hinted at bringing Gemini for Home features into its security systems.

articles.title: Trump accepts the blue tsunami, despite months of election legal battles, threats
articles.description: Ahead of the midterms, Democrats wargamed dozens of scenarios looking at how President Donald Trump might try to undermine the election, everything from seizing voting machines to falsely declaring a foreign attack. But when the blue tsunami arrived Tuesday night, Trump seemed to let it wash right over him. In a series of late-night interviews, […]
articles.content: Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach speaks alongside President Donald Trump at a Nov. 1, 2026, rally in Salina, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)Ahead of the midterms, Democrats wargamed dozens of scenarios looking at how President Donald Trump might try to undermine the election, everything from seizing voting machines to falsely declaring a foreign attack. But when the blue tsunami arrived Tuesday night, Trump seemed to let it wash right over him. In a series of late-night interviews, the president said he would accept the results. He acknowledged that Democrats had performed well as they retook the House and Senate. And while he refused responsibility for Republicans’ newfound misfortune, he also spoke of cutting deals with Democrats. “Yes, I’ll accept them,” Trump said on Fox News when asked about the results. He added a short time later, “Congratulations to the Democrats, they did a good job.” The comments marked a stunning departure for a mercurial president with a long history of alleging elections were stolen in response to unfavorable results. They also stood out because this year’s midterms were his first election while in office since 2020, when he led a campaign to overturn his loss that helped spur the mob that sacked the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. “My first thought was, ‘Well, I’m glad that’s on tape,’” Pamela Smith, president and CEO of the election security nonprofit Verified Voting, said in an interview. Fears of federal interference Election officials spent months planning for the possibility of federal election interference on Election Day. After the FBI seized ballots from the 2020 election in Fulton County, Georgia, in January, state and local leaders across the country weighed how they would respond if the Trump administration tried to take their ballots or voting equipment. They mapped out what poll workers would do if federal agents showed up at the polls. Some states even passed new limits on federal law enforcement and military servicemembers at the polls, even though federal law already prohibits armed personnel at election sites. “There have been so many different kinds of threats and it’s just been so far to get to this day, far too hard for the election officials,” Smith said Wednesday. None of those extreme scenarios came to pass on Election Day. Instead, Democrats won resounding victories up and down the ballot. As of midday Wednesday, Democrats had secured 54 Senate seats, according to The Associated Press. Democrats had also won at least 228 seats in the House, well above the 218 necessary to control the chamber. The not-close race for control of Congress and a high voter turnout “made it impossible to challenge these results,” David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, told reporters. Trump blamed the loss on his absence from the ballot, even though he had exhorted Americans to vote as if he were on the ballot. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war with Iran. “The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026,” Vance wrote on social media. Both men sought to explain Republicans’ deep losses — not claim that they didn’t happen. Ballot fight consumed officials But despite Trump’s pledge to accept the results, voting rights advocates said the Trump administration very much attempted to interfere ahead of Election Day and influence how states ran their elections. The U.S. Department of Justice sued California over the ballots of 20,000 suspected noncitizens and Alaska over alleged voter confusion in the U.S. Senate race. California election officials had warned the Justice Department’s demand would have thrown the election into chaos and the U.S. Supreme Court rejected the request Monday. Meanwhile, a federal judge tossed the Alaska lawsuit on Sunday. Justice Department lawyers raised the possibility that election officials could be prosecuted if they counted the ballots of noncitizens or if they failed to follow federal recordkeeping laws. They issued subpoenas to election workers in Los Angeles County, demanding records that suggest prosecutors are examining whether election officials were “aiding and abetting” noncitizen voters. The DOJ also sued dozens of states for unredacted copies of their voter rolls containing sensitive personal data. Federal judges have rejected those lawsuits in at least 27 decisions so far, and the Trump administration has won none of its cases. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security ran election-related field operations that federal judges found could intimidate voters. The department also launched a powerful computer program to identify possible noncitizen voters, but Democrats and election experts said its results were unreliable and prone to falsely flagging U.S. citizens. More broadly, Trump urged GOP state lawmakers across the country to redraw their congressional maps to be more favorable to Republicans — a process that accelerated after the Supreme Court weakened limits on racial gerrymandering. But in Alabama, North Carolina, Texas and elsewhere, the new maps did little to shield GOP candidates. Earlier this year, Trump also pushed the U.S. Postal Service to impose restrictions on mail ballots, a move blocked by the Supreme Court. And he unsuccessfully demanded Congress pass the SAVE America Act, which would have immediately imposed stringent rules requiring voters to prove their citizenship, leaving states with no time to prepare. “Despite unprecedented executive branch efforts to interfere in election administration, state and local officials responsible for running our elections have continued to do their jobs and uphold the process,” Michael McNulty, senior policy director at Issue One, a group focused on protecting American democracy, said in a statement. Some legal wrangling continues Trump’s admission of defeat may not fully end his administration’s pressure campaign over elections. Late on Election Day, the Justice Department secured a rare court victory when the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed a decision by a three-judge panel removing limitations on the Trump administration threatening election workers with prosecution. The decision came after a federal judge in California last week issued an order prohibiting the DOJ from threatening election officials with criminal charges if they didn’t comply with demands related to setting aside the ballots of alleged noncitizen voters. “We will conduct our criminal investigations without fear or favor,” Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote on social media Tuesday. The Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to require California to set aside the ballots of 20,000 suspected noncitizens also remains unresolved. Even though the Supreme Court declined an emergency request by the DOJ, a federal judge has scheduled a hearing on Nov. 13 to examine the list that could include witness testimony. The consequences of any ruling now aren’t clear. California’s ballots are currently being counted, meaning it would be effectively impossible now to identify whether a ballot came from a suspected noncitizen. The hearing will take place several weeks before election officials must certify results, however. The hearing could reveal new information about how the Trump administration developed the list. The DOJ has said Homeland Security compiled it based on a public copy of California’s voter roll that was checked against government records and data from the Lexis Nexis research service. California election officials have said they’ve found evidence that U.S. citizens are on the list, and in a court hearing on Monday, a Justice Department attorney acknowledged it has a “high error rate.” Jonathan Miller, chief program officer of Public Rights Project, which represents Los Angeles County in the lawsuit, in a statement framed the dispute in simple terms. “State and local officials run our elections — and the federal government cannot interfere,” Miller said.

UAW’s Shawn Fain: The 2026 election results were a case of the ‘many versus the mighty’
articles.description: DETROIT — The political outreach efforts of Michigan’s labor movement played a significant role in the 2026 elections as Democrats helped elect candidates who put the plight of working people first in their campaign messages and policy planks, said UAW President Shawn Fain on Tuesday evening. In an interview with Michigan Advance, the leader of […]
articles.content: United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain speaks at the Michigan Democratic Party's election night watch party in Detroit on Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — The political outreach efforts of Michigan’s labor movement played a significant role in the 2026 elections as Democrats helped elect candidates who put the plight of working people first in their campaign messages and policy planks, said UAW President Shawn Fain on Tuesday evening. In an interview with Michigan Advance, the leader of one of the nation’s largest unions said the gains made in the Nov. 3 election — which saw several of the movement’s endorsed candidates sail to victory — were a testament to the on-the-ground efforts of labor over the past year, including its get out the vote effort within UAW’s own ranks. “We mobilized our membership. We have 350,000 members here in Michigan, and over 200,000 voted early,” Fain told the Advance while he was watching election night returns at the Michigan Democratic Party victory event in downtown Detroit. “Our members have been out with 500,000 phone calls, 100,000 doors knocked on. We’ve seen double digit percentages of support. What that means for me, and working class Michiganders, is that we’re going to have people who stand behind working class people who are struggling to afford to live right now.” Fain said the election, and its efforts in 2026, was a true case of “the many versus the mighty.” “You had a lot of rich people who tried to inject a ton of money, outside groups who came to Michigan, to buy a seat, to buy these races,” Fain added. “Michiganders are smarter than that and they’re telling these people they’re not for sale.” Michigan Democratic Party members and supporters watch election night returns on Nov. 3, 2026, at a watch party in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Many of the UAW’s endorsed Michigan candidates won on Tuesday, including Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson, Secretary of State-elect Garlin Gilchrist, U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, Attorney General-elect Eli Savit, and Michigan Supreme Court Justices Meghan Cavanagh and Noah Hood. The UAW had also endorsed Christina Hines, Sean McCann and Will Lawrence — all of whom were elected to congressional seats. Fain said those gains have the potential to change or improve labor laws, as well as policies that address affordability, both here in Michigan and nationally. The focus on working people from several candidates, particularly from the El-Sayed campaign, showed Fain that the union had done what was necessary to elevate working class needs and issues to the very top of Democratic politics. “We’ve served notice,” he said. “We’re done getting behind candidates just because of a party label. The days of just endorsing people are over. They’ve got to do the work, and we have expectations. We expect that they are going to be there for working class people. We laid that standard down back in 2023, and we’ve really focused our efforts here in 2026 to mobilize our membership and mobilize our people like we’ve never done in my lifetime, and you’re seeing the results of that tonight.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Now that Democrats control the whole of Michigan government, and also control both chambers of Congress, Fain said he wants them to focus on adequate wages, healthcare and retirement security. Any efforts to create an economic environment where people who are already working 12 hours a day, seven days a week and don’t have to work two or three jobs would also go a long way, he said. “That’s not a life. Working class people deserve better,” Fain said. “We expect the Democratic Party to get back to their roots. Some of those Democrats forgot about that over the years. … Working class people are sending a message tonight that they are fed up with struggling to afford to live. If these candidates can get behind those issues, they’re going to be there for a long time. If they don’t, no matter which party they belong to, they’ll be out of the way the next round.”

A smooth Election Day delivers a strong rebuke, several history-making results
articles.description: After months of campaigning, polling and prognostication, voters across the country had their say in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday. And despite fears about possible trouble at polling places, millions of votes were cast, mostly without incident. Voters administered a sharp reprimand to President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans, with Democrats capturing comfortable majorities […]
articles.content: Americans broke early voting records leading up to the Nov. 3 elections that saw Democrats take control of Congress in a public rebuke of Republican President Donald Trump’s policies in the first half of his term. (Photo by Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star)After months of campaigning, polling and prognostication, voters across the country had their say in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday. And despite fears about possible trouble at polling places, millions of votes were cast, mostly without incident. Voters administered a sharp reprimand to President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans, with Democrats capturing comfortable majorities in the U.S. Senate and the House. Democrats also are poised to control the majority of governor’s offices for the first time in 16 years following major GOP losses. It was a historic day: Voters chose the first female Black governor in U.S. history in Georgia, the first Native American woman for the U.S. Senate in Minnesota, the first Black Republican governor in Florida and the first Muslim as a U.S. senator in Michigan. Here is a look at how Election Day played out in states from coast to coast. Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms celebrates her victory on Nov. 3 in Atlanta. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder) Janice Martin says, “Thank you, Jesus,” after the news broadcast announced Democrat Adam Hamilton’s win for U.S. Senate at Cindy Holscher’s watch party Nov. 3, 2026, in Lenexa, Kansas. (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector) Voters wait in line outside the Department of Elections in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance) People stuck their “I voted” stickers to the memorial for Alex Pretti in Minneapolis on Nov. 3, 2026. Pretti was shot and killed by federal agents in January during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown on Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer) Deb Haaland, a former U.S. interior secretary who previously represented New Mexico in Congress, made history Tuesday night as the first Native American woman in the nation to be elected governor. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM) Multnomah County election workers sort through submitted ballots at the county election office in Portland, Oregon, on Nov. 3, 2026. Before any ballot can be counted, workers verify that voters signed their ballot envelope and that their signature matches the signature on their voter registration file. (Photo by Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle) Poll workers wait for voters at a polling place in a garage on Willett Road in Brentwood, Pennsylvania, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star) Velma Farris, 102, votes at Shelby Community Center in Nashville, Tennessee, aided by her daughter, Vicky Greve. Farris’ first election was in 1944, when she voted for Franklin D. Roosevelt for president. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout) Barret Peterson drops off his ballot in a drop box outside the Main Library in Salt Lake City before the polls close on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Jamie Macias votes during the 2026 election at the El Zagal Shrine Hall in Fargo, North Dakota, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Dan Koeck for the North Dakota Monitor) Volunteers with Just Vote Colorado on Tuesday handed out “know your rights” cards in Adams County, Colorado, where the Trump administration had deployed Justice Department election monitors. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline) Harmony, a volunteer with DJs at the Polls, spins music outside of the polling place at Emmanuel Presbyterian Church in Phoenix. She said voters thanked her for helping entertain them as they waited in line. (Photo by Jim Small/Arizona Mirror) U.S. Rep. Mike Collins addresses supporters after losing his run for U.S. Senate in Georgia. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder) Rebecca Bennett’s daughter Millie, 4, dances during Bennett’s election night watch party at the Bridgewater Manor on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor) Dr. Amy Acton became the first Democrat in 20 years to lead Ohio after winning the governor’s race Tuesday, Nov. 3, at a rally in Cleveland. (Photo by Nick Evans/Ohio Capital Journal) Mary Peltola supporters celebrate results on election night, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at a Mary Peltola watch party in downtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon) Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford handily defeated Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo to become Nevada’s first Black governor. (Photo by April Corbin Girnus/Nevada Current) U.S. Sen. Darline Graham gives a concession speech Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the State Fairgrounds in Columbia after she was defeated by Dr. Annie Andrews. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/SC Daily Gazette) Shortly after polls close, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins thanks her family and staff, and prepares the crowd gathered at the GOP watch party in Bangor, Maine. Voters in five states back bans on noncitizen voting while one state bucks trend
articles.description: Voters in five states approved new citizenship voting requirements on Tuesday while Arizona voters rejected theirs. Proposals to explicitly bar noncitizens from voting were on the ballot this week in six states: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia. Arizona voters defeated Proposition 144, which would have mandated that only citizens could register […]
articles.content: A Star Wars-themed campaign sign opposing Proposition 144 at a Phoenix intersection. Arizona voters defeated Proposition 144, which would have mandated that only citizens could register and vote in Arizona elections. (Photo by Jim Small/Arizona Mirror)Voters in five states approved new citizenship voting requirements on Tuesday while Arizona voters rejected theirs. Proposals to explicitly bar noncitizens from voting were on the ballot this week in six states: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia. Arizona voters defeated Proposition 144, which would have mandated that only citizens could register and vote in Arizona elections. Arizona’s measure was much broader than those in other states. The citizenship voting requirement was included in a more sweeping proposal that would have required government-issued ID to cast in-person and mail-in ballots, banned foreign contributions in elections, and allowed voters to have their ballots counted at their polling precinct on election day. Opponents were surprised the measure was defeated, reported the Arizona Mirror. Republicans and other supporters said it would make state elections faster and more secure. But critics including voting rights groups worried it would lead to the end of no-excuse mail-in voting. Federal law already bars noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and no state currently allows noncitizens to vote in statewide elections. Most states, including Arkansas, Kansas and South Dakota, already have citizenship voting requirements in state law or their constitutions, making the ballot measures seem redundant at first glance. But sponsors of the citizenship voting requirements — primarily Republicans — said they wanted to preemptively bar cities or other local governments from allowing noncitizens to vote in local elections, as municipalities in California, Maryland and Vermont have done. Legal experts say that some state laws that seem to require citizenship to vote can be interpreted to allow noncitizen voters in certain elections. Voters in West Virginia overwhelmingly supported adding the amendment to the state constitution to bar noncitizens from voting. The amendment “would ensure that no future legislature could just simply change the election law with only a bill,” said West Virginia state Sen. Patricia Rucker, a Republican who sponsored the legislation that proposed the amendment, in September. Rucker said Tuesday that she was “proud that West Virginia’s voters chose to protect the integrity of our elections” by voting yes on the amendment, reported the West Virginia Watch. Critics of Kansas’s newly approved ballot measure worry it could make it harder for people to legally vote in the future. “The supermajority in our legislature has a documented history of attempting to restrict voting in various ways,” Amii Castle, a law professor at the University of Kansas, told the Kansas Reflector. “My concern is that they’re going to use that to justify or as a pretext to say, ‘Well, wait a minute. We amended our constitution. Now it says only citizens can vote, therefore, prove your citizenship. Bring your documents.’” This year’s ballot measures are the latest in a flurry of similar initiatives in recent years: Between 2018 and last year, states put 15 citizenship requirement measures on their ballots and voters approved all of them. Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org. Abdul El-Sayed: Michigan rejected ‘hateful, spiteful campaign’ after months of Republican attacks
articles.description: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed tells The Associated Press that voters have rejected a “hateful, spiteful campaign” after months of Republican attacks on his Muslim identity.
articles.content: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks to a crowd during a rally, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Kristen Norman)(Kristen Norman/AP Photo/Kristen Norman / FR171985 AP)WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed told The Associated Press on Wednesday that Michigan voters had rejected “a hateful, spiteful campaign” after months of Republican attacks on his Muslim identity in one of the nation’s most closely watched Senate races.El-Sayed said he was “running on adrenaline and caffeine” after his race with Republican Mike Rogers was called early Wednesday, giving Democrats another significant victory in a premier swing state as they won a substantial majority in the Senate in Tuesday’s midterms.Throughout the cycle, Republicans sought to demonize El-Sayed, who was born in the U.S. after his parents immigrated from Egypt. President Donald Trump repeatedly called him a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists.”“Michigan proved just how big we are. Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face,” El-Sayed said. “Michiganders rejected that. Every single county, every single one, pushed against that.”In a sign of how combative the race had become, Rogers and El-Sayed had not spoken as of Wednesday afternoon, even after Rogers issued a statement conceding the race. In 2024, Rogers called then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin to concede on Wednesday morning, before the AP had even called the race.El-Sayed, who will become the nation’s first Muslim senator, told the AP by phone that the morning was “a moment of reflection,” including about what his victory would mean to his two young daughters. His 3-year-old, he said, has no idea what happened, while his 8-year-old understands but sees it as normal.“Now, this is something they read about in the history books,” he said.With approximately 97% of the vote in, El-Sayed held a 7 percentage point lead over Rogers. Every county in the state shifted toward Democrats compared with 2024, according to AP voting data.The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of more than 4,500 voters in Michigan, showed that Michigan Senate voters were roughly split on whether El-Sayed’s views were “too extreme,” with about half saying they were.El-Sayed rose from a double-digit defeat eight years ago in the state's Democratic gubernatorial election to an upset victory of an establishment-backed candidate in the primary after being outspent by tens of millions. He said his campaign proved that “old-fashioned politics can work if you’re willing to do the work.”El-Sayed quickly pivoted, though, toward the future, saying his victory is “not the success” and that “the success is what you're able to do with the seat.”He would not commit to supporting Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer for another term, saying he did not yet know who else might run. Schumer is expected to retain the leadership position.“I do believe we need new leadership and I think people are hungry for it,” El-Sayed added.

articles.title: DuckDuckGo pitches itself to schools amid backlash over Google’s AI policy
articles.description: DuckDuckGo is courting schools frustrated by Google's AI restrictions, pointing educators to its search engine and options to disable AI features.
articles.content: DuckDuckGo is pitching itself to schools after Google created an opening for the alternative search engine. On Tuesday, Google told schools they could turn off Gemini, but it said shutting off its other AI features would cost schools Google Search, as well. DuckDuckGo, a company that focuses on user privacy by limiting data collection, clearly sees this as a moment to make inroads in education, where Google has historically dominated. According to figures Google has published in previous years, there are around 50 million Chromebooks in schools, used by students and educators, and its Google Classroom platform serves over 150 million users globally. On X, DuckDuckGo’s founder and CEO, Gabriel Weinberg, pointed to the company’s online documentation, explaining how schools can switch their default search engine to DuckDuckGo’s service instead, adding, “get in touch for help.” Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo’s chief public affairs officer, Kamyl Bazbaz, issued a stronger statement, writing, “Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong.” Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless.Prove Google wrong. https://t.co/Ta6ibmFdb9 In an email to TechCrunch, DuckDuckGo chastised Google for its decision, adding that Google could easily turn off Search’s AI features for schools if it wanted to. The company’s comments come as the American public is weighing how much AI they want to allow into their lives. As Tuesday night’s elections indicate, they don’t want AI data centers built in their towns. But using AI at work and school has become a common practice and requires a more nuanced discussion. Knowing that educators have struggled with AI, Google developed technology called “Guided Learning” that is meant to help kids learn by walking through problem-solving steps rather than just providing them with an answer. But educators are still asking for tools that let them remove AI from the learning process altogether. After the backlash on Tuesday, Google defended its decision, saying it was just responding to schools’ feedback. It said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search would be off by default, and schools could choose to enable them individually. We want to clarify what we announced today about our education services. Today’s announcements give schools more choice, not less. Here’s what we announced:– Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search will be OFF 🔴 by default. This is based on K-12 schools asking for more control… The problem, of course, is that Google Search now heavily uses AI, through AI Overviews and a conversational AI Mode that answers users’ queries. DuckDuckGo isn’t anti-AI, to be clear — it offers its own set of AI features, including a chat interface called Duck.ai and an AI search assistant. However, unlike Google, it provides options to disable these features in both its search and browser settings, the company says. It also offers a dedicated website, noai.duckduckgo.com, where AI-assisted answers, AI-generated images, and AI feature suggestions are all turned off. That flexibility may be driving demand for its services, as the company reported earlier this year that its app installs were up 30% as users rejected being force-fed Google’s AI Search. articles.title: Vance and Trump blame midterm GOP elections loss on their war in Iran
articles.description: The fingerpointing is coming from inside the house. Vice President JD Vance said in a lengthy social media post Wednesday that Republicans’ shellacking in the midterm elections the night before was mainly due to the administration’s war in Iran. Though Vance sought to soften the blow to President Donald Trump by ascribing the same opinion to […]
articles.content: Vice President JD Vance spoke May 18, 2026, about the importance of bringing manufacturing jobs back to the United States at the Milbank Manufacturing company in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)The fingerpointing is coming from inside the house. Vice President JD Vance said in a lengthy social media post Wednesday that Republicans’ shellacking in the midterm elections the night before was mainly due to the administration’s war in Iran. Though Vance sought to soften the blow to President Donald Trump by ascribing the same opinion to the president, the post was an unusual public distancing by a sitting vice president and marked a significant first step in a post-Trump Republican political landscape that Vance will likely seek to lead. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Vance served as a U.S. Marine in Iraq and later heavily criticized that Middle East war, calling it “an unforced disaster,” in a 2023 social media post. ‘Largely true’ Speaking to reporters Wednesday afternoon, Trump said Vance’s view was mostly correct. “I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” he said when asked about Vance’s post. “Probably it’s true. But at the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear” weapon. “I know how he feels about it,” he said later. “I thought it was fine.” He repeated that he’d expected the war to have a negative effect on the midterms, but that it was worth pursuing. Trump launched military operations in Iran in February, despite no apparent active threat from the Islamic republic. He promised the conflict would soon end, but when polls closed Tuesday night, it was still active and Iran maintained a block of the critical shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz that has squeezed the global supply of oil. 2028 message? Vance is seen as a frontrunner for the GOP presidential nomination in 2028, but Tuesday’s drubbing, in which Republicans lost Senate seats and governorships in states Trump and Vance carried by double digits in 2024 and ceded a large House majority to Democrats, could demonstrate a need to distance himself from Trump to stand a chance in the general election. In his post, Vance noted that Republicans’ problem on Tuesday was not turnout, but that many voters who supported the Republican ticket in 2024 flipped to Democrats this year. He said those voters identified four issues that drove their switch: end the war, focus on the cost of living, “Put America First” and change the United States’ “relationship to Israel.” “Our voters showed up,” he wrote. “And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats.” Vance also predicted calls would come for significant changes to immigration policy after some analysts said that an aggressive — sometimes deadly — enforcement campaign led to backlash among some Trump 2024 voters. Vance rejected any major overhaul, while again signaling some daylight between himself and Trump on the administration’s signature issue. “Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty,” he said. “I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.”

articles.title: Michigan election firsts: Muslim, LGBTQ, Democratic socialist wins
articles.description: In a series of firsts, Michigan will send a Muslim to the US Senate, Native American and openly gay members to the US House, a transgender woman to the state Legislature and more.
articles.content: Michigan’s midterm elections marked a number of historic firsts Voters elected country’s first Muslim US Senator in Abdul El-Sayed, state’s first openly gay US Representative in Jeremy Moss Benson, Brinks make history as first female duo to win governor, lieutenant governor. First transgender woman elected to state House LANSING — From the first all-female gubernatorial duo in state history to the nation’s first Muslim senator, Michigan voters on Tuesday elected candidates who made history in more ways than one. Propelled by record turnout for a midterm election and voter frustration with President Donald Trump, Democrats won big, sending majorities to Washington and a new governing “trifecta” to Lansing. “We showed the nation that in our democracy, the power of the people will always rule the day,” Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson said in her victory speech. Here’s a look at some of the historic firsts: State’s first all-female governor, lieutenant Benson and running mate Winnie Brinks became the state’s first all-female ticket to win election as governor and lieutenant governor, a milestone Benson touted in her victory speech. Related: How El-Sayed, Benson won Michigan: Big turnout, Democratic shifts Democrats take full control of Michigan government. What to expect Voters approve Proposal 2; opponents file lawsuit to try to block It Benson is also the first candidate to succeed a governor from her own party since the 1960s. The last to do so was John Swainson, in 1961, who succeeded G. Mennen “Soapy” Williams as the 42nd governor of Michigan. Benson will be the 50th, succeeding term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Nation’s first Muslim US Senator There’s been much ado about El-Sayed, whose win over Republican Mike Rogers made him the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate. But other notable wrinkles: He’ll take over a seat previously held by Michigan’s first Jewish US Senator, Carl Levin. Levin retired in 2014 and was succeeded by retiring US Sen. Gary Peters, D-Bloomfield Township.Donate US Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Holly, is also Jewish, meaning Michigan will now have its first ever Jewish/Muslim duo in the US Senate. Detroit House seats go full DSA For the first time ever, Detroit will be fully represented in the US House by Democratic socialists. Incumbent US Rep. Rashida Tlaib waltzed into a fifth term in office on Tuesday, winning her race against Republican James Hooper by roughly 55 percentage points. She’ll be joined in the US House by state Rep. Donavan McKinney, who beat incumbent Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar in the primary and on Tuesday defeated Republican TP Nykoriak by 57 points. Both Tlaib and McKinney are members of the Democratic Socialists of America. “My constituents voted for Democratic Socialism this election because they feel the devastation of corporate greed in their lives – poisonous air, unaffordable housing, job loss, lengthy power outages, medicaid cuts, and more,” McKinney said in a statement. First transgender woman in Michigan Legislature Democrat Joanna Whaley also made history Tuesday night by winning election to the state House, making her the first transgender woman elected to the serve in the Michigan Legislature. Whaley, who will represent the Downriver-based 2nd House District, is a Lincoln Park clergy member and clinical spiritual care provider who campaigned on lowering utility bills, medical debt relief and improving job training programs, among other things. The district is currently represented by Democratic state Rep. Tullio Liberati, who did not run for reelection. His brother Frank Liberati, also a former lawmaker, lost to Whaley in the August primary after unsuccessfully trying to force her to run under her birth name, which she had legally changed. Michigan’s first openly gay member of Congress State Sen. Jeremy Moss also made history by winning election to the US House. He’ll be the state’s first openly gay congressional lawmaker. Moss easily won election in the Oakland County-based 11th US House district. He succeeds outgoing US Rep. Haley Stevens, who ran for the US Senate but lost to El-Sayed in the primary. State’s first Native American in Congress State Sen. Sean McCann ousted US Rep. Bill Huizenga in Michigan’s 4th Congressional District and made history in the process. The Kalamazoo Democrat is believed to be Michigan’s first ever Native American in Congress. He’s a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation and has said he learned of his Native ancestry as an adult.
