articles.title: Michigan Dems flip three US House seats as Huizenga, Barrett fall
articles.description: Michigan Democrats flip three US House seats, ousting GOP Reps. Bill Huizenga and Tom Barrett in the process.
articles.content: Michigan Democrats won all three of the state’s ‘toss up’ US House races in the midterm election In the process, two GOP incumbents were ousted: Tom Barrett in the 7th District and Bill Huizenga in the 4th District Democrats also picked up 10th District seat held by John James, who ran for governor rather than seek reelection to Congress LANSING — Michigan Democrats flipped three US House seats in Tuesday’s midterm election, ousting incumbent Republican Reps. Bill Huizenga and Tom Barrett in the process. Sean McCann’s victory over Huizenga in southwest Michigan’s 4th Congressional District and Will Lawrence’s win over Barrett in mid-Michigan’s 7th District helped solidify a Democratic majority in the House for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term. Democrat Christina Hines also defeated Republican Mike Bouchard to win the Macomb County-based 10th District seat held by John James, who lost his bid for governor. In a statement, Hines said she “could not be more excited to get to work” on things like lowering costs and fighting to “ensure everyone has access to affordable, quality healthcare.” Related: Michigan election results: Governor, Senate, US House, proposals, more Michigan governor’s race election results: Jocelyn Benson vs. John James Michigan US Senate election results: Abdul El-Sayed vs Mike Rogers Barrett, in a statement released mid-day Wednesday, said he had conceded the race to Lawrence shortly after 2 am, adding that he was “disappointed in the outcome” but proud of his team and campaign. Bouchard also conceded to Hines early Wednesday, before the vote tallies were finalized. Huizenga had not yet publicly acknowledged defeat when the Associated Press called his race at 1:13 p.m. The results mean Democrats will hold a nine out of the state’s 13 congressional seats next term, ending what had been a 7-6 GOP advantage. Barrett and Huizenga join another ousted incumbent this cycle: Detroit Democrat Shri Thanedar lost in the primary to state Rep. Donovan McKinney, who easily won election on Tuesday because the 13th District is considered one of the most progressive in the nation. In other races, Democratic state Sen. Jeremy Moss won Oakland County’s 11th District, which incumbent Democrat Haley Stevens vacated to unsuccessfully run for US Senate. Donate Several incumbents also won reelection, including Democrats Debbie Dingell of Ann Arbor and Rashida Tlaib of Detroit, as well as Republicans Tim Walberg of Tipton, John Moolenaar of Caledonia and Jack Bergman of Watersmeet. Here’s what to know about the three seats Democrats flipped: 4th District Huizenga, a Zeeland Republican, served in the US House since 2011, which should have given him an incumbent’s advantage as he sought reelection to a ninth term. But McCann, a Kalamazoo Democrat, benefited from name recognition because he has represented parts of southwest Michigan in the state Legislature on and off since 2011. Like many other Democratic nominees this election season, McCann had sought to play up Huizenga’s ties to Trump while Huizenga has positioned himself as a workhorse focused on affordability. “This victory belongs to the people all across Southwest Michigan, and it’s the people that I will work every day to serve — to take on the corruption and policies shortchanging our families, and work with anyone to make life better and protect the American Dream for our children,” McCann said in a victory statement. “Michigan families deserve nothing less, and I look forward to getting right to work for the people of this district.” 7th District Lawrence bested Barrett in a mid-Michigan district that experts had called a bellwether for national control of a US House, where Republicans held a four-seat advantage ahead of Nov. 3. But that advantage is now gone. Democrats flipped 29 seats nationally, including Barrett’s. Race results in some contests are still pending, though Democrats are certain to have a chamber majority. The politically purple 7th District includes Clinton, Shiawassee, Ingham and Livingston counties and parts of Eaton and Oakland counties. Lawrence, a progressive Democrat and community organizer who beat out two centrist candidates in the August primary, campaigned against high prices, the Iran War and data centers in an attempt to woo voters angry with Trump — and by extension Barrett. Barrett, meanwhile, sought to distance himself from Trump while describing Lawrence’s past support for defunding the police and loosening immigration restrictions as “extreme” and too far left. Lawrence’s win represents a key victory for progressive Democrats. Despite his primary win, some onlookers had openly wondered whether a progressive could succeed in the general election, which wound up becoming one of the most expensive US House races in the nation this cycle. “We built an unprecedented movement here in Mid-Michigan, powered by thousands of volunteers, and we showed that you can beat an incumbent Republican without taking a dime of corporate PAC money,” Lawrence said in a statement. He added: “Our people-powered movement took on the richest and most powerful people in the world, and we won.” 10th District Hines beat Bouchard in the 10th District, a politically diverse region spanning southern Macomb County and the Oakland County communities of Rochester and Rochester Hills. In a victory statement sent just before 4 am Wednesday, Hines said she “could not be more excited to get to work” in the US House. “I’ll work to lower costs, ensure everyone has access to affordable, quality healthcare, and fight against the corruption in DC so that Congress starts delivering real results for working people,” she said. “My responsibility will always be to the people of this district, and no matter if you voted for me or not, I look forward to serving you.” James won the district by six percentage points as an incumbent in 2024, but his decision to run for governor created an open lane for a newcomer from either major party. Hines, a former prosecuting attorney in Macomb and Oakland counties, had campaigned on eliminating tariffs, lowering health care costs and getting corporate money out of politics. Bouchard, a US Army veteran and son of Oakland County Sheriff Mike Bouchard, ran on promises to prioritize border security, strengthen the US military and levy tariffs on other countries (excluding Canada) in hopes of boosting Michigan manufacturers. Even before the race was called by the Associated Press on Wednesday, Bouchard congratulated Hines on her victory in a statement posted to Facebook just before 4:30 a.m. “I pray for her and her family as they step up to represent us all,” Bouchard wrote.

articles.title: Most expensive House race, most doors knocked: How William Lawrence won
articles.description: In a news conference Wednesday outside of his Michigan Avenue election offices, William Lawrence said he took a concession call from U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett early in the morning and […]
articles.content: In a news conference Wednesday outside of his Michigan Avenue election offices, William Lawrence said he took a concession call from U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett early in the morning and is getting ready to take office. Lawrence won a tight race, which he said was the most expensive House race in the nation, against U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett. Secretary of State results show Lawrence winning with 51% of the vote to Barrett’s 47.7%. “We showed that you can beat an incumbent Republican in a hotly contested frontline race without taking a dime of corporate PAC money,” Lawrence said. He said getting money out of politics would be one of his priorities. Inn a Facebook post Wednesday afternoon, Barrett acknowledged disappointment in the loss and also cited the spending in the race, “the most spending against me of any Republican member of Congress in the nation, we came closer than any competitive district in the country.” Lawrence said his campaign knocked on more doors than any other in the nation – 250,000 in the general election and 100,000 in the primary – and he credited more than 1,000 door-knockers with pushing his message across the finish line. “They spent more against me than any House campaign in the country,” Lawrence said. Lawrence’s campaign rejected PAC funding, which he said – in a later conference call with the Congressional Progressive Caucus – was another key. Data centers erupted as an issue during the campaign, Lawrence said. “Because we weren’t taking any corporate tech money from PACS, we were able to respond to residents and make it a cornerstone of our campaign,” Lawrence said. Several data center proposals came up during the campaign, including for downtown Lansing and Mason as well as a Delhi Township proposal that was floated a week before Election Day. Lawrence made an appearance and spoke at a crowded town meeting on Friday, days before the election. Lawrence will be joining a progressive caucus that swelled in the Tuesday vote. U.S. Rep. Greg Casar said, on a call with newly-elected candidates including Lawrence, that the progressive ranks will grow by at least 25 House members and end up with more than 100. Casar said progressives leveraged good positions but, critically, did tremendous outreach and he cited Lawrence, who recognized the biggest door-knockers. Casar said Lawrence’s father was #2 and Lawrence said the top door-knocker went to an average of 60 doors a day for 90 days. Casar said progressives won big and led the way in the national election results by forcing votes on a war powers resolution, which more moderate Democrats leveraged as well, and bringing wildly popular issues like controlling AI and opposing data centers to the forefront. Will Lawrence declares win in one of nation’s most-watched U.S House races “This is a mandate for dramatic change,” Casar said. “But it is not a sign that all of Democrat’s problems are solved. This is not an endorsement of tinkering around the edges. This people is giving Dems a shot to show them. We’ve seen how a party can go from a big victory to crushing defeat if they sell out and refuse to deliver.” Lawrence said one of his priorities will be constituent services and setting up an office. He said he plans to keep the campaign office on Michigan Avenue, but will need to sign a new lease. Asked if he thought Tuesday’s vote was a mandate against Trump or for Democrats, Lawrence said the president is clearly unpopular and has done many things to make life more difficult for Americans. “All he’s done over the last two years is make things more difficult, diminish our national standing around the world, set us at odds with each other while making everything more expensive. We have work to do to bring people back together, here from the bottom up, who have been torn apart. We’ve got a mandate to deliver on affordable housing and health care and ending the war to lower the cost of all of our commodities.” In the CPC call, he gave a similar answer: “We have a sweeping mandate around the entire country and we have a duty to pass bills in the House and Senate, to end the distarous war and invest in housing we can afford and protect Social Security.” Gallery: William Lawrence election watch party U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett watch party gallery

articles.title: Jocelyn Benson lays out priorities as she prepares to lead Michigan’s new Democratic trifecta
articles.description: Few details were offered as the governor-elect begins putting together a transition team and plan for her first 100 days in office.
articles.content: "Kids and their future will be a central part of my vision for our state as a mom," Governor-Elect Jocelyn Benson said Wednesday. "And so you will continue to see us amplifying the needs for our young people in the state, making sure they are protected, safe and above all, have an opportunity to thrive in whatever they want to do."(Adam Yahya Rayes / Michigan Public)Three things are at the top of Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson’s priority list as she prepares to take Michigan’s top office in January: unity, economic growth, and public schools.“Today, we will begin identifying where we can deliver quick relief in the early days of our new term, beginning with the bills families feel every month,” Benson said in a post-election news conference Wednesday, one day after defeating Republican John James. “Together, we will deliver on our plans to create well-paying jobs in the state, strengthen Michigan's workforce, and make sure every kid is college or career ready when they graduate any public school in the state.”Democrats won back control of Michigan’s House and expanded their majority in the Senate in the general election.Benson’s running mate, Grand Rapids Democrat Winnie Brinks, is the current Michigan Senate majority leader. There’s been a lot of friction between her chamber and the Republican-led House, but Brinks said she still sees a path to a “productive” last few months of this legislative session“Real progress doesn't come from one office or one party alone. It comes when people sit down at the same table and focus on what works for the families that we serve,” Brinks said. “I'm ready to partner with anyone in either party in either chamber to get things done for Michigan and turn Governor-Elect Benson's agenda into real results for people.”Benson said she looks to move past the “hateful rhetoric in this election” and is willing to work with Republicans at all levels of government. Her predecessor, Gretchen Whitmer, has had an unusually cordial relationship with Republican President Donald Trump in his second term.“I will work with anyone to provide relief for the people of Michigan, including President Trump and the federal government,” Benson said. “If we can work together to protect the people of Michigan from the harm that these tariffs have caused, I would love to and I'm open to that.”Benson reiterated her commitment to opening up the office to Freedom of Information Act requests. State law shields the governor from those requests, but Benson said she plans to willingly open her office to requests.Benson said her campaign will release more details about her transition team and plans for the first 100 days in office in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Money out of Politics ballot measure faces First Amendment challenge
articles.description: The Mackinac Center for Public Policy argues provisions of the proposal violate the First Amendment. It filed a federal lawsuit Tuesday evening.
articles.content: According to the Michigan Secretary of State, more than 1.2 million Michiganders have already voted in the general election.138,000 cast early in-person ballots over the weekend. (Steve Carmody / Michigan Public )Less than 24 hours after voters overwhelmingly approved a ballot measure to limit election spending in Michigan, the Mackinac Center for Public Policy has filed a lawsuit to block it.The non-profit, free-market think tank argues parts of the proposal violate the First Amendment. Its lawsuit asks a federal judge to block parts of the proposal, not overturn it entirely.More than 80% of Michigan voters supported the measure in Tuesday’s election.“We think that the law needs to be defined and its scope understood rather quickly,” said Patrick Wright, the Mackinac Center’s Vice President for Legal Affairs. “We don’t care to be on the receiving end of a criminal complaint, we want to make sure and understand what is and isn’t legal as soon as possible. And that applies for all 10 million Michigan citizens.”Maura Cowley, campaign manager for Michiganders for Money out of Politics, the group that supported the ballot proposal, said the lawsuit didn't come as a surprise."We are prepared for the challenge, we feel confident about Proposal 2 moving forward," Cowley said Wednesday on Stateside. "We’re also just taking a moment to just celebrate the historic win.”A spokesperson for the Michigan Secretary of State's office said the office couldn't comment on pending litigation.The proposal would prohibit regulated state utility companies and their executives from donating to campaigns for many Michigan offices or political action committees. Wright said the Mackinac Center is not challenging that provision of Proposal 2.Instead, the Center is asking a federal judge to prohibit the state from enforcing the proposal’s reporting requirements around “electioneering communications” within 100 days of an election.The Mackinac Center argues in its lawsuit that, though it does not endorse candidates or issues, some of its research and advocacy could be labeled “electioneering communications” under the proposal, which would force the Center to disclose a donor list to the state.“Mackinac has historically been free to discuss candidates within the context of its issue-focused advocacy,” the center argues in its complaint. “Now Mackinac will have to consider the risks and burdens from the disclosure requirements when deciding whether to refer to a candidate, even just indirectly, in its public communications. Mackinac will likely refrain from referring to some candidates to minimize the amount of disclosure required.”The Mackinac Center argues the reporting provisions would require it to list the names of all of its supporters, violating their privacy.It’s also asking a federal judge to block the state from forcing it to disclose its finances as a “political committee.”The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan by the Institute for Free Speech, which is representing the Mackinac Center.

The election is over. What’s supposed to happen next for Congress?
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Voting ended Tuesday in this year’s midterm elections, leaving officials and volunteers counting tens of millions of ballots to determine which U.S. House and Senate candidates will take the oath of office in January. The post-election process includes numerous steps and varying deadlines for when ballots have to be certified, since each state […]
articles.content: The U.S. Capitol on Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — Voting ended Tuesday in this year’s midterm elections, leaving officials and volunteers counting tens of millions of ballots to determine which U.S. House and Senate candidates will take the oath of office in January. The post-election process includes numerous steps and varying deadlines for when ballots have to be certified, since each state has different laws governing not only what happens on Election Day but what happens afterward. Once local and state election officials wrap up their work, the process moves to Congress, which has its own rules and procedures. The Constitution also gives the House and Senate final say over whether to seat someone. Here’s a look at what’s next and where issues could arise, aside from lawsuits that may be filed or already in progress. When will there be official results? Counting ballots and certifying the results takes at least a week in most states, often longer. Kyle Yoder, research director at The Center for Election Innovation & Research, said that is exactly the type of deliberative process voters should want and expect. He also cautioned the results news organizations report in the hours and sometimes days after Nov. 3 aren’t final totals. “Results aren’t official until every ballot has been counted by every eligible voter,” he said. “That process takes time, and when you sit back and think about it, you want it to take time because what we want is for that count to be correct, for it to be accurate, for it to be complete.” Yoder added that the “biggest point of confusion that we run into when we’re talking to voters about all this is they think the results they’re seeing on their TV on election night are the final results.” The Associated Press, which many news organizations look to for race calls, explains how its experts decide when to announce a winner and when to wait for more ballots to be counted. The Election Law Program, a collaborative effort between William & Mary Law School and the National Center for State Courts, has timelines for the various state deadlines. How long can states take to recount ballots? After election officials certify the first count of ballots, especially close races can head into a recount. Some state laws require it automatically if the margin of victory is under a certain percentage. In other circumstances, specific people can request a recount, typically the runner-up, though some state laws allow voters or even political parties to request another count. “In many states, election recounts, legal challenges to the results, etcetera, can only begin once results have been certified,” Yoder said. “So it is in the interest of politicians who may be saber-rattling to allow certification to happen, so that they can begin those recounts, legal challenges.” States have various deadlines for how long those recounts can last. But they can drag on amid lawsuits and Congress has the authority in some cases to conduct its own recount. Who decides which candidate wins an election and can the official decide not to send a certificate of election to Congress? James Alcorn, senior director of the Election Law Program at the William & Mary Law School, said “it depends” on the state law, but that statewide races are typically certified by a secretary of state or a state board of elections. “For an office that is not statewide, that may be certified at a local level, and in some states, congressional races are going to be similar,” he said. There are very few modern examples of a local or state election official not sending a certificate of election before the new Congress convenes in early January. And those were due to ongoing lawsuits. New York Republican Rep. Claudia Tenney wasn’t sworn in until February 2021, more than three months after the election, amid a lawsuit over the outcome. The election was ultimately resolved when a state Supreme Court justice ordered election officials to certify the race and her opponent decided not to appeal the decision. Following an especially contentious election in North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District in 2018, the state board of elections decided not to certify either candidate as the winner and called for a special election. That seat had no representative in the U.S. House from early January until September. It took nearly eight months following the 2008 election for Democratic Sen. Al Franken to join the upper chamber of Congress amid a legal fight over the vote tally that ended at the Minnesota Supreme Court. What happens once a state sends the certificate of election to the House or Senate? The House Clerk uses the certificates to compile the list of members-elect that is used on the first day of the new Congress to determine who can vote for Speaker. Once that first step is complete, members normally take their oaths and move on to other matters. Certificates of election must be sent to the Secretary of the Senate before newly elected or reelected members can take their oath in early January. “After the opening prayer and recitation of the pledge, the vice president of the United States, who serves as the president of the Senate, announces the receipt of certificates,” according to a post from the Senate Historical Office. “Following established tradition, senators-elect are then escorted down the center aisle of the Senate Chamber to the presiding officer’s desk.” Only newly elected or reelected senators, about one-third of the chamber, are sworn in since it’s what’s known as a “continuing body.” That’s a very different set of rules than in the House, where every lawmaker typically takes the oath on the first day. Can either chamber of Congress refuse to seat someone with a certificate of election? Yes. The Constitution grants each chamber of Congress the power to be the “Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members.” The Federal Contested Elections Act, a 1960s law, gives the House Administration Committee the ability to investigate the results of certain elections and make a recommendation to the full chamber about which candidate to seat. The law, which doesn’t apply to the Senate, gives the committee the authority to accept the certified results from election officials or conduct its own recount. Any recommendation would need to be approved or rejected by a majority vote on the House floor. Complaints have been filed under the FCEA several times during the past few decades, including after the 2020 election, when Iowa Democratic candidate Rita Hart asked the House to decide whether Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks won the race. The panel investigated for months before Hart withdrew the complaint in April 2021. A report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service says that “FCEA contests rarely change election results, as doing so typically requires the House to overturn a state-certified election result.” There is a separate process on the first day of a new Congress that allows any member-elect to object to another member-elect taking the oath. Texas Republican Rep. Chip Roy tried this unsuccessfully in January 2021. It was rejected following a 371-2 vote of members-elect who had yet to take their oaths. Roy voted in favor of the resolution, which directed the speaker “to administer the oath of office to all Representatives-elect.” The Senate also holds the ability to look into and ultimately decide the winner of a contested election, likely through the Rules and Administration Committee. The chamber’s official website on disputed elections notes that “a senator with the proper credentials against whom a challenge had been filed would be seated ‘without prejudice.’” “Under this arrangement, if a committee investigation later determined that for some reason the individual was not entitled to a seat, he could be ‘excluded’ from the Senate by a simple majority vote, as opposed to having to be expelled, which required a two-thirds majority,” the webpage continues. The post later adds that the Senate historically has not intervened “where legal action in the federal or state courts was appropriate, and it seldom took very seriously the claims of a contestant who had failed to follow these avenues of redress. “Similarly, when a losing candidate demanded a recount of ballots, the Senate preferred to become involved only if the state law made no provision for such a recount. Still, in some cases the Senate felt impelled to act, and the sealed ballot boxes were shipped to Washington where staff members, carefully observed by representatives of both candidates, scrutinized the ballots and election records for possible irregularities.”

articles.title: Jocelyn Benson is Michigan’s next governor. Here’s what education will look like in her administration.
articles.description: Jocelyn Benson, Michigan secretary of state, will take the reins from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, whose second term is expiring.
articles.content: Michigan voters have elected a new governor, Jocelyn Benson, who promises to transform education and guarantee that when students graduate from the public school system, they are college and career ready. This story also appeared in Chalkbeat Detroit The Associated Press called the race between Benson and U.S. Rep. John James at 1:45 a.m. The results show Benson winning with 55% of the vote. Benson, the daughter of special education teachers, has a plan for addressing the state’s current literacy crisis by taking steps similar to what the state already has been doing: Investing in curriculum and training for teachers based on the science of reading, a longstanding body of research about how children learn to read. Her education plan says she would also “enable statewide tracking of literacy rates and improvements.” Benson would also ensure first-year teachers receive starting salaries of $60,000 a year minimum. Currently, the average in Michigan is around $41,000 annually. What she calls her “Michigan Education Guarantee,” which she touted as she campaigned, would be an ambitious promise, particularly when it comes to college readiness. Just 24% of students met the SAT’s rigorous definition of being college ready on the exam taken earlier this year. Benson will take office in the midst of an education crisis in Michigan. Just 44% of Michigan students in grades 3-8 were proficient in reading on the Michigan Student Test of Educational Progress, according to results released in August. The proficiency rate for third graders on the exam was at its lowest level in the 12-year history of the M-STEP. Meanwhile, Michigan ranks 42nd in the nation in education in the most recent Kids Count report. She and James have opposing views on many education issues. For instance, James said on his first day as governor, he would sign on to the federal scholarship tax credit program. Benson said opting in would be reckless, citing a lack of clear guidance for how the program will be implemented. James favors bringing back a law requiring schools to retain third graders struggling with reading. Benson says teachers are the ones who should be making calls about retention. Here’s what Michigan can expect on education in Benson’s administration. A right to a world-class education In addition to her Michigan Guarantee, Benson says she will push to establish a constitutional right to “a world-class education for every young Michigander.” She said this would give parents and educators with “an enforceable pathway to hold lawmakers accountable to our education excellence goals.” Expanding early childhood education and tax cuts to pay for childcare Benson would expand Michigan’s PreK for All program, which provides free preschool for 4-year-olds, regardless of their family’s income, to 3-year-olds. She plans to Increase the availability of high-quality childcare by streamlining the approval and certification process. And she says she will ensure increased pay for early childhood workers. Tax cuts for parents paying for childcare are also part of Benson’s plan. “I believe childcare costs need to go down if we’re going to improve education and give our kids a good start and support the hardworking parents who are supporting their kids,” Benson said during an Oct. 6 gubernatorial debate with James. A funding system focused on student needs Benson has said she believes Michigan’s schools have been underfunded for years. She wants a system that is focused on funding student needs. She favors the weighted funding system, which lawmakers have experimented with in recent years and codified into state law this year, because it provides additional funding for students who need greater resources, such as students from low-income homes and students who are English language learners. She also plans to stop the practice of Michigan lawmakers funding higher education out of the School Aid Act, which advocates say was intended solely for K-12 schools. She would do that by creating separate funding for the state’s colleges and universities. She wants to mandate that if lawmakers fail to enact a state budget by the required July 1 deadline, an inflation-adjusted version of the previous year’s education budget would go into effect. Improving outcomes for students with disabilities Multiple pieces of Benson’s education plan focus on students with disabilities. She wants to create a strategic plan “for how Michigan will improve the education level and employment rates … so that they are able to thrive,” she says in her plan. She’ll create an independent state office that will have the authority to provide advocacy support and resolve disputes between families of children with disabilities and school districts. She also plans to fix funding for special education, citing in her plan an overhaul proposed by the Autism Alliance of Michigan. Creating an education cabinet Governors usually have a cabinet made up of the heads of key state agencies and departments. Benson would create a separate cabinet focused on education. The cabinet would include the heads of the Department of Education, the Department of Lifelong Education, Advancement, and Potential, the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity, and the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, her plan says. This cabinet will be focused on using disaggregated student data to set a statewide strategy aimed at improving schools. Lori Higgins is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat Detroit. You can reach her at lhiggins@chalkbeat.org. Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

Blue wave washes over Michigan as Dems flip key congressional battlegrounds
articles.description: The success of Democrats across the nation in Tuesday’s election manifested itself squarely in Michigan’s congressional delegation, which saw three districts change hands from Republicans to Democrats. What had been a 7-6 GOP majority has now been reversed to a 9-4 Democratic advantage starting in 2027. Here are the unofficial results from the U.S. House […]
articles.content: A "Vote Here" sign on Nov. 3, 2026, outside of Bethlehem Lutheran Church in Lansing, Mich., one of several local polling places in Ingham County. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)The success of Democrats across the nation in Tuesday’s election manifested itself squarely in Michigan’s congressional delegation, which saw three districts change hands from Republicans to Democrats. What had been a 7-6 GOP majority has now been reversed to a 9-4 Democratic advantage starting in 2027. Here are the unofficial results from the U.S. House races across Michigan’s 13 congressional districts: 1st Congressional District Fending off a push from Democrats at the local and national level, U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Watersmeet) won a sixth term. In a rematch against Traverse City Attorney Callie Barr, Bergman had won over 53.2% of voters when the Associated Press called the race at 1:09 a.m. Wednesday, while Barr received 44.7%. 2nd Congressional District Emerging victorious against Marine Corps veteran Ben Ambrose, U.S. Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Caledonia) will serve a seventh term in the U.S. House of Representatives. According to unofficial results from the Associated Press at 10:45 p.m. Tuesday, Moolenaar received 62.9% of the vote, while Ambrose received 35.8% 3rd Congressional District U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids) has defeated former broadcast meteorologist Terri DeBoer, winning a third term as representative for Michigan’s 3rd Congressional District. Unofficial results at 12:54 a.m. Wednesday showed Scholten with 57.3% of the vote while DeBoer received 41.2%. 4th Congressional District Building on gains in 2022, Democrats have continued to make headway in Western Michigan as state Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo) claimed victory Wednesday against U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Holland Township) for his seat in Congress. Who is Hakeem Jeffries? Meet the likely first Black speaker of the US House. Unofficial results from the Associated Press, which finally called the race at 1:13 p.m. Wednesday, show McCann had 50.1% of the vote while Huizenga received 48.3%. McCann will conclude his time in the state Legislature and serve as representative for the state’s 4th Congressional District, which includes Allegan and Van Buren counties, and portions of Ottawa, Kalamazoo, Calhoun and Berrien counties. “I am honored and humbled that the people of Southwest Michigan have put their trust in me to represent and serve this amazing district,” McCann said in a statement. “Thank you to the voters, and to every volunteer and supporter who knocked on doors and made phone calls, talked to their neighbors, and helped out in ways big and small. I will be forever grateful for your support, because you are the heart and soul of this campaign. And thank you to Congressman Bill Huizenga for his years of service to our community.” 5th Congressional District U.S. Rep. Tim Walberg (R-Tipton) was easily reelected for a ninth term. Unofficial results show Walberg bested educator and labor organizer Christian Vukasovich with 64.4% of the vote, according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press, which called the race at 11:11 p.m Tuesday. 6th Congressional District Voters overwhelmingly reelected U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) for a seventh term. Dingell defeated her Republican challenger, Heather Smiley, with 71.8% of the vote according to unofficial results. Smiley received 25.8%. 7th Congressional District In a tight race for Michigan’s politically purple 7th Congressional District, Lansing area political organizer William Lawrence declared himself the victor against incumbent Congressman Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte). Return of the trifecta: Michigan Democrats reclaim full control of state government Lawrence’s campaign shared their proclamation of victory at 2:49 a.m. Wednesday, with the Associated Press finally calling the race at 2:05 p.m. The final tally, with 97% of the votes counted, had Lawrence at 51% and Barrett at 47.7% While Barrett was leading through most of the evening and into the night, Lawrence’s campaign began making gains in the early hours of the morning. Barrett departed his election night watch party at 2:39 a.m. without speaking to the media. As of 6:29 a.m., Lawrence was leading by 3.2 percentage points. “We built an unprecedented movement here in Mid-Michigan, powered by thousands of volunteers, and we showed that you can beat an incumbent Republican without taking a dime of corporate PAC money,” Lawrence said in a statement. “We united people from every corner of this district – and found common ground in opposition to war and data centers, and in favor of good housing and healthcare, social security, jobs and education. Our people-powered movement took on the richest and most powerful people in the world, and we won.” 8th Congressional District U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City) defeated retired GM engineer Thomas Smith, winning a second term in the House of Representatives. First elected in 2024, McDonald Rivet received 54.4% of the vote according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press at 1:48 a.m. Wednesday, while Smith received 43%. While the 8th Congressional District was a key target for Republicans and Democrats in 2024, Smith was never a serious threat to McDonald Rivet’s reelection chances, having won the GOP primary despite dropping out just weeks before. 9th Congressional District U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township) will serve a fourth term in Congress, with unofficial results at 11:45 p.m. Tuesday showing she defeated CNC Machinist Ray Pooley with 61.7% of the vote. McClain serves as the U.S. House Republican conference chair. 10th Congressional District In the early hours Wednesday morning, former prosecutor Christina Hines announced her victory over Army National Guard veteran Michael Bouchard Jr. While Hines declared victory at 3:52 a.m., the Associated Press officially called the race shortly before 12:30 Wednesday afternoon with unofficial results showing Hines with 52.4% of the vote to 45.3% for Bouchard. The district is currently held by U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), who opted against seeking reelection to run for governor, which was unsuccessful, as he lost to Democrat Jocelyn Benson. Encompassing southern Macomb County, the district also includes Rochester and Rochester Hills in eastern Oakland County. A former prosecutor in Wayne and Washtenaw counties, Hines focused her campaign on bringing down costs, emphasizing that as a mother of three and a Macomb county resident, she understood the hardship families in the district are facing. “This campaign started with a simple truth: that working families in our district are sick of being left behind by corrupt politicians in Washington and deserve someone who will actually put their needs first,” Hines said in a statement. “Over the last 18 months, I have been moved by the thousands of people who have told me their stories, shared their struggles, and demanded more from their leaders. Your words have stayed with me throughout this entire campaign and I will carry them with me to Washington.” Hines’ win is one of three GOP-held congressional districts in Michigan to flip to Democratic control. Democrat William Lawrence declared victory in the 7th Congressional District early Wednesday over incumbent Republican Congressman Tom Barrett of Charlotte and state Sen. Sean McCann did the same against his opponent, incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga of Holland Township. 11th Congressional District Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield) emerged victorious against Troy Mayor Ethan Baker, receiving 59.6% of the vote, according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press at 9:33 p.m. Tuesday. Moss, the state’s first openly gay state senator, will be Michigan’s first openly LGBTQ+ representative in Congress. He will succeed U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), who unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate and then stunned Democrats when she endorsed Republican Mike Rogers just days before the election. In a statement celebrating his victory, Moss said Michiganders need a Congress that can put a check on the president. “I will work hard every day to lower costs, protect and expand our healthcare, dismantle ICE, and hold the Trump administration accountable,” Moss said. 12th Congressional District U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit) will serve a fifth term in Congress, easily defeating Republican James Hooper, who she previously faced in 2024. Unofficial results from the Associated Press at 9:33 p.m. Tuesday, show Tlaib with 84.8% of the vote and Hooper with 12.7%. 13th Congressional District State Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) will succeed U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar to represent Michigan’s 13th Congressional District. McKinney defeated Republican T.P. Nykoriak with 75.5% of the vote, according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press, which called the race at 10:33 p.m. Tuesday. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel congratulated McKinney on his victory in a statement. “As a labor organizer and state representative, Donavan has the values and experience we need to fight and deliver for Detroiters in the halls of Congress. His leadership will be key to making the wealthy pay their fair share, expanding access to healthcare and housing, and making sure every Michigander has a fair shot, no matter their zip code.” The Working Families Party, a minor political party backing progressive candidates, also cheered McKinney’s victory. “WFP champion Donavan McKinney defeated a sitting Congressman in the primary, despite millions in spending from corporate and crypto interests,” Branden Snyder, state director for the Michigan Working Families Party, said in a statement. “ Now he’s heading to Congress to fight for the community that raised him. We know that Donavan will fight with everything he has to protect the rights of workers and unions, stand up to corporate greed, and bring back investments to Michigan’s 13th Congressional District.”

articles.title: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test
articles.description: It won't win the specs race, but it will actually fit in your hand.
articles.content: The first modern smartphones had 3.5-inch screens, which can be hard to remember in today's world of gargantuan glass slabs. Sure, people talk about wanting smaller phones, but will they buy one? Enough Phone is betting they will. The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics. The company's cheeky name is reflected in its approach to phone design. A flagship killer this is not, but it's probably "enough" for most people. It has a mid-range MediaTek processor, a single rear-facing camera, a polycarbonate body, and a fingerprint sensor in the power button. Specs at a glance: Enough Phone ($399 for a limited time, $599 MSRP) SoC MediaTek Dimensity 7500 Memory 8GB Storage 128GB with microSD Display 5.3-inch 1520x720 HD+ LCD Cameras Sony IMX766 50 MP, 32 MP selfie Software Android 17 or OdysseyOS Battery 3500 mAh (removable) Connectivity 5G, LTE, Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth, NFC, SIM+eSIM Measurements 133×64×12 mm With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone. While it's a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini. Thinness takes a hit, as the designers have opted to make the battery user-replaceable. Like the Fairphone, you'll just have to remove a few screws to get the back cover off.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Progress against neglected tropical diseases requires sustained action
articles.content: The World Health Organization (WHO) today reported major global progress against neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), with 63 countries having eliminated at least one NTD by June 2026, up from 42 at the end of 2020. WHO’s Global report on neglected tropical diseases 2026, a midterm assessment of the 2021–2030 NTD road map, shows that more countries are eliminating NTDs and fewer people need treatment. Findings reveal that the number of people requiring interventions fell to 1.41 billion in 2024, down 36% since 2010 and 19% since 2020. Cases of sleeping sickness have dropped by 98% since 1999, while Guinea worm disease fell to a record low of just 10 human cases in 2025. “Elimination of neglected tropical diseases is one of the standout success stories of global health," said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “However, the hard-won gains we have made could easily be lost, so countries and partners must step up, not step back, by increasing domestic financing, sustaining external support and integrating NTD services into primary health care. The goal is not only to eliminate diseases, but to free communities from disability, disfigurement, death and generational poverty.” Advances in science offer new tools to prevent and treat NTDs, such as WHO-prequalified child-friendly arpraziquantel for schistosomiasis, generic miltefosine for leishmaniasis and a dengue vaccine. Two chikungunya vaccines and new medicines for onchocerciasis and human African trypanosomiasis have also received regulatory approval. While the report signals major progress against many diseases, it also highlights uneven progress and shows that these diseases continue to disproportionately affect the world’s poorest and most vulnerable communities. Dengue cases reached a record 15.1 million in 2024, deaths from vector-borne NTDs have risen, and yaws eradication is off track. Only three disease-specific indicators reached their 2025 milestones. Gaps in comprehensive and timely data , including data disaggregated by gender, also make progress difficult to measure. International development assistance for NTDs remains highly concentrated, with a small number of donors accounting for nearly 80% of the total between 2018 and 2024. This concentration has made NTD programmes particularly vulnerable to abrupt reductions in support, which have disrupted mass treatment, case management, surveillance and vector control, and put donated medicines at risk of expiring. Overall, resources available for NTDs remain 30% below pre-COVID-19 levels, and dedicated funding for some programmes has all but disappeared. At the same time, countries are demonstrating how progress can be made more sustainable. More countries where NTDs are prevalent are mainstreaming NTDs into national health strategies, essential service packages, and domestic budgets. Efforts to improve efficiency by delivering interventions for several NTDs through shared services are also gaining ground: the number of countries adopting the WHO-recommended skin NTD strategy has already exceeded the 2030 target. The report concludes that faster and sustained action will be needed to meet the 2030 targets, while recognizing the progress achieved despite limited resources. It calls on affected countries to increase domestic financing and integrate NTD interventions into universal health coverage and adapt programmes to conflict settings and climate change where needed. It also calls on donors to broaden their support across NTD interventions, and on recipient countries to diversify their funding sources to reduce dependency and vulnerability. With five years remaining to 2030, accelerated action is needed to protect fragile gains and close persistent gaps. Neglected tropical diseases are associated with devastating health, social and economic consequences. Their burden is mainly experienced in impoverished communities. Public health targets for the control, elimination and eradication of these conditions were defined in the road map for neglected tropical diseases 2021-2030. It aims by 2030 to reduce by 90% the number of people requiring NTD interventions, reduce NTD-related disability and premature death by 75%, enable 100 countries to eliminate at least one NTD, and eradicate Guinea worm disease and yaws. Through science and health innovation, WHO works with countries and partners to advance better diagnostics, medicines and vaccines, strengthen surveillance and data, and integrate NTD prevention and care into national health systems, helping translate scientific progress into healthier lives for the communities most affected. Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations’ agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations – leading the world’s response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care. Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. “Together for health. Stand with science”, the theme of World Health Day 2026, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide.

Russian attacks disrupt power in Kyiv, while the death toll in a stricken village rises to 40
articles.description: Russian attacks disrupt power in Kyiv, while the death toll in a stricken village rises to 40 AP News Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 3, 2026 Institute for the Study of War Ukraine and Russia trade hundreds of drones overnight, as Moscow continues targeting energy infrastructure ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos Russia hits power stations in Ukraine's regions of Kyiv, Zhytomyr Reuters U
articles.content: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russian attacks triggered power and water outages for hours Wednesday across Kyiv and surrounding regions while President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the death toll in a stricken village in southern Ukraine rose to 40 in one of the deadliest strikes there in nearly five years of war. On Monday, multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region, as residents waited for humanitarian aid. In addition to those killed, Zelenskyy said 30 more people could still be buried in the rubble. “Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack,” he said in a post on X. “But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response. Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered.” Elsewhere, Moscow showed no signs of letting up its aerial assaults. Before water and power were restored, residents in the capital of Kyiv were urged to use public drinking water fountains. Emergency centers were set up hastily in the worst-hit areas, offering hot tea and power for people seeking to charge electrical devices. Russia attacked overnight with 310 drones, including 81 jet-powered drones, according to Ukraine’s air force. In its daily social media report, the air force said it downed or suppressed 272 drones of various types. Such attacks are a regular feature of wartime life in Ukraine despite arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court in 2024 for two senior Russian officers whom prosecutors accuse of overseeing strikes on civilian infrastructure. Officials from the United States, Germany, France, Britain, NATO, the World Bank and the European Union met Wednesday at the European Commission’s headquarters in Brussels to discuss the massive reconstruction effort that will be required once the war ends. The commission said in a brief statement after the closed-door meeting that it “focused on refining the scenarios for Ukraine’s postwar economic development and prosperity.” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she wanted the meeting to discuss European demands for Russian concessions in any negotiations. She said previous talks have been focused only on “what Ukraine should give away or what concessions they should make.” The Brussels talks came ahead of a new round of U.S.-brokered peace negotiations next week, more than 4 1/2 years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor. Russian drones were hampering the search for victims in the village of Komyshuvakha, said Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the regional military administration, but he added that operations there would continue. Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the regional defense council, said 12 bodies pulled from the rubble had been identified so far. The National Police of Ukraine said in a Telegram post that visual identification of some bodies was not possible and that specialists were working with relatives of the dead to collect DNA samples. Body camera footage recovered from a police officer killed in the attack shows the devastating impact of the Russian guided bomb. The video was recorded Monday as the officer descended stairs into the shelter after the nearby aid distribution center was struck. In the video, the officer speaks to survivors of the initial attack, urging them to seek shelter. “Go down! Why are you gathering here?” he is heard saying. Moments after the officer enters a low-ceilinged underground room, a brief rumble is heard as the video cuts to black. On Tuesday, Baptist pastor Vladyslav Makhovskyi joined the search for survivors. But as the day wore on, bodies wrapped in white plastic sheets were carried from the ruins and laid in rows as smoke drifted across the shattered landscape. “When the bombs hit, people could no longer get out,” Makhovskyi told The Associated Press. “I understand that many were killed immediately. Even if some were still alive, they probably couldn’t breathe.” The attack followed the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the southwestern Ukrainian region of Kherson. It was the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since 2022, and allowed the evacuation of residents from the shattered city. Zelenskyy awarded U.S. first lady Melania Trump the Order of Princess Olga, 1st class — an honor for women who have made an outstanding contribution to the Ukrainian state. She was recognized for her humanitarian support, including human rights and charitable activities aimed at helping Ukrainian children, according to the presidential website. She was credited with brokering the ceasefire to allow those trapped in Oleshky to leave. The Kremlin, meanwhile, expressed hope that U.S. President Donald Trump will continue his efforts to end the war in Ukraine regardless of the outcome of the midterm elections that saw Democrats take control of Congress, spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine said Wednesday it had uncovered a criminal plot involving senior officials from the country’s security service, prosecutor general’s office and national police who were alleged to have taken kickbacks from the criminal underworld in exchange for protecting fraudulent call centers, drug sales and illegal cigarette and currency operations. It was the latest in a series of graft scandals that have plagued Zelenskyy’s presidency. In September, former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko resigned after investigators accused one of his subordinates of running a scheme linked to fraudulent call centers. Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that it shot down 709 Ukrainian drones overnight. The major online retailer Ozon said that a drone attack caused a fire to break out at its logistics center in Adygeysk, in Russia’s Adygea region, but that there were no casualties. Corder reported from The Hague, Netherlands. Associated Press writers Derek Gatopoulos in Kyiv, Elise Morton in London and Lorne Cook in Brussels contributed.

Th
articles.content: AI agents won’t be stealing Uber’s lunch any time soon. Only four rides were arranged by third-party AI agents during the third quarter of 2026, Uber executives disclosed during an earnings call this morning. The volume of Uber Eats orders fulfilled by AI agents was a little higher, with the company recording “around 500” during the week of Halloween, out of a total 320 million Uber rides and Uber Eats deliveries. This is the first time that Uber has disclosed the number of third-party AI agents that have arranged deliveries or rides on its platform. With the rise of AI agents like Meta’s Muse or OpenAI’s Dots, some experts are predicting that platforms like Uber and DoorDash are at risk of disintermediation, in which customers use AI agents to order food or book a ride, rather than visiting the app itself. But in these early days, it seems like the risk is still very small. During the call, Uber’s executives expressed an openness to working with third-party AI companies to make things easier for agents to use their platform — while also expressing confidence that their customers will continue to prefer the experience of using the Uber app directly. “We hope that there will be more traction,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the call. “We do think that we want to make services that are available to consumers in a delightful, easy way. We think our direct services are going to be the most delightful and easy, but we will work with these third parties.” He continued, “It is just very, very early, and we want to make sure we are not dependent on any one player, and I think we are very well positioned in this environment going forward.” As we’ve noted before, this first wave of AI agents still have a long way to go before people begin seeing them as a viable way to order food or book a ride somewhere. There still is a lot of friction points. And platform operators like Uber or DoorDash have little incentive to allow these agents to barge in and replace their own customers. Which is not to say the AI companies won’t inevitably figure it out! These companies know this is one of their primary use cases, and their best path to a more profitable future. But getting Uber to agree to more disintermediation will be a tough ask. Uber is developing its own AI tools that are designed to keep customers using its own platform. Earlier this year, the company rolled out a new Cart Assistant for Uber Eats, in which an AI bot will build a grocery list based on an image of a recipe or a text prompt.

articles.title: Lansing Police identify human remains found earlier this year
articles.description: Lansing Police said Wednesday that they had identified the human remains that were discovered in September and the remains belong to Antonio McPherson. Police have previously sought public help in […]
articles.content: Lansing Police said Wednesday that they had identified the human remains that were discovered in September and the remains belong to Antonio McPherson. Police have previously sought public help in locating a 27-year-old named Antonio McPherson, who was reported to be missing and endangered in summer 2025. Police did not release any information about McPherson in the Wednesday statement: “The victim has been identified as Antonio McPherson. The Lansing Police Department is investigating this as a suspicious death. We are awaiting the Medical Examiner’s Office’s determination of the cause of death.” Police said those three sentences were an update to the September discovery of human remains in the 2400 block of Tecumseh River Road. At that time, police were dispatched to the location for a suspicious situation and noticed the apparent human remains, according to the earlier statement. The department said in September that forensic officials from LPD and Michigan State Police as well as the Michigan State University Anthropology team were looking into apparent human remains. The condition of the remains were initially believed to be several years old, according to police. At around the same time, police also retrieved a prosthetic leg from the Grand River, which was not related.

articles.title: Who is Hakeem Jeffries? Meet the likely first Black speaker of the US House.
articles.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries got one step closer to becoming the next speaker after Democrats delivered a sweeping victory in the midterm elections. If elected by a majority of House members, Jeffries would make history as the first Black person to hold the gavel. The 56-year-old Brooklynite would lead Democrats’ charge against President […]
articles.content: U.S. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York speaks to reporters at the U.S. Capitol on Oct. 3, 2023. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries got one step closer to becoming the next speaker after Democrats delivered a sweeping victory in the midterm elections. If elected by a majority of House members, Jeffries would make history as the first Black person to hold the gavel. The 56-year-old Brooklynite would lead Democrats’ charge against President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans’ policies, while pursuing an affordability and accountability-focused agenda. Democrats are set to control both the House and Senate in the new Congress after a blue tsunami tore through the country on Election Day. Jeffries — who’s represented the Empire State’s 8th Congressional District since 2013 — would have to navigate a challenging terrain that includes internal divisions in his caucus and a president all but certain to veto many of the party’s measures. Jeffries would be the first Democratic speaker since Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California. How hard to push Trump Since Trump returned to office in January of last year, Jeffries, whom House Democrats elected as minority leader in late 2022, has stood at the forefront of Democrats’ pushback against the administration, a difficult project amid Republican control of both chambers of Congress and the presidency. As that pushback ramps up under a Democratic House majority that has campaigned in part on holding the administration accountable, Jeffries will have to decide whether his party will seek to impeach Trump. That undertaking could compete with a slew of policy priorities on tap in the next Congress. Trump was impeached twice in the House during his first term, and acquitted both times in the Senate. Jeffries was one of the seven House impeachment managers during Trump’s first Senate impeachment trial in 2020. Healthcare a top issue While leading House Democrats in opposing the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law, Jeffries in July 2025 broke the record for the longest House floor speech. Speaking on the floor for almost nine hours, Jeffries blasted the package, including its sweeping healthcare cuts that axe roughly $1 trillion in Medicaid spending over 10 years. Just months later, Democrats shut down the government over their healthcare demands in October 2025 and urged Republicans to negotiate on an extension of the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits. The 43-day shutdown is the longest in U.S. history. The enhanced tax credits were used by individuals who buy their own health insurance through the Affordable Care Act Marketplace. Democrats established them in 2021 as part of a massive COVID-19 relief package and extended them in 2022 through their own sprawling party-line law, but the credits expired in late 2025. Jeffries led a discharge petition in the House to force a vote on legislation to extend the credits for three years. The effort reached the 218-signature threshold needed to trigger a vote in December 2025 after garnering the support of a handful of moderate GOP members in the House. The bipartisan bill passed the House in January but stalled in the Senate. The nonpartisan health research organization KFF has noted that the enhanced tax credits’ expiration has “sharply increased” individuals’ out-of-pocket costs toward premiums. Democrats campaigned heavily on affordability, and one of their main agenda items in the next Congress will be to permanently restore the credits. Navigating Medicare for All Meanwhile, Jeffries would also have to navigate intra-party divisions regarding “Medicare for All,” a movement popular among progressives to extend single-payer national health care to all Americans. Jeffries has co-sponsored Medicare for All legislation in prior years but stopped putting his name behind the measure once he became the Democratic leader. He rejected Medicare for All in an interview with NBC News in August, saying “it’s not legislation that I currently am co-sponsoring or that I support.” Historic figure Jeffries made history as the first Black lawmaker to lead a party in Congress when he became minority leader in January 2023. He has also been chair of the House Democratic Caucus, whip of the Congressional Black Caucus and co-chair of the House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee. Prior to joining Congress, Jeffries served in the New York State Assembly from 2007 to 2012 and also spent several years as a corporate litigator. Jeffries was born in Brooklyn, New York, in 1970 and grew up in the Crown Heights neighborhood. Jeffries is married, and he and his wife have two sons. He received his bachelor’s degree from the State University of New York at Binghamton, a master’s degree in public policy from Georgetown University and a law degree from New York University.

articles.title: What I learned driving the Slate electric truck prototype
articles.description: After 45 minutes behind the wheel, I am more optimistic about the $25,000 EV.
articles.content: If my 45-minute drive yesterday morning is anything to go by, I think Slate Auto will have quite the hit on its hands. The startup had one of its prototype trucks in town and asked if I wanted to check it out—no jumping on a plane or having to spend yet another night in an interchangeable hotel room, just a drive from southwest DC to Rockville, Maryland. Easy-peasy. The prototype truck had been well-used, with almost 6,000 miles (9,656 km) showing on the small and minimalist but very legible digital display that also shows your speed and, if you engage reverse, the backup camera. And while the cabin layout was representative of the production version, the surfaces most certainly weren’t—the prototype instead uses a lot of hard and shiny black plastic, with strips of Velcro here and there left over from when the interior had to be camouflaged when the vehicle was out in public. Getting acquainted with the Slate was refreshingly easy. The Morris Marina-like door handles open with a pleasing mechanical action. The seat and steering column adjust manually but with plenty of reach, something many budget models used to leave out to save on cost.Read full article Comments

articles.title: With 5 seats up for grabs, Detroit voters elect familiar faces and one newcomer
articles.description: The election comes at a pivotal time for Michigan's largest school district and could shape its direction for years to come.
articles.content: This story also appeared in Chalkbeat Detroit Sign up for Chalkbeat Detroit’s free newsletter to keep up with the city’s public school system and Michigan education policy. Voters elected two former board members, an incumbent, a newcomer, and a familiar face to the Detroit school board Tuesday in a pivotal election that may change the direction of the district for years to come. Detroiters cast ballots to fill five open at-large seats on the Detroit Public Schools Community District’s seven-member board, including four seats with full four-year terms and one with a two-year partial term. The election comes as parents and community members push district leaders for more urgency in improving academic achievement, building conditions, and transparency. The unofficial results showed winners of the four-year terms are Georgia Lemmons, Jameel Smith, LaMar Lemmons and Bessie Harris. The election was a referendum of sorts on the 9-year tenure of Superintendent Nikolai Vitti,who has in recent months faced harsher criticism from board members concerned that students aren’t improving enough on state and district exams. While the election of two new members critical of Vitti makes more board clashes likely, his most vocal critics didn’t get elected. And it’s unclear whether Vitti’s job is at stake because not all candidates or sitting members have been clear about their opinions. LaMar Lemmons was a Detroit Public Schools board member during state emergency management from 2012 to 2016. He was elected to the newly formed DPSCD board in November 2016 and left office in 2018. He has been critical of Vitti over the years. He initially voted against hiring Vitti in 2017, but later changed his vote because he said he wanted the new school leader to have unanimous support from the board. Most recently, LaMar Lemmons decried the accelerated closures of small schools. His wife, Georgia Lemmons, is a retired DPS teacher who served on the DPSCD board from 2017 to 2022. She voted against extending Vitti’s contract in 2020. Smith, director of psychotherapy services behavioral health service line at Henry Ford Health. Incumbent Harris is a retired special education teacher and principal. She was appointed to the board in October 2025 to fill a seat after the resignation of a member. Terry Whitfield, a self-employed nonprofit consultant, was just shy of earning a four-year term, losing by just 56 votes. Aliya Moore, a self-employed DPSCD parent, won the two-year partial term. Moore is a longtime critic of Vitti and his administration who has called for his removal from the district for years. The future of the district was on the mind of voters such as Elizabeth Gist. She said she spent a lot of time researching since she hadn’t heard much from any campaign and selected about seven school board candidates she planned to vote for. She hopes they can improve Detroit’s educational system and its children’s outcomes. “Children are the future … and I’m concerned. Because critical thinking seems to be a lost art. Even basic phonics, reading, arithmetic,” Gist said. Thirty-one names are on the ballot for the four full-term seats. Three of them — Natalie Bien-Aime, Henrietta Ivey, and Darious Morris — have said they are no longer running. Three candidates — Ijazz Jackson, Aliya Moore, and Shawn Vaughn — are running for the two-year seat. With so many candidates on the ballot, some voters said they were confused about who to vote for Tuesday. Katherine Jackson, a retiree, said that while her grandchildren attend DPS schools she is not as informed on the candidates as she hoped she could have been. “I really wish there was someone or something to help me so I just voted for the names I recognized,” she said. Nichelle Williams, 33, a southwest Detroit home healthcare worker, has a freshman daughter attending the University Preparatory Academy charter school, and described herself as not being familiar with the dozens of candidates. But she is sure of one thing — that it’s time to “shake things up.” She cited the district’s decades-long struggles with literacy rates. “They need a change when it comes to reading, a lot of students are really far behind where they have to be and can’t read,” Williams said. “Then they turn into adults who can’t read … something has to change.” Read more of our DPSCD board election coverage here: This November’s Detroit school board election may drastically change the district’s direction. Here’s how. Some Detroit school board candidates spent campaign contributions on clothing, travel, and meals 1 Detroit school board candidate raised nearly 80% of campaign money, finance statements show 4 Detroit school board candidates have felony convictions, analysis finds 5 Detroit school board candidates run as a slate backed by ‘militant’ ‘anti-fascist’ activism group Statewide races on Tuesday’s ballot will also affect education for Detroit students, including the governor’s race and the battle for two seats on the State Board of Education. Amelia Benavides-Colón from BridgeDetroit and Beki San Martin of the Detroit Free Press contributed to this report. Hannah Dellinger covers Detroit schools for Chalkbeat Detroit. You can reach her at hdellinger@chalkbeat.org.

The DEA banned a drug some opioid users called a miracle
articles.description: Researchers say the Schedule I ban could kill studies of a promising opioid treatment.
articles.content: In 2012, as the driver of deaths in the opioid crisis began moving from prescription pills to heroin, Laura Bohn was tasked with finding safer drugs to manage pain. Funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, in 2017 she and other scientists revealed in the science journal Cell that several compounds—including a particularly promising one called SR-17018—could relieve pain in mice without causing respiratory depression. That’s a big deal, because respiratory depression is typically what causes people using opioids to stop breathing and die. Bohn, senior associate vice president of research at University of South Florida Health, says her team filed a patent on SR-17018. They went on to discover that mice using the chemical did not develop a high tolerance for it and that mice already dependent on morphine—a powerful opioid—could consume SR-17018 to reset their tolerance without suffering from painful withdrawal symptoms.Read full article Comments

articles.title: The blue tsunami sweeps the US, as Democrats land huge gains in Congress
articles.description: Voters across the country administered a sharp reprimand to President Donald Trump and Republicans who hold majorities in Congress, with Democrats gaining comfortable majorities in the Senate and the House. Several U.S. Senate and House races remained uncalled by The Associated Press as Election Day ended on the East Coast. But by Wednesday morning, Democrats […]
articles.content: The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025, just hours before a federal government shutdown. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Voters across the country administered a sharp reprimand to President Donald Trump and Republicans who hold majorities in Congress, with Democrats gaining comfortable majorities in the Senate and the House. Several U.S. Senate and House races remained uncalled by The Associated Press as Election Day ended on the East Coast. But by Wednesday morning, Democrats had notched 54 Senate seats to control that chamber and 228 House seats, clearing the thresholds needed to win majorities in each chamber as the party swept virtually all of the races that were expected to be competitive. Those wins included Senate contests in states Trump won by double digits just two years ago, some of which had not elected Democrats in decades: Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina, Ohio and Texas. Democrats also won a seat left open by retiring Republican Thom Tillis in North Carolina, bringing their total of Senate pickups to five, with leads in a handful of other states. And they retained their seat in Minnesota, electing Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan to the Senate. By the early hours of Wednesday, they’d netted 25 new House seats, putting them on track to start next Congress with a majority that will give House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, whom Democrats are expected to make speaker, some room to maneuver. The AP had not yet made a call by midnight that Democrats had control of the House. Democrats also flipped four governorships, in Georgia, Texas, Ohio and Iowa. Republicans had not flipped any Democratic-held governorships, U.S. House or Senate seats by midnight, according to race calls by AP.
