McCann declares victory against Huizenga, delivering Michigan’s 4th Congressional District for Dems
articles.description: Building on gains in 2022, Democrats have continued to make headway in Western Michigan as state Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo) claimed victory Wednesday against U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Holland Township) for his seat in Congress. Unofficial results from the Associated Press, which finally called the race at 1:13 p.m. Wednesday, show McCann had 50.1% of […]
articles.content: State Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo) is joined by U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, at left, during a stop in Kalamazoo of the "Sick of It! Fix Health Care Now" bus tour on Oct. 20, 2026. (Campaign photo)Building on gains in 2022, Democrats have continued to make headway in Western Michigan as state Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo) claimed victory Wednesday against U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Holland Township) for his seat in Congress. Unofficial results from the Associated Press, which finally called the race at 1:13 p.m. Wednesday, show McCann had 50.1% of the vote while Huizenga received 48.3%. Return of the trifecta: Michigan Democrats reclaim full control of state government McCann will conclude his time in the state Legislature and serve as representative for the state’s 4th Congressional District, which includes Allegan and Van Buren counties, and portions of Ottawa, Kalamazoo, Calhoun and Berrien counties. The win would be at least the third Michigan congressional district to flip to the Democrats, following wins by William Lawrence in the 7th District and Christina Hines in the 10th District. “I am honored and humbled that the people of Southwest Michigan have put their trust in me to represent and serve this amazing district,” McCann said in a statement. “Thank you to the voters, and to every volunteer and supporter who knocked on doors and made phone calls, talked to their neighbors, and helped out in ways big and small. I will be forever grateful for your support, because you are the heart and soul of this campaign. And thank you to Congressman Bill Huizenga for his years of service to our community.” Huizenga released a statement conceding the election on Wednesday evening. “While this election did not turn out the way we had hoped, I’m incredibly proud of the campaign we ran and want to congratulate Sean McCann on his victory. God has blessed me with the honor of a lifetime to represent the people of Southwest Michigan in Congress,” Huizenga’s statement said. “To my amazing family, our volunteers, our campaign team, and everyone who knocked on doors, made phone calls, put up a yard sign, or supported our campaign, I couldn’t be more grateful. I’ve worked hard to make a difference for our communities, and I’ll always be proud of what we’ve accomplished together. I know God will keep calling me to serve, and I look forward to what comes next.” While the nonpartisan Cook Political Report initially rated the district as a likely win for Republicans, its rating gradually shifted to “toss-up,” meaning either party had a good chance of winning. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said McCann ran a “vigorous and impressive campaign” to defeat Huizenga, which spoke to his dedication to delivering results for working people. “Sean’s lifetime of service is simply continuing with a new, well-deserved title: Congressman. In Washington, Sean will continue to fight for working people and take on Republicans. I served with state Senator McCann, and I know Michiganders in the southwest corner of our state are in good hands,” Hertel said in a statement. During a canvass launch organized by McCann’s campaign five days before Election Day, U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly), said a Democratic victory in the 4th Congressional district would signal that “when Democrats compete, they win,” reflecting on U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten’s 2022 win in the neighboring 3rd Congressional District, previously considered to be a conservative stronghold. “This victory belongs to the people all across Southwest Michigan, and it’s the people that I will work every day to serve – to take on the corruption and policies shortchanging our families, and work with anyone to make life better and protect the American Dream for our children. Michigan families deserve nothing less, and I look forward to getting right to work for the people of this district,” McCann said. 6:56 pmA statement from Congressman Huizenga was added to this story. 1:16 pmThis story has been updated with word that the Associated Press had officially confirmed McCann as the winner.

OpenAI to acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc.
articles.description: OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer Company, expanding Codex’s tools for building, understanding, and reviewing code.
articles.content: Expanding Codex’s tools for building, understanding, and reviewing code. Today we're announcing that OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc(opens in a new window). (“Pierre”), the company behind Code Storage(opens in a new window) and a family of standout open-source developer tools. If you’ve browsed files or reviewed a change in the Codex app, you’ve already used Pierre’s Trees and Diffs libraries. We’re excited to work with the Pierre team to build on the Git workflows that developers already rely on and adapt them to how teams work with coding agents. We’ve seen in our own engineering work how the systems around Git need to evolve as more of that work happens in parallel. Earlier this week, we shared how we’re scaling Git at OpenAI with Pando, our in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. With the Pierre team, we wish to set the standard for modern software development: from the first branch an agent creates to that magic moment when code is deployed to the world. We want to make Codex the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects. We’ve long appreciated the care Pierre brings to another part of working with Git: how developers review code. You can see that care in the libraries we use in Codex today. Trees lets developers quickly navigate a project’s files, and Diffs makes it easy to see what changed. Both of these tools make it easy to review and navigate large volumes of code with uncompromising performance. That same attention to detail runs through Pierre’s other work. Diffs’ Edit mode lets a reviewer fix a line of code right where they spot the problem. Pierre recently released Highlights, an extremely fast syntax highlighter that updates as a developer types or an agent streams code. The same small team that put an editor inside a diff also designed the API for Code Storage, a service that lets apps store code and track its history using Git. Pierre has built tools that developers love, and together, we will ship new products and platforms that benefit all. Once the acquisition closes, our ambition is to advance the future of source control across the industry. We want Codex to connect the code a company ships with the decisions its people make, at the scale the future demands. Pierre’s open-source projects will remain open-source, and we’ll continue to contribute to them. Customers can continue using Code Storage after the acquisition closes while we work to bring its features and functionality into Codex. The closing of the acquisition is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of regulatory approvals. Until closing, OpenAI and Pierre will remain separate and independent companies.

How Abdul El-Sayed, Jocelyn Benson won Michigan: Big turnout, Democratic shifts
articles.description: Record turnout for a midterm and statewide shifts towards Democrats meant a big night for Abdul El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson. Here’s how they won Michigan.
articles.content: This story also appeared in Bridge Michigan High turnout, Democratic shifts helped senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and governor-elect Jocelyn Benson win Michigan Benson, El-Sayed both outperformed Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 Republican US Senate nominee Mike Rogers lost ground in Detroit, while El-Sayed fared well in college towns Democrats Abdul El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson rode a “blue wave” to win Michigan’s US Senate and governor’s races, respectively, outperforming recent party performance in an election that was a rebuke of President Donald Trump. Benson, a Democrat, will succeed outgoing Gov. Gretchen Whitmer after beating Republican John James by more than 10 percentage points, according to unofficial results. El-Sayed, a progressive who campaigned on universal healthcare and taxing the rich, defeated Republican Mike Rogers by about seven points, defending the seat to help Democrats retake control of the US Senate. Here’s a look at how they secured victory: High turnout, broad Democratic shifts El-Sayed and Benson both benefited from relatively high turnout across the state, particularly among Democratic voters. According to unofficial results, more than 4.8 million voters cast ballots in Michigan. That appears to be a midterm record, topping the 4.5 million Michiganders who voted in 2022 but shy of the 5.7 million who cast ballots in the 2024 presidential election that Trump won. Benson won 18 counties, while El-Sayed won 14, including several of the most populous counties that helped make up for losses in more rural areas. But even in the counties they lost, Benson and El-Sayed exceeded expectations. All 83 Michigan counties shifted toward Democrats compared with the 2024 election, according to an analysis by the Associated Press. That included a 14-percentage point shift in Wayne County, the state’s largest, but also double-digit shifts in more rural areas like Dickinson, Branch and St. Joseph counties. In Wexford County, where Rogers won by a smaller margin than two years ago, retired Manton voter Jerrilyn Mathews, a former Republican, said she voted for El-Sayed, other Democrats and “anything against Trump.” Detroit and Wayne County As of 7 a.m., about 93% of all Wayne County ballots had been counted with El-Sayed and Benson each getting more than 70% of the vote in their respective races, according to unofficial results. Both outperformed 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris, who topped Trump with 63% of the Wayne County vote in 2024. In Detroit, the state’s largest city, Benson won about 93% of the vote and El-Sayed won about 92%, according to unofficial results. Both topped the 90% Harris won in Detroit two years ago. Rogers spent considerable time in Detroit and touted inroads with Democrats, including outgoing state Rep. Karen Whitsett. But he received only 5% of the city vote in Tuesday’s election, down from the 7% he won there in his 2024 loss to US Sen. Elissa Slotkin. “I voted to go against Trump. When it all comes down to it, we are trying to vote against Trump,” said Henry McCoi of Detroit, who cast his ballot at Mayberry Elementary School. With nearly all ballots counted in Washtenaw County, El-Sayed won there with 74% of the vote. Benson received about 75%. Both outperformed Harris, who had won 71% of Washtenaw County votes in 2024. El-Sayed and Benson also outperformed Harris in Ingham, Kalamazoo, Isabella and Kent counties, all home to universities and large groups of young voters. Jack Morean, a 19-year-old Michigan State University student from Grand Rapids, voted in his first general election Tuesday morning at an on-campus precinct in East Lansing. Morean said he voted for Democrats up and down his ballot. “We’re in a time where divisiveness is very apparent,” he said. “Our current government is honestly abhorrent. I’m here to vote for change.” Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan.

articles.title: Democrats take full control of Legislature, Michigan government. What to expect
articles.description: Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson can expect smooth sailing for her agenda, as Democrats win the state House, grow their Senate majority and maintain control of the Supreme Court, attorney general and secretary of state.
articles.content: Michigan Democrats have again won a legislative trifecta, flipping not just the state House but also growing their Senate majority With some race results still pending, it appears House Democrats will hold an at least 60-seat majority Senate Democrats, meanwhile, are likely to have a 23-15 majority by the time all races are called — their largest margin in decades LANSING — For only the second time in more than four decades, Democrats will control both chambers of the Michigan Legislature after flipping the state House and growing their majority in the state Senate, according to unofficial election results. With Jocelyn Benson also winning the governor’s race, Democrats are poised to have a governing “trifecta” in Lansing for the next two years, a power they last enjoyed in the 2023-24 session. In the 110-seat House, Democrats secured at least 60 seats, in part by ousting at least five GOP incumbents, with several race results still outstanding. And in the 38-member Senate, Democrats grew their majority from 20 to 23 seats, ousting two GOP incumbents in the process. That will give Democrats their largest majority in the Michigan Senate since 1982, according to Gongwer subscription news service. “Our Democratic trifecta is going to go to Lansing and pass a voting rights act for the state of Michigan to ensure that every citizen in this state is protected at the ballot box in every election,” Benson promised early Wednesday morning in a victory speech. The last time the Democrats held complete power, they acted quickly to pass gun reforms, clean energy laws and protections to union and gay rights. Related: 10 races to watch: Democrats, Republicans battle for Michigan Legislature Michigan elections: What Democrats, Republicans say they’d do if they win big Michigan elections: Voters decide on Proposal 2 Money Out of Politics question Democrats told Bridge last month to expect an encore, focusing this time on affordability, reining in drug costs and addressing housing affordability. Benson has promised a new tax on vacation rentals and tax subsidies for the construction of starter homes. Not only will Democrats control the Legislature and governor, but Tuesday balloting ensured they will maintain control of the state Supreme Court, university boards, the state Board of Education and secretary of state and attorney general. “Voters have given us a mandate to address the cost of living crisis head-on,” state Sen. Darrin Camilleri, D-Trenton, said Wednesday.Donate Flipping the House Democrats entered into Election Day with a 52-58 minority in the state House — and were able to defend their incumbents, but flip several hotly contested races as well. In the 55th House district, state Rep. Mark Tisdel, R-Rochester Hills, lost by about 4 percentage points to Democrat Alex Hawkins, a US Army veteran. Tisdel has served since 2021 and has won re-election by 4 to 7 percentage points, even as Democrats like outgoing Gov. Gretchen Whitmer won by double digit margins. Other Republican House incumbents ousted Tuesday night include Rylee Linting in the Wayne County-based 27th district and Jamie Thompson in the 28th district, which includes parts of Monroe and Wayne counties. Steve Frisbie in the Calhoun County-based 44th district and David Martin in the 68th district, which includes parts of Genesee and Oakland counties, also lost their reelection bids. Democrats also defended the 61st district, where incumbent Rep. Denise Mentzer withstood a challenge from Republican Robert Wojtowicz. With all precincts reporting, Mentzer won reelection to the Macomb County seat by more than 5,000 votes — outperforming her 2024 contest, also against Wojtowicz, where she only won reelection by a few hundred votes. Republicans had invested heavily in this district, as had Democrats, with spending cumulatively topping at least $863,000 between the two major parties, according to the Capitol research service MIRS News. Big gains for Democrats in the House on Tuesday include: House District 27: Former Democratic state Rep. Jaime Churches beat Linting by roughly 1,641 votes according to unofficial totals Wednesday. Linting had unseated Churches in 2024 by about 2,300 votes and was part of the successful push by Republicans to end the 2022 Democratic trifecta. House District 46: Democrat Jan Maino toppled incumbent Kathy Schmaltz, R-Jackson, for control of a House district which includes parts of Jackson and Washtenaw counties. Republicans spent heavily on Schmaltz, who lost to Maino by more than 2,800 votes. House District 54: Democrats secured one of the two open House seats this cycle, with Democrat Sarah Pounds beating out Republican Roman Gaskey in the Oakland County-based district. Republican Rep. Donni Steele currently holds the seat but chose not to seek reelection, instead successfully running for the state Senate. Retaining the Senate Both Senate Republicans and Democrats in October told Bridge there were five races to watch on election night which could determine chamber control. Of those, Democrats won four and appear poised to take the final one, according to unofficial vote totals Wednesday. Should they secure all five, that would give Democrats a 23-15 seat majority over Republicans in the state Senate — the largest margin in almost 50 years. Based on unofficial results, the competitive districts Democrats won include: Senate District 9: Democrat Dr. Theresa Brooks ousted incumbent state Sen. Michael Webber, R-Rochester Hills, by nearly 8,300 votes. Webber won the seat by just 795 out of 115,111 votes in 2022. The district includes parts of Oakland and Macomb counties. Senate District 12: Incumbent state Sen. Kevin Hertel, D-Saint Clair Shores, defended his seat from Republican John Goldwater by more than 9,000 votes. Hertel won the seat by just 404 out of 125,140 votes in 2022. The district includes parts of Wayne, Macomb and St. Clair counties. Senate District 13: Democrat Sean Carlson beat former Republican state Rep. Ryan Berman by nearly 8,200 votes. The district, which includes part of Oakland County, was an open seat after incumbent state Sen. Rosemary Bayer, D-West Bloomfield, chose not to run for reelection. Senate District 30: Incumbent state Sen. Mark Huizenga, R-Walker, fell to state Rep. Carol Glanville by more than 13,400 votes. Huizenga won the seat by just 391 out of 129,633 votes in 2022. The district includes parts of Kent and Ottawa counties. Senate District 32 has still not yet been called, though Democrat Rebecca Amidon seems likely to beat out Republican Kim Cole for an open seat being vacated by term-limited state Sen. Jon Bumstead, R-North Muskegon. Unofficial returns show Amidon leading Cole by more than 13,400 votes with 88% of the district’s precincts reporting as of time of publication. Bumstead won the district by about 5 percentage points in 2022, and Democrats believe his departure gives them a good chance to close that gap.

Fix speech to text accuracy problems with a smarter workflow
articles.description: Learn why speech to text accuracy drops and how to fix it, from audio quality and accents to keyterm prompting, plus how to measure it with WER.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Speech to text (STT) accuracy depends on three things: the quality of your audio, how people speak, and the words they use. Noise and heavy compression strip detail from a recording, with even strong models struggling with overlapping voices or unfamiliar jargon. This guide shows where each STT problem comes from and how to fix it. Transcription errors rarely stay in the transcript. A misheard drug name in a clinical note or a wrong account number in a call log carries into every system that uses that text, from search and analytics to AI agents that act on what was said. Poor accuracy also adds review time, because someone has to find and correct the mistakes by hand. The good news is that most STT accuracy problems are fixable. Many of these fixes only require slight changes to your existing configurations or recording setups, which means you can fix your problem without having to change your model settings. You may also see this topic called speech recognition accuracy, ASR accuracy, or transcription accuracy. Speech to text, speech recognition, and automatic speech recognition (ASR) all describe the same process of converting spoken audio into written text. The fixes in this guide apply whichever term you use. Imagine someone asks you to transcribe an audio recording of a thickly accented professor describing complex theoretical physics, recorded in a crowded restaurant with background music and ambient chatter. Digital computer systems aren't natively attuned to acoustic variability. It takes significant training and fine-tuning to make STT work effectively, and while modern AI tooling is very effective, many issues can still impact output. But by understanding what they are, you can address them in your transcription workflows. There are three main causes for inaccurate speech to text conversion: Each cause needs a different fix, which the sections below cover in turn. First, the audio recording itself can have issues. Microphone issues could lead to speech becoming distorted or clipped. Reverb due to the acoustics of the venue, a poor signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the recording, or a low sampling rate on the recording could all potentially strip away important phonetic information from recordings. A single speaker with a neutral accent, speaking in a quiet venue, will be relatively easy to transcribe. But that’s rarely the type of recording we want transcribed. Unfamiliar accents and choppy or simply non-traditional speaking cadence can throw off an STT model trained on standardized speech. Cross-talk or overlapping speakers can also disrupt a model’s ability to accurately parse what’s being said. Lastly, speech content can also challenge some STT models. Industry jargon and new product names might not be language an STT model has encountered in training. As it selects the most statistically likely output, speech that’s unfamiliar may not be a top prediction. Numerical or mathematical expressions, or speech that might otherwise be written numerically, also might not transcribe clearly. Homophones are words that sound the same but are spelled differently. An STT model needs enough contextual understanding to distinguish between them. For example, “the bear ambled across the bare mountainside.” The model would need to know the animal is spelled “bear” and the adjective for an uncovered surface is spelled “bare.” Speech to text processing occurs in a series of well-defined steps. To fix an accuracy issue, you need to identify where in that pipeline you can make a change. Broadly speaking, the STT process breaks down into: Each stage has its own failure modes and its own fixes. There could be issues with the environment in which you’re recording. Common issues here include background noise or echoes. The recording equipment could also be the source of an issue if it’s faulty. Fixing issues in this stage typically involves isolating what is causing the problem and resolving it. For example, if you know that the STT tool struggles with loud backgrounds, then hosting conversations in an environment that you have more control over is a good idea. For any noise you can’t avoid, apply voice isolation before the audio reaches the model. How you configure your API to an STT engine can affect processing. Prompt structure and the model you choose can also affect quality and the number of inaccuracies. Fixing issues in this stage means testing your setup against your own audio. Run the same sample recordings through each candidate model, compare their word error rates, and then change one setting as a time to refine. If a model keeps missing one type of speech, such as a noisy call or a certain regional accent, test out different models for their accuracy in the exact environment you’ll be using. This is your quality-control layer, where specialized processes clean up transcription errors and ambiguities your primary engine might have missed. STT pipelines regularly use rule-based pattern matching to standardize formatting (e.g., changing “ten dollars” to “$10.00”), a process called inverse text normalization (ITN), but if a speaker uses one of those terms in a non-standard way or mispronounces it, a rigid find-and-replace matching tool won’t catch it. There’s also the question of whether a human-in-the-loop (HITL) checks the quality of the output. If not, inaccuracies may make their way into production output. As with any activity, if a human performs it, there’s a chance for human error. At this stage, fixing issues means catching the errors that your primary engines leave behind. You can compare transcripts against a reference sample to find which mistakes repeat, then add targeted rules or a custom dictionary for those terms. Especially for high-stakes transcriptions, always add in a human review step. Improving audio quality while recording can reduce many downstream accuracy issues. Use a higher sample rate, apply minimal or no compression, and maintain as clear a recording environment as possible. Use 16 kHz or 44.1 kHz audio for recording. 8 kHz legacy telephone-grade audio sampling and lower can be challenging for STT models to parse. To the models, it sounds muffled and garbled, and they can’t ask speakers to repeat themselves like a person can on a call. A sampling rate can only reproduce frequencies up to half of its sampling rate. This is called the system’s Nyquist frequency. At only 8 kHz, that would cut off anything above 4 kHz, and specifically make it challenging for an STT model to tell the difference between fricatives (“s” versus “f” sounds) and plosives (“p” versus “t” sounds). Recording to lossy formats, such as MP3 and AAC, can also strip away speech subtleties. There’s less signal for the model to work with. Stick to lossless or uncompressed formats, such as FLAC or PCM WAV. Follow best practices in audio engineering for microphone use. Omnidirectional mics work best in controlled environments. Otherwise, directional mics are better for isolating speech. Position microphones four to six inches (10-15cm) from a speaker’s mouth and try to prevent speakers from leaning closer, which will create a proximity effect and muddy the recording with boosted low frequencies. Also use a pop filter on your microphone whenever possible. Pop filters diffuse puffs of air created when speaking plosive consonants (e.g., “p” and “b” sounds). As noted in the previous section, you want to use close-mic recording wherever possible, ideally four to six inches from a speaker’s mouth. Avoid white noise and background noise that will muddy recordings. Common sources you might not notice without experience doing field recordings include hum from HVAC systems, keyboard clicking, and general street noise. All of these can challenge an STT model's ability to parse speech. However, it’s often not possible to avoid background noise, in which case you will want to apply voice isolation as a preprocessing step before you send your audio to an STT model. Voice isolation uses software algorithms or a lightweight, specialized neural model to filter background audio from speech recordings. Modern multilingual models are trained on diverse speech sets, but their accuracy levels still vary when working with real-world audio. Run your own benchmarks on different models using sample audio from your relevant demographics. If you have historical service calls you can use, run those through transcription, ones that feature the accents, cadences, and speech patterns you want transcribed in the real world. Check the outputs for errors and identify any relevant patterns. Is the model struggling with slang used by younger age groups? Does it stumble over a specific regional accent you commonly encounter? Your two main tools to accurately transcribe overlapping speech are diarization and multichannel recording. A diarization process takes a raw audio input and segments it by individually recognized speakers. It works well when speakers take clear turns. Instead of blending all voice streams into one audio track, native multichannel recording allows you to keep each speaker on a separate channel, which the STT model can identify and process independently. Each speaker is partitioned natively in the recording so there’s nothing for a speech model to diarize post hoc. Brand names, new product names, industry jargon, and other unique terms often will not transcribe accurately if they were not in an STT model’s training data. Keyterm prompting is the process of supplying an STT model with specific spellings you want it to favor. They’re usually not one-for-one replacement prompts, you’re just biasing the model towards selecting the custom spelling you want based on context. Numbers, account IDs, postcodes, and drug names are where a small error costs the most. A model can mishear “fifteen” as “fifty,” or confuse two drug names that sit one syllable apart, such as hydroxyzine and hydralazine. Test these fields separately, because a low overall WER can hide errors on exactly the words that matter most. Word error rate (WER) is a useful metric to assess an STT engine's accuracy. You can compare the WER across different model tests you perform to get a sense of their relative accuracy. It’s important to note that WER weights all errors equally. For example, substituting “took” for “look” counts equally to misrecognizing your brand name or an important figure, like the size of a medication dose. Check the WERs for different models. There is no single good WER, because the right target depends on your audio and your use case. Clean, single-speaker audio produces much lower error rates than noisy calls with overlapping speakers. Compare models on your own recordings rather than relying on a headline number. For a reference point on specialized audio, Scribe v2 Medical is among the top-performing models on public medical ASR benchmarks. Check current benchmark results for the latest figures. Benchmark results change as new models are released. Check current results before you compare. Accuracy is how closely the transcription output matches the spoken “ground truth” input. Word error rate measures accuracy. Precision is how reliable the STT model’s positive predictions are. A highly precise model will select the same word for complex speech across multiple runs. If the model outputs a word, you can trust that word was present in the speech. But a highly precise model can still have low accuracy, meaning it deletes many words. ElevenAPI gives you access to Scribe v2, ElevenLabs’ speech to text model, along with features that address the accuracy problems in this guide: keyterm prompting for names and jargon, multichannel transcription for overlapping speakers, and speaker diarization. If you want to transcribe without using the API, you can also access ElevenCreateive STT. Get started today generating high-quality speech to text with ElevenAPI or learn

articles.title: AI voice agent pricing: What it costs for your business
articles.description: See AI voice agent pricing from $0 to custom Enterprise, what sets your price per minute, and how to calculate ROI against staffing costs.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. AI voice agent pricing depends on three line items: the platform that runs the agent, the large language model (LLM) that powers each conversation, and the telephony provider that connects your calls. Most pricing pages lead with a monthly plan fee, but that fee covers only the first of those three. This guide explains how AI voice agent pricing works, what sets your price per minute, and how to calculate ROI against your current staffing costs. We use real ElevenAgents pricing throughout, so you have concrete figures to plan with. ElevenAgents uses tiered monthly plans. Each tier includes a set number of call minutes, a concurrent call limit, and features that scale with team size. Workflow builder, knowledge base, widget 10 workspace seats, 10 Professional Voice Clones Custom DPA and SLAs, BAAs for HIPAA customers, custom SSO, discounts at scale Divide any paid plan's price by its included minutes, and you get the same platform rate: $0.08 per minute. Additional minutes on Creator and above bill at that same $0.08 rate, and text messages cost $0.003 each. Prices exclude taxes. Because every paid tier shares the same platform rate, volume discounts come through custom Enterprise pricing. The table shows platform cost only. LLM usage and telephony sit on top, which the next two sections explain. The providers of AI voice agents tend to price their offerings in one of three main ways, with many often blending more than one. These models include: ElevenAgents combines all three. Each plan has a fixed monthly fee with included minutes, per-minute billing for additional usage, and workspace seats on the Scale and Business tiers. When you compare AI voice agent pricing models, check one detail first: whether the advertised per-minute rate is all-in or platform-only. A platform-only rate with LLM and telephony billed at cost gives you visibility into each line item. A bundled rate hides the split, which makes it harder to optimize. Your effective price per minute is the sum of three separate line items. Treat them as distinct budgets, because each one responds to different decisions. Total monthly cost = (call minutes × platform rate) + LLM usage + telephony The platform rate covers the voice and conversation layer. On ElevenAgents, that includes text to speech, speech to text, turn taking, knowledge bases, and RAG. Voice quality sits inside this rate. Eleven v4 Turbo in ElevenAgents runs at a median inference latency of about 100 ms across more than 90 languages. The LLM reasons through each turn of the conversation, and its cost varies by model. ElevenAgents bills LLM usage at cost, so a larger reasoning model costs more per minute than a lighter one. Match the model to the task. Routine requests such as order status or appointment changes rarely need the most capable model, while complex troubleshooting often does. Telephony connects your agent to the phone network. Carriers bill at their own rates, and ElevenAgents passes those through at cost. Your telephony spend depends on your provider, number type, and call direction. Web and in-app voice conversations through the widget skip carrier charges entirely. Concurrency is the number of calls your agent handles at the same moment. A plan with 20 concurrent calls supports 20 simultaneous conversations, no matter how many minutes remain in your allowance. Size your plan against peak hour traffic, not monthly totals. ElevenAgents also lists a burst rate of $0.16 per minute for call spikes beyond standard capacity, and Enterprise plans offer elevated concurrency limits. No single average exists, because the range from $0 to custom Enterprise pricing reflects different use cases rather than inconsistent pricing. A useful way to estimate is to translate plan minutes into calls. Assuming a four-minute average call, here is how the tiers map to real workloads: Add your LLM and telephony estimates to the platform figure for each tier to see the full monthly number. Voice AI is free to test, but not free at production scale. The ElevenAgents free tier includes 15 minutes per month, four concurrent calls, the workflow builder, a knowledge base, and the embeddable widget. That covers building and testing a working agent before you commit to a budget. Startups get even more room here. The ElevenLabs Startup Grants Program gives qualifying new products 12 months free with 33M characters to build, launch, and test conversational agents. That allowance covers over 680 hours of Agents usage. Once an agent handles real customer volume, LLM and telephony costs apply alongside platform minutes. Plan for all three before you move from pilot to production. AI voice agent ROI comes from comparing two numbers for the same call volume: the total cost of running the agent, and the fully loaded cost of human staffing. A single universal ROI figure would mislead you, because the answer depends on your volume and on how many calls the agent resolves without escalation. Work through these five steps with your own figures. Together, these steps give you a like-for-like comparison. The example below applies them to sample figures. The figures below are assumptions for illustration. Replace them with your own. Subtract your LLM and telephony estimates from that net figure to get your monthly savings. Then check that your plan's concurrency covers your busiest hour. Cost is only part of the return. articles.title: WHO Health Emergencies EPI-WIN webinar: Launch of WHO guidelines for clinical management of arboviral diseases: dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever
articles.content: Wednesday, 4 November 2026, 13:00 –14:00 (CET) Arboviral diseases are caused by viruses that are transmitted by arthropods (such as mosquitoes and ticks) to humans. Due to climate change, urbanization, and other factors, there have been increasing epidemics of arboviral diseases and emergence in historically unaffected regions. Presently, 5.6 billion people globally are estimated to be at risk of infection from arboviruses, and this number is estimated to increase by 2050. Epidemic-prone arboviruses transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes include dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses. In addition, Aedes aegypti can transmit urban yellow fever. A global dengue upsurge has occurred in recent years, and since 2024, epidemics of chikungunya are occurring after a hiatus of two decades in the Indian Ocean islands, while yellow fever outbreaks are occurring in the Americas Region. In alignment with the strategic objectives of the Global Arbovirus Programme, the WHO guidelines for clinical management of arboviral disease focuses on the updated recommendations for clinical management of dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever for which there are no approved specific treatments, and management of these diseases is mostly symptomatic and supportive. Most cases of arboviral diseases are mild and self-limiting, however, if worsening or severe cases are not recognized and managed appropriately, it can lead to negative patient outcomes, including death. As such, this guideline includes recommendations on the management of patients requiring admission to health care facilities as well as recommendations for patients who can be managed in an outpatient setting. While the new guidelines provide a robust framework for managing patients effectively, their impact will be limited unless they are supported by policies that improve referral pathways and expand access to like-saving hospital-based care. Promoting good clinical practices is only one part of the solution. To reduce mortality, particularly from severe cases of yellow fever, countries must also strengthen their health systems to ensure timely access to hospital care, including intensive care services. This is especially critical given that most yellow fever cases occur in remote and underserved areas. Introduction of EPI-WIN, housekeeping and slido: Dr Supriya Bezbaruah, Lead, EPI-WIN Science and Knowledge Translation, WHO headquarters Welcome remarks: Dr Maria Van Kerkhove, Director, Pandemic and Epidemic Management (EPM), WHO Health Emergencies Programme (WHE) Introduction to the launch: Dr Diana Rojas Alvarez, Global Arbovirus Programme, WHE Importance of an integrated clinical guideline for arboviruses: Prof Kleber Luz, Pediatrician and Infectious Disease Specialist, Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil Summary of WHO guideline for clinical management of arboviral diseases and implementation tools:Dr Jamie Rylance, Clinical Management Expert, Safe and Scalable Care Unit, WHE Closing remarks: Dr Janet Victoria Diaz, Unit Head, Safe and Scalable Care, WHE Closing of EPI-WIN: EPI-WIN Science and Knowledge Translation, WHO headquarters

articles.title: Election 2026: Detroit museums, zoo millages approved by voters
articles.description: Voters in Wayne and Oakland counties support a millage to fund two Detroit cultural institutions preserving Black history, according to unofficial vote tallies.
articles.content: Voters in Wayne and Oakland counties support a millage to fund two Detroit cultural institutions preserving Black history, according to unofficial vote tallies. The “Yes to Our Story” campaign from the Detroit Historical Society and Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History is seeking approval of a 10-year, 0.2-mill levy to support operations. With all of the votes counted, 68% of Wayne County voters supported the millage. In Oakland County, 53% of voters backed the millage, with of the unofficial vote tallied. “Generations of Detroiters built this museum because they believed our stories deserved a home,” Neil A. Barclay, president and CEO of the Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History said in a Wednesday statement. “Yesterday, the people of Wayne and Oakland Counties honored that legacy and made sure every child in this region can learn from it. We are grateful for their trust, and we intend to earn it every day.” Historical Society President and CEO Elana Rugh formerly said, when the millage plan was unveiled in August, that the proposal would bring financial stability to both museums while allowing the institutions to focus on what they do best – preserving local and Black history while ensuring everyone can experience it. “For more than a century, the Detroit Historical Society has kept the story of this region, and yesterday voters made sure we can keep telling it,” Rugh said in a statement. “This victory belongs to the volunteers, staff and partners who carried our story into every corner of both counties. We will show them what their investment makes possible.” The tax will amount to $30 per year for the owner of a home with an average value of $300,000 and support operating costs for both museums. The museum millage was placed on the ballot by the Southeast Michigan Public Historical Museum Authority, a joint public authority established in July by Wayne and Oakland counties, according to the “Yes to Our Story” website. Barclay has noted that the millage will allow both museums to have a more prosperous and unified future and more money to cover operating costs. The proposal also calls for free transportation to the two museums for students and seniors. The millage also would ensure that residents of both Wayne and Oakland counties receive free admission to the Wright Museum and the Historical Society, which operates the Detroit Historical Museum in Midtown and the Dossin Great Lakes Museum on Belle Isle. Currently, only small children and museum members receive free admission. To thank the community, the three museums will offer free admission from Wednesday, Nov. 4 through Sunday, Nov. 8. Results will become official after the county canvass. In the coming months, the Wright and DHS will share the timeline for the first levy and plans for reporting to taxpayers on how the funds are used. Detroit Zoo millage renewal Meanwhile, another long-standing regional institution will continue to receive support from residents in the tri-county area. The Detroit Zoo asked residents in Wayne, Oakland and Macomb counties to renew a 10-year, 0.1 mill levy for its “Renew Your Zoo” campaign. Unofficial results in all three counties showed the millage renewal passed with 75% support in Wayne County, 71% in Oakland County and 69% in Macomb County. “This is an incredibly meaningful week for us, as voters across Wayne, Oakland and Macomb counties have renewed their support for the Detroit Zoological Society,” a Wednesday post on the zoo’s Facebook page reads. “We are deeply thankful for the confidence our community has placed in us.” The millage will allow the zoo to continue caring for more than 2,000 animals and 200 different species. For a homeowner with a home worth $200,000, the average cost will remain about $10 a year, said Hayley Murphy, executive director and CEO of the Detroit Zoological Society. The nonprofit operates the Detroit Zoo and the Belle Isle Nature Center, which is also included in the millage. The Detroit Zoo’s 100th anniversary is in 2028. “The millage is a real stable source of funding for us,” Murphy said. “It’s about a third of our revenue, so that helps cover both the zoo and the Belle Isle Nature Center. It helps us pay for the amazing animal care that we do.” Residents in the three counties first approved the Detroit Zoo tax in 2008 and again in 2016.

articles.title: Will Lawrence declares win in one of nation’s most-watched U.S House races
articles.description: U.S. House candidate William Lawrence is planning a noon news conference to discuss flipping Michigan’s 7th district, which is held by U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett. While final tallies have not […]
articles.content: Earlier in the evening Lawrence mingled with supporters. Photo by Raymond Holt for City Pulse U.S. House candidate William Lawrence is planning a noon news conference to discuss flipping Michigan’s 7th district, which is held by U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett. While final tallies have not been called, Lawrence maintains a lead and his campaign declared a victory in the early hours. Gallery: William Lawrence election watch party According to the Michigan Secretary of State’s tracker, Lawrence had 51% of the vote and Barrett had 47%, with most of the state’s votes counted. U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett watch party gallery Barrett, an Army veteran and helicopter pilot, ran a tricky final few months as he worked to separate himself from the increasingly unpopular Iran War and show independence from the Trump administration but he simultaneously showed off his close ties by bringing more than half of the Trump cabinet to his district in the six months before the election, as well as several visits from close administration allies like U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson. Congressional candidate William Lawrence outside a data center meeting in Delhi Township on Oct. 30, 2026. Photo by Mike Ellis/City Pulse In a statement, Lawrence’s campaign said, “As of Election Day morning, no candidate faced more Republican ad spending than Lawrence. Republican groups spent $23.3 million in general election advertising in Michigan’s 7th district, close to $1 million more than the next closest district (NY-17). Overall, Democrats were outspent by several million dollars in MI-07’s general election. Lawrence, who has never held elected office, is a community organizer who grew up in East Lansing and co-founded the nationally-known Sunrise Movement and the Mid-Michigan Tenant Resource Center. His campaign focused on prices, data centers and corporate political funding, drawing progressive backing. He won the Democratic primary against well-funded and casting-call-ready candidates Ukraine Ambassador Bridget Brink and retired Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam. Lawrence’s supporters met at The Venue in Lansing to watch the returns. Lawrence told his supporters to go home around 2:30 a.m., with a narrow lead. A Lawrence supporter reacts to Abdul El-Sayed’s announcement of victory in the Michigan senate race. Photo by Raymond Holt for City Pulse Supporters of Michigan’s 7th Congressional incumbent Rep. Tom Barrett gathered in the conference room of the Crowne Plaza hotel in Lansing. NBC’s live election broadcast was projected on three screens across the room, courtesy of a YouTube Premium subscription. Throughout the night, the crowd cheered when the live vote count, consistently showing Barrett in the lead, flashed across the screen. Barrett was absent at the beginning of the event, with scattered appearances throughout the night. The room filled with supporters, who were hopeful for the results. Tom and Lisa Jelenek are Michiganders for over two decades. From Lainsberg, the couple both voted for Barrett by absentee ballot. Tom Jelenek told City Pulse he appreciates Barrett’s military service. Lisa Jelenek said that the incumbent’s votes against the war in Iran set him apart from other Congressional Republicans. Reporting from ABC News noted that one of the measures Barrett voted for in opposition to the war, which passed the House and the Senate, was largely symbolic and lacked any real teeth to end the conflict. Lisa Jelenek said that, ultimately, she will sleep fine with whoever takes the seat. “The way this goes down is the way this goes down.” Guests gradually filed out as the night continued. Tables were left deserted with empty beer bottles and glasses half-filled with water. Around 2:15 a.m., live election coverage was turned off, and the screens turned dark. A member of the campaign team took down the “Tom Barrett for Congress” themed backdrop from the stage. About a dozen supporters, mostly members of Michigan State University’s College Republican chapter, lingered in the space, milling about and waiting for direction from Barrett. At 2:39 a.m., Barrett walked near the event space doors, spoke quietly with MSUCR members and subsequently left without making any official closing remarks or speaking to the press. MSUCR members told City Pulse that Barrett was not ready to concede the race and that they would wait to see what the coming hours bring. However, they said that Barrett would not contest the results if they favored his opponent.

Return of the trifecta: Michigan Democrats reclaim full control of state government
articles.description: DETROIT — Michigan will have a new Democratic Party majority in the state Legislature after Tuesday’s election, according to unofficial returns. The party and its top incumbent officials in the state Legislature declared victory on Wednesday morning after it became clear that they would have a new trifecta, as Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson was […]
articles.content: State Rep. Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) steps to the podium in Detroit with Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) after Democrats retook the majority on the Michigan House and retained control of the Senate. Puri is likely to be the next Speaker of the House, while Brinks was elected at lieutenant governor earlier Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — Michigan will have a new Democratic Party majority in the state Legislature after Tuesday’s election, according to unofficial returns. The party and its top incumbent officials in the state Legislature declared victory on Wednesday morning after it became clear that they would have a new trifecta, as Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson was also elected to the office of governor on Nov. 3. As of early Wednesday morning, Michigan Democrats have secured 19 seats in the state Senate while the Republicans secured 14 seats, the Associated Press reported. The AP also reported that the Democrats secured 51 seats in the state House, compared to the 43 seats that GOP secured on election night. Those unofficial returns show that the balance of power in the legislative branch will return to where it was in 2023 and 2024, when the party held both chambers of the Legislature and the governor’s office. Democrats’ main priority was protecting their state Senate majority and preventing it from falling into Republican hands in a demonstrably favorable year for the party. Democrats also aimed to capitalize on their momentum in 2026 to retake the House. With a Democratic wave cresting in Michigan on Tuesday, the party achieved both victories. “Since winning back the majority for the first time in nearly 40 years in 2022, we knew we would have a new mission in 2026 – defending and expanding that majority. And today, Senate Democrats have done just that,” Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks said in a statement. “This newly expanded majority will allow Senate Democrats to reach new heights.” Brinks will join Benson in the executive office as the lieutenant governor-elect. In that role, she will still retain a top leadership position in the chamber she is now leaving, as the lieutenant governor is the president of the Senate and breaks ties, if needed. “I look forward to working with our new caucus as Lieutenant Governor to drive costs down and wages up throughout this great state,” Brinks said. Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) steps to the podium in Detroit after Democrats retook the majority on the Michigan House and retained control of the Senate. Puri is likely to be the next Speaker of the House, while Brinks was elected at lieutenant governor earlier Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Michigan Senate Democrats must also choose a new leader going into the 2027 legislative session. Current House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) is the likely pick for House speaker now that Democrats have also taken back the state House. He will replace current Republican House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township), if elected to the position by his caucus as expected. Puri said what Michigan experienced on Tuesday night was not a “blue wave,” but a “tsunami.” “For the last two years, I served in the Michigan House as a minority leader, and I watched the institution be driven into the ground,” Puri said at the Democrats’ watch party in Detroit. “I watched healthcare be ripped away from our sick. I watched food and benefits taken away from our needy, and I watched tax cuts to billionaire corporations. The people of Michigan spoke up tonight and said that they’ve had enough, and they delivered a House Democratic majority.” Puri will become the first Indian American and Sikh speaker of the Michigan House. State Rep. Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) speaks to supporters in Detroit after Democrats retook the majority on the Michigan House and retained control of the Senate. Puri is likely to be the next Speaker of the House. Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Following the momentous win, state Rep. Jason Morgan (D-Ann Arbor), said the victory was the culmination of intense focus on the issues of affordability and the damage that they said the Republicans had done to their gains during the last Democratic trifecta. Morgan added that Republicans in Washington, D.C. also had a hand to play in creating the environment that made 2026 such a favorable year for the opposing party. “The hard work for us was just showing the people of Michigan that we will actually make their lives better. We will make their lives more affordable. We will create opportunity, and we will make our state better for the long term,” Morgan told Michigan Advance. “And I believe that people saw that, and they also looked at Washington D.C. and realized that everything Donald Trump was doing was hurting their daily life. Morgan said he was “extremely excited about what we can do over the next years to make life better for every Michigander.” Brinks on Wednesday morning said that the Senate’s top priority would be to push for a Michigan Voting Rights Act, which they have had in mind through the period of divided government from 2025 and 2026. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Morgan said that the House’s first priority was to focus on making life more affordable for for Michiganders — at the rest would fall into place. That includes potential Freedom of Information Act reform to extend the law to the governor’s office and the Legislature, and other accountability issues. But affordability would come first. “Government transparency, ethics, and accountability, those are critical … but the most important thing that I’ve heard consistently from voters while knocking doors all over the state of Michigan is that people need life to be more affordable,” Morgan said. “That’s what we’re focused on as priority number one.” Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said that, “when Democrats are in power, we make progress for working people.” “With our last trifecta, we restored workers’ rights, cut taxes for families, fed kids at school, and lifted tens of thousands of children out of poverty,” Hertel said in a statement. “Now, we will continue that critical work. With the leadership of Governor-Elect Benson and the future leaders of the state legislature, we will keep building toward a Michigan where every person has a chance to thrive.”
