articles.description: Fowlerville Community Theatre’s upcoming production of “Mary Poppins” is a family show in more ways than one. Not only does the cast include several sets of family members, but parents […]
articles.content: Fowlerville Community Theatre’s upcoming production of “Mary Poppins” is a family show in more ways than one. Not only does the cast include several sets of family members, but parents and other relatives are also pitching in to help prepare for opening night. One such volunteer is Okemos resident Robin Young, who helped paint the sets and is assisting with promoting the show around Greater Lansing. Her granddaughter Addison Smith plays Jane Banks, while her daughter Stacey Smith is part of the tap-dancing ensemble in the “Step in Time” number. “I’m just doing what I can to help,” Young said. “I saw how hard they all work. The participants are all members of their communities who have day jobs and are doing this, too, so it’s truly for love of the theater.” November and early December theater productions: “Clybourne Park” Nov. 5-8 and 12-15 7 p.m. Thursday 8 p.m. Friday-Saturday 2 p.m. Sunday Riverwalk Theatre 228 Museum Drive, Lansing riverwalktheatre.com “Antigone” Nov. 6-15 7:30 p.m. Tuesday-Saturday 2 p.m. Sunday Wharton Center Pasant Theatre 750 E. Shaw Lane, East Lansing theatre.msu.edu “Emily Brontë: Teenage Necromancer”Nov. 6-8 7 p.m. Friday 3 p.m. Saturday-Sunday Eastern High School 626 Marshall St., Lansing allofusexpress.org “Eurydice” Nov. 6-8 and 13-14 7 p.m. Friday-Saturday 2 p.m Sunday LCC Dart Auditorium 500 N. Capitol Ave., Lansing lcc.edu/showinfo “Witch” Nov. 6-8 and 12-15 7 p.m. Thursday-Saturday 3 p.m. Sunday; Nov. 14 Stage One 2200 Lake Lansing Road, Lansing peppermintcreek.org Manual Cinema’s “The 4th Witch” 7:30 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 10 Wharton Center Cobb Great Hall 750 E. Shaw Lane, East Lansing whartoncenter.com “What Do You Do with a Problem?” 4 p.m. Nov. 15 Wharton Center Cobb Great Hall 750 E. Shaw Lane, East Lansing whartoncenter.com “O Christmas Tea: A British Comedy” 7:30 p.m. Nov. 18 Wharton Center Pasant Theatre 750 E. Shaw Lane, East Lansing whartoncenter.com “Rhinoceros” Nov. 18-22 7:30 p.m. Wednesday-Sunday 2 p.m. Sunday Studio 60 Theatre 542 Auditorium Road, East Lansing theatre.msu.edu “A Lansing Christmas Adventure” Nov. 19-Dec. 27 Preview weekend showtimes: 7:30 p.m. Thursday-Friday 2 p.m. Saturday-Sunday Rest of run showtimes: 2 p.m. Thursday, Saturday-Sunday; Nov. 27; Dec. 23 7:30 p.m. Friday-Saturday; Dec. 23 No performances Nov. 26, Dec. 24 and 25 Williamston Theatre 122 S. Putnam St., Williamston williamstontheatre.org “Mary Poppins” Nov. 20-22 7 p.m. Friday 2 p.m. Saturday-Sunday Fowlerville High School Address fowlervillecommunitytheatre.com Giving Tuesday Play-a-Thon Dec. 1 11 a.m., 3 p.m. and 7 p.m. Williamston Theatre 122 S. Putnam St., Williamston williamstontheatre.org “Six” Dec. 1-6 7:30 p.m. Tuesday-Saturday 2 p.m. Saturday 1 and 6:30 p.m. Sunday Wharton Center Cobb Great Hall 750 E. Shaw Lane, East Lansing whartoncenter.com There are nearly 90 people in the cast, with Mandy Stone in the lead as Mary Poppins. Stone runs Lansing’s Alive Theatre with Christine Hall, who plays Mrs. Banks. According to Stone, the large cast makes this version of “Mary Poppins” much more immersive than other productions, especially the ensemble numbers. “Fowerville is a very family-oriented theater,” she said. “I’d say they lean more into having fun than stressing people out. One of the ways this occurs is they don’t cut people in auditions. They like having everyone involved.” Although the stage show has all the classic Disney songs fans know and love, audiences may be surprised at how different it is from the movie. The plot deviates more toward the storyline of the original books by P.L. Travers, especially in how the characters are portrayed. “Mary is a little less happy. Julie Andrews makes everything kind of sparkly and shiny. This Mary is a little more direct and not quite so smiley.” Stone explained. “Mr. and Mrs. Banks’ relationship is a lot more in the forefront: how Mr. Banks is the clinical, absent father that he is and how they fix that. Mrs. Banks is not the fluffy suffragette; she’s a mom trying to be heard and doesn’t know how to get through to either her kids or her husband. So, the character growth in them is wildly different from the movie.” Stone said that due to budget restrictions, she will not be physically “flying” in the show. The company will use other tricks to pull off the effect. However, when pressed for details, all she would tease was, “I know how it will work, but I can’t tell you. That’s Disney magic, darling!” Stone praised the rest of the cast, especially Addison Smith and Ezra Webber as Jane and Michael Banks. “They don’t have a ton of theater experience, but they’re naturals. Addie has the perfect English accent straight out of the gate, and Ezra is just the sassiest little bugger. They insisted on naming my umbrella Geoffrey.” Young can attest to how good her granddaughter’s British accent is, having watched snippets of rehearsals and listened to her practicing songs in the car. She is amazed by how quickly the cast and crew have come together. “There’s such joy that comes from the performers,” she said. “Even in the rehearsals, when it’s getting harder and more uncomfortable, they’re all so full of joy, working and pulling together. These are little kids painting sets alongside their parents and their grandmothers — three generations painting sets. It’s such a welcoming situation, truly a community.” She added that she can’t wait to see the finished show and is confident that everyone who comes to see it will love it. “It has such great family values, hope and love that reflects this whole cast,” she said. Stone echoed that sentiment. “I know that ‘Mary Poppins’ is special and nostalgic to a lot of people, and I think that nostalgia will carry through,” Stone said. “It’s an absolute honor to play her. She means the world to me. It feels surreal every time I get to put on the heeled boots and become her. In my heart of hearts, I just want to make Julie Andrews proud, even though she has no idea who I am.”

articles.title: From ‘Star Wars’ to ‘Star Trek’
articles.description: After 35 years of playing in the “Star Wars” sandbox, Timothy Zahn is making the jump to another sci-fi franchise. Zahn is hard at work on an original “Star Trek: […]
articles.content: After 35 years of playing in the “Star Wars” sandbox, Timothy Zahn is making the jump to another sci-fi franchise. Zahn is hard at work on an original “Star Trek: Deep Space Nine” graphic novel for IDW Publishing, slated for a late 2027 release. Timothy Zahn, courtesy photo “I started watching classic ‘Star Trek’ when I was in high school, so this is kind of like a homecoming for me,” he said. He didn’t reveal too much about the plot. What he did say is that a priceless artifact is destroyed upon arrival at DS9. A covert team is sent in to figure out what happened and who is responsible. Of course, things aren’t what they seem. “Things keep unraveling. Hopefully, it’ll be a twisty plot for people to enjoy,” Zahn said. “We needed a space station, and DS9 is the best one for this story. Mostly it’s my own characters, who interact with some of the classic ‘DS9’ characters.” https://lansingcitypulse.com/star-wars-novelist-timothy-zahn-is-grateful-for-the-fans

articles.title: In Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, Hines claims victory
articles.description: In the early hours Wednesday morning, former prosecutor Christina Hines announced her victory over Army National Guard veteran Michael Bouchard Jr. While Hines declared victory at 3:52 a.m., the Associated Press officially called the race shortly before 12:30 Wednesday afternoon with unofficial results showing Hines with 52.4% of the vote to 45.3% for Bouchard. The […]
articles.content: Former prosecutor and Democratic congressional candidate Christina Hines in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)In the early hours Wednesday morning, former prosecutor Christina Hines announced her victory over Army National Guard veteran Michael Bouchard Jr. While Hines declared victory at 3:52 a.m., the Associated Press officially called the race shortly before 12:30 Wednesday afternoon with unofficial results showing Hines with 52.4% of the vote to 45.3% for Bouchard. The district is currently held by U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), who opted against seeking reelection to run for governor, which was unsuccessful, as he lost to Democrat Jocelyn Benson. Encompassing southern Macomb County, the district also includes Rochester and Rochester Hills in eastern Oakland County. A former prosecutor in Wayne and Washtenaw counties, Hines focused her campaign on bringing down costs, emphasizing that as a mother of three and a Macomb county resident, she understood the hardship families in the district are facing. “This campaign started with a simple truth: that working families in our district are sick of being left behind by corrupt politicians in Washington and deserve someone who will actually put their needs first,” Hines said in a statement. “Over the last 18 months, I have been moved by the thousands of people who have told me their stories, shared their struggles, and demanded more from their leaders. Your words have stayed with me throughout this entire campaign and I will carry them with me to Washington.” Hines’ win is one of three GOP-held congressional districts in Michigan to flip to Democratic control. Democrat William Lawrence declared victory in the 7th Congressional District early Wednesday over incumbent Republican Congressman Tom Barrett of Charlotte and state Sen. Sean McCann did the same against his opponent, incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga of Holland Township. In a statement shared to social media, Bouchard congratulated Hines on her victory, offering his assistance as she steps into the role of the 10th Congressional district’s next representative. “I got into this race because I love this country,” Bouchard said. “America is the greatest country that has ever existed and election results going to the other party, do not diminish America’s shine. I will endeavor to ensure we remain that beacon on the hill throughout the world. Our promise is not political, it is in you. It is in freedom and our democracy.” 12:34 pmThis story was updated with word that the Associated Press had officially declared Hines the winner.

articles.title: ‘Star Wars’ novelist Timothy Zahn is grateful for the fans
articles.description: For 35 years, Michigan State University alumnus and New York Times best-selling novelist Timothy Zahn has been synonymous with his most famous creation: Grand Admiral Thrawn from “Star Wars.” Just […]
articles.content: For 35 years, Michigan State University alumnus and New York Times best-selling novelist Timothy Zahn has been synonymous with his most famous creation: Grand Admiral Thrawn from “Star Wars.” Just who exactly is Thrawn? A blue-skinned, red-eyed member of the alien race called the Chiss, Thrawn is a brilliant yet calculating leader in the Galactic Empire, on par with Darth Vader. “I wanted someone who wasn’t like the Emperor and who wasn’t like Vader, who could inspire trust and loyalty in the troops,” Zahn, 75, explained. “That wound up being someone who cares about his people and generally will not waste them in any failed attempts. They would win almost every battle Thrawn led them into. Vader led by fear, Thrawn led by loyalty.” Thrawn by MSU alumnus Timothy Zahn An Illinois native, Zahn earned a bachelor’s degree in physics from MSU and a master’s degree in physics from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He began to pursue doctoral studies in physics but decided to become a full-time writer instead. He lives in the Pacific Northwest. The deluxe edition of Zahn’s 2017 novel “Thrawn” (Random House Worlds, $50), released Oct. 28, features a white slipcase with a triangular cutout shaped like a Star Destroyer, a wrap-around cover with special foiling and artwork of Thrawn, blue-and-gold sprayed edges, endpapers illustrated with Star Destroyer schematics and a satin ribbon bookmark. Zahn’s last book about Thrawn was 2021’s “Lesser Evil,” the final installment in the “Thrawn Ascendancy” trilogy. “It’s about Thrawn before he joins the Empire. It explores the origins of Thrawn and his rise through the military ranks of the Chiss Ascendancy, located in the chaotic and uncharted Unknown Regions of the galaxy,” he said. “I got to create the entire Chiss culture. It was an exercise in world building, along with having Thrawn in it. What more could you ask for?” https://lansingcitypulse.com/from-star-wars-to-star-trek Since his debut more than 35 years ago, Thrawn has proven to be one of the “Star Wars” franchise’s most popular characters. Several action figures of him have been made over the years, and he appeared in two seasons of the animated TV series “Star Wars Rebels,” in which he was voiced by Lars Mikkelsen (“House of Cards,” “The Witcher”). “A writer tries to make the best characters he or she can. It’s up to the readers who they particularly grab on to,” Zahn said. “I’m very grateful to the fans for keeping Thrawn and his legacy alive all these decades. It’s great to see him on the little screen. He might even appear on the big screen — who knows?” Thrawn first appeared in 1991’s “Heir to the Empire,” written by Zahn. Hard as it is to believe, the “Star Wars” franchise — which debuted in 1977 with visionary filmmaker George Lucas’ “A New Hope,” — was in a period of lethargy. At the time, the last movie released in the franchise was 1983’s “Return of the Jedi.” The long-awaited prequel films didn’t debut until 1999, starting with the commercially successful yet fan-maligned “Phantom Menace.” Marvel Comics lost its license to create “Star Wars” comics in 1986. Timothy Zahn, courtesy “Heir to the Empire” debuted in the Top 10 of The New York Times’ best-sellers list and rose to No. 1, remaining there for several weeks. In its first week alone, the novel sold 70,000 copies and was sent back to press for an additional 70,000. Dark Horse Comics, which acquired the rights to create new “Star Wars” comics in 1991, later adapted the “Heir” trilogy. However, Zahn refuses to take credit for revitalizing “Star Wars.” “The books sold not because of my name, but because it was ‘Star Wars.’” he said. “It was a risky venture. In 1991, no one knew if anyone even cared about ‘Star Wars.’ The interest was still out there, but there was really nothing new. People say I revived ‘Star Wars.’ Not true. I just stuck a fork in the pie crust to see if any steam would come out, and it did.” Fellow “Star Wars” author John Jackson Miller disagreed with Zahn. “Timothy Zahn helped prove that people were still interested in ‘Star Wars’ long after the original films had ended, and everyone benefited, from readers to future writers,” Miller said. “He’s been a part of the scene ever since. I don’t think the ‘Star Wars’ tie-in scene would be anything close to what it is today were it not for his contributions.”

articles.title: ‘Dressing’ is out and seafood stuffing is in this Thanksgiving
articles.description: Thanksgiving, as we observe it today, doesn’t have much in common with the original feast of 1621. The vibe between the Pilgrims and Wampanoag was tense at the dinner table, […]
articles.content: Thanksgiving, as we observe it today, doesn’t have much in common with the original feast of 1621. The vibe between the Pilgrims and Wampanoag was tense at the dinner table, with some participants arriving ready to rumble. Come to think of it, maybe today’s Thanksgiving table hasn’t strayed too far, being notable for bringing together people from warring political tribes, with notoriously mixed results. Seafood stuffingPhoto by Ari LeVaux There was no pumpkin pie, because butter and flour were unheard of or sorely missed, depending on one’s affiliation, but wild fowl was likely on the menu, which leads me, among others, to conclude there was stuffing. Historians point to their evidence, while I point to the simple fact that both Pilgrims and Indians are human beings, and human beings know how to cook. And cooks don’t let an empty body cavity go unstuffed, especially during a three-day feast. Unfortunately, we seem to take this for granted in today’s America, where we think nothing of passing around savory bread pudding that has never seen the inside of a bird. That’s the fight I’ll pick this year. Technically, this never-stuffed material is “dressing,” not “stuffing.” The reason this distinction is important is because the stuff that comes out of the bird is so much better than the side pan, even if the same went into both vessels. The juices from a baked bird impart an unmistakable, irreplaceable joy to the stuffing. On the East Coast, the local diet was heavy on seafood like clams, scallops, oysters, mussels, eels and fish. I grew up in coastal Massachusetts, where we would sometimes dig a hole in the beach and fill it with ingredients like those above, in addition to hot rocks, and have a clambake. Somewhere along the way in my Thanksgiving experimentations, I decided it would be a good idea to stage a clambake inside a bird. In order to make it taste more like stuffing, I add breadcrumbs, herbs, lemon and aromatic veggies. This recipe depends on a diversity of quality seafood. It’s good to have at least one with the shell on, like clams or mussels, because that makes it seem more like a real clambake. Scallops and shrimp work great, too. And I really like imitation crab. It soaks up the juices like a thirsty sponge. Chickens, ducks and turkeys all work fantastic. Rabbit tastes like chicken, so that should work, too. But whatever bird you choose, large or small, you might find yourself with more stuffing than you can possibly cram into your bird. The easiest thing to do is to stuff it around the bird, along with potatoes, and let it melt in the pan juices. Although not literally stuffed, it sucks up enough of the juices to potentially rule out gravy. Another option for too much stuffing: pull the skin away from the bird and stuff it on up between the skin and bird. If basted properly, this layer of stuffing can help keep the bird moist. The skin might split, especially if you cram shells up there, but the crusted stuffing becomes a new skin, absorbing as many bastings as you care to pour. Finally, we can do the almost unthinkable: bake that excess stuffing in a side pan. Put a bunch of chicken wings on top and cook until they melt into the dressing. And just like that, after all of my huffing and puffing, I’ve figured out a way to make dressing taste like stuffing. My favorite part of this fishy bird dish is the clam juice brine. You’ve probably heard of clam juice as a mixer, adding deep umami notes to your bloody mary. And we can thank James Beard for nationalizing the idea that you should brine a chicken before baking it, because salty meat absorbs more water than non-salty meat, so it stays moist. My salty clam brine combines the two concepts. It flavors the stuffing via the fat and adds delicious authenticity to the feast. It may not dissolve the animosity at the table, but perhaps it will at least help keep everyone’s mouths too stuffed with food to talk. And that, my friends, is the true point of Thanksgiving. The right stuffings Some clam juice is salty, some isn’t. Sometimes the salty ones don’t mention salt in the ingredients, but it will show up in the RDA values for sodium. I’ve seen it with zero grams, 40 grams and 100 grams of added sodium. So, the salt can be a little tricky. Taste your clam juice, and if it’s really salty, reduce the added salt by a teaspoon or two. Serves six One 4-pound birdOne 10-ounce bottle clam juice6 teaspoons salt2 tablespoons olive oil2 cups minced onion2 cloves minced garlic1 cup chopped celery1 cup chopped carrotsOne chopped apple, red or green1 teaspoon black pepper3 tablespoons chopped fresh sage2 tablespoons chopped fresh thyme1 tablespoon chopped fresh rosemary2 pounds seafood1/2 cup white wine1 cup crouton-sized breadcrumbsThree lemons, cut into quartersFour potatoes, cut into quarters, to surround the bird Rinse the bird, take out any giblets stashed in the cavity and brine it in the clam juice with the salt and 2 cups of water. Push down on the bird hard, so the body cavity fills with brine. Marinate it for at least four hours in the fridge, turning occasionally. Rinse the bird, pat it dry and put it in a roasting pan. Add the oil to a frying pan on medium heat and sauté the onions, garlic, carrots, celery and apple with the black pepper, thyme, rosemary and sage. After 10 minutes, add the seafood, wine, lemon juice and squeezed lemons and cook a few minutes longer, but don’t try to cook all the seafood. Add the breadcrumbs, stir it all together and stuff it into the bird. Place the potatoes around the bird, along with extra stuffing if you go that route. Cover with foil and place in a 350-degree oven. After 90 minutes, remove the foil. The skin of an extra-stuffed bird will have receded like the tide. The stuffing on top, including the seafood, will hold the baste like a sponge. Turn the oven down to 300 degrees. Baste every 15 minutes until done. After about an hour, use a meat thermometer to make sure the bird’s internal temperature is at least 165 degrees. Rest, serve and eat.

articles.title: Lawrence declares victory in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District
articles.description: In a tight race for Michigan’s politically purple 7th Congressional District, Lansing area political organizer William Lawrence has declared himself the victor against incumbent Congressman Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte). Lawrence’s campaign shared their proclamation of victory at 2:49 a.m. Wednesday, with the Associated Press finally calling the race at 2:05 p.m. The final tally, with 97% […]
articles.content: Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence announces his final push to mobilize voters as he stands outside of U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett's (R-Charlotte) former office in Lansing on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)In a tight race for Michigan’s politically purple 7th Congressional District, Lansing area political organizer William Lawrence has declared himself the victor against incumbent Congressman Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte). Lawrence’s campaign shared their proclamation of victory at 2:49 a.m. Wednesday, with the Associated Press finally calling the race at 2:05 p.m. The final tally, with 97% of the votes counted, had Lawrence at 51% and Barrett at 47.7% While Barrett was leading through most of the evening and into the night, Lawrence’s campaign began making gains in the wee hours of the morning. Barrett departed his election night watch party at 2:39 a.m. without speaking to the media. At 2:40 a.m., Lawrence was leading by 2.2 percentage points. “We built an unprecedented movement here in Mid-Michigan, powered by thousands of volunteers, and we showed that you can beat an incumbent Republican without taking a dime of corporate PAC money,” Lawrence said in a statement. “We united people from every corner of this district – and found common ground in opposition to war and data centers, and in favor of good housing and healthcare, social security, jobs and education. Our people-powered movement took on the richest and most powerful people in the world, and we won.” Prior to his run for Congress, Lawrence had co-founded the Sunrise Movement, a youth-led climate action group which helped shape President Joe Biden’s climate policies. Lawrence also advocated for housing reforms as a founder of the MI Rent is Too Damn High Coalition. Lawrence will serve as the U.S. representative for the state’s 7th Congressional District, which includes Clinton, Shiawassee, Ingham and Livingston counties and parts of Eaton, Genesee and Oakland counties. Prior to Barrett winning the seat in 2024, the district had been represented by Democrat Elissa Slotkin, who ran for and won a U.S. Senate seat that same year. 2:23 pmThis story has been updated with word that the Associated Press had finally officially declared Lawrence as the winner.

articles.title: Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, will become first Muslim senator
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — Progressive favorite Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Republican Mike Rogers in a bitter campaign for Michigan’s open Senate seat, giving the Democratic Party’s left wing a breakthrough victory in one of the nation’s most important swing states. El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, will become the nation’s first Muslim senator. A former public health official who has never held elected office, he rose from a double-digit defeat in Michigan’s Democratic gubernatorial primary eight years ago to win a seat in the U.S. Senate. “You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed told a Detroit crowd early Wednesday as he declared victory. “Thank you. This is all yours.” El-Sayed overcame massive outside spending in both the Democratic primary and general election with a grassroots campaign built around universal health care, removing outside money from elections and sharp criticism of Israel. Backed by progressive leaders including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, his victory may bolster the movement ahead of the 2028 presidential election, offering evidence that candidates embracing its agenda can win in critical battleground states. Democrats across the country secured sweeping victories, winning in both battleground and deep-red states to claim control of both chambers of Congress. Republicans had cleared the field for Rogers, a former congressman who narrowly lost a Senate race to then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin two years ago. But Rogers struggled to balance his loyalty to President Donald Trump with concerns over rising prices tied to the war in Iran and economic turmoil from the president’s tariffs. The campaign also featured bitter attacks over El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel. Trump and other Republicans repeatedly sought to link him to terrorist organizations, despite no evidence of such ties, and questioned his loyalty to the United States. In his victory speech, El-Sayed said Republicans “went all in on one of the ugliest campaigns that we’ve seen in our lifetimes.” “They might have been pointing to my name and my faith, but we all know my name and my faith are not why you can’t afford your gas,” he said. The race became a focal point in the national battle for Senate control after two-term Democratic Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek reelection. El-Sayed emerged from a bruising August primary against the establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens that drew nearly $60 million in outside spending. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, spent nearly $30 million opposing El-Sayed, its largest investment in a single race. El-Sayed has been a staunch critic of Israel. The primary exposed divisions within the Democratic coalition. El-Sayed faced criticism from some in Michigan’s Jewish community over his rhetoric, including his statement that “hurt people hurt people” following an attack on a Michigan synagogue earlier this year. He later apologized, saying he was “sorry” to “anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful.” His campaign appearances with Hasan Piker, a popular political streamer who has made inflammatory comments about Israel, Jews and the Sept. 11 attacks, also became a target of criticism. The discord culminated two days before the election when Stevens endorsed Rogers after appearing at church with him, saying that El-Sayed had not done enough to address the concerns of some communities. Some Democrats worried about Black voter turnout in Detroit after Stevens carried Wayne County in the primary. Former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris were among the high-profile Democrats who campaigned with El-Sayed in the city to help mobilize voters. El-Sayed campaigned on an unapologetically progressive platform that made some moderate Democrats uneasy. Central to his campaign was Medicare for All, which would replace the current mix of private and public health insurance with a government-run, single-payer system. Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders helped build momentum for El-Sayed early in the campaign, while Ocasio-Cortez joined him for a final campaign swing through Michigan’s Upper Peninsula and the Detroit area. The victory will give progressives a powerful argument heading into the 2028 presidential election that their agenda can win, even in the nation’s most competitive battleground states. Republicans opted to run it back with Rogers after his razor-thin 2024 loss, when Slotkin prevailed even as Trump won Michigan by more than a percentage point. Once a CNN contributor who criticized Trump, Rogers has aligned himself more closely with the president in recent years. Rogers tried to expand his support among Democrats and independents, particularly Black and Jewish voters. But the political environment raised a fresh challenge for the Republican nominee. Rogers, who chaired the House Intelligence Committee and built much of his career around national security, had to navigate high fuel prices and an unpopular war with Iran while remaining aligned with Trump. “The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Rogers wrote on social media in September. El-Sayed relished in his victory, telling the Republican to enjoy his “retirement.” “You chose hate and Michigan chose hope,” El-Sayed said. “May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again.”

Democrats win majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years
articles.description: Democrats have won the majority of governor’s offices for the first time in 16 years after the GOP racked up major losses across the country. Democrats flipped governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas and defended competitive races in Maine, Michigan and Wisconsin, according to unofficial results from The Associated Press and Decision Desk […]
articles.content: Dr. Amy Acton speaks at a campaign rally in Cleveland ahead of her successful campaign for Ohio governor. Acton will become the first Democrat elected to lead Ohio in 20 years during a midterm election cycle that saw huge Democratic gains in states. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal)Democrats have won the majority of governor’s offices for the first time in 16 years after the GOP racked up major losses across the country. Democrats flipped governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas and defended competitive races in Maine, Michigan and Wisconsin, according to unofficial results from The Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ. As of 10 a.m. Eastern time on Wednesday, Democrats were set to hold 28 governor’s offices compared with Republicans’ 20. Races in Alaska and Kansas have not yet been called. In a historic night, voters elected a record number of four Black governors, including the first Black woman and first Black Republican ever elected governor. Midterms are always tough for the party that holds the White House, but high prices and growing disapproval of President Donald Trump delivered even stronger than expected results for Democrats Tuesday. “It’s a blue wave that was bigger than anyone had expected, and it’s having consequences across the country, including here in Texas,” said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston. “Overall, Donald Trump has single-handedly turned many red states blue — or at least purple.” By late Tuesday, Democrats had won races for attorney general and lieutenant governor for the first time in decades and flipped the Texas House. “One of the real questions will be what do Democrats do with this power, and will they be able to retain it,” he said. “This has effectively opened a door for Democrats across the country.” Gubernatorial races proved historic for both Democrats and Republicans on Tuesday with the election of the nation’s first Black woman governor and the first Black Republican governor. But the Democratic party made major gains coast to coast, particularly in reliably conservative states, that could reshape state policy for years to come. In Iowa, the election of Democrat Rob Sand ends more than a decade of Republican control of the legislature and the governor’s office. In Ohio, Democrat Dr. Amy Acton’s win marks the first time in 20 years that Ohio voters have selected a Democrat to lead the Buckeye State. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will become Georgia’s first Democratic governor since 2002 and the nation’s first Black woman governor. While governors were on ballots in 36 states, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter had only identified a dozen races for governor as competitive. Those included: Alaska, Georgia, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Wisconsin. Republicans have controlled a majority of state governments since 2010. Before Tuesday’s election, Republicans boasted a 26-24 gubernatorial advantage over Democrats. But the GOP’s state legislative advantage was even stronger, with Republicans controlling 28 state legislatures and Democrats controlling 18 with divided control of chambers in three states, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. By Wednesday morning, Democrats had notched major legislative wins. Democrats broke the GOP supermajority in Florida, flipped control of the Wisconsin state Assembly and Senate, and flipped the North Carolina state House. In Pennsylvania, Democrats won the GOP-held state Senate, seizing a trifecta – control of the governor’s office and both chambers of the legislature – in Harrisburg. “Tonight’s earth-shattering victory is undeniable proof that voters are fed up with the MAGA agenda,” Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said in a news release. In Arizona, Democrats declared victory in a yearslong effort to win control of the legislature, proclaiming that Republicans would be in the minority at the state Capitol for the first time in 60 years. Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org. This story was originally produced by Stateline, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Michigan Advance, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed beats Mike Rogers in US Senate race: ‘Michigan, we did it’
articles.description: Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeats Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s fiercely contested US Senate race.
articles.content: Michigan voters have cast their ballots in the US Senate race between Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers Contentious from the start, the race has attracted record outside spending and could decide which party controls Congress This story will be updated with the latest results as election officials across the state tally votes DETROIT — Buoyed by favorable national tailwinds, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed overcame party infighting to defeat Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s fiercely competitive US Senate race. El-Sayed, a progressive who campaigned on universal healthcare and taxing the rich, is the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate. He’ll be part of a new majority for Democrats, who flipped several seats in other states in a national rebuke of Republican President Donald Trump. The Associated Press called the race for El-Sayed at 2:27 a.m, declaring him the winner over his Republican rival. He led Rogers by nearly 6 percentage points with 85% of all ballots counted. See the latest vote tally here: El-Sayed had already declared victory an hour earlier, thanking supporters for taking a chance on the “unlikeliest of candidates.” “Michigan, we did it,” he told supporters at a Michigan Democratic Party watch party in Detroit. “I cannot wait to serve you with the same big-heartedness, open-mindedness, grit and earnestness that you’ve shown me.” He also had harsh words for President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Rogers, who had each claimed he or his family were associated with the Muslim Brotherhood. “You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope,” he said. “May we never have to see the likes of you in the state again.” El-Sayed’s victory is a watershed moment for the left wing of the Democratic Party, which viewed the Michigan race as a proving ground for progressives’ viability in competitive swing states. Related: Donate Jocelyn Benson beats John James in governor’s race Voters OK Proposal 2 to get ‘money out of politics’ More Michigan election results Addressing the outside spending that poured in during the primary and election cycle to defeat him, El-Sayed said voters “built something bigger than a bank account.” “We built a movement, government of the people, by the people, and for the people,” he said. “We showed that in a battle between the money and the many, that the many really can win.” Despite a highly public feud with former Democratic primary rival Haley Stevens, who endorsed Rogers two days before the election, a majority of voters chose El-Sayed to try to address high costs of living and put a check on the Trump administration. “I am definitely voting Democrat just because the Republicans did nothing to stop” Trump, said Jerrilyn Mathews, a Manton retiree and former GOP voter who left the party when the president took it over. Mathews had “doubts” about El-Sayed but ultimately voted for him and other Democrats up and down the ticket. “Considering who the opposition was, I think I’d have voted for a tin can,” she said of Rogers after casting her ballot Tuesday. Rogers, a former member of Congress, also ran for the Senate in 2024 and narrowly lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. Who is Abdul El-Sayed? A former public health official and doctor by training, El-Sayed’s core message became a campaign slogan and rallying cry for supporters: “Money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for All.” Drawing from his experiences in public health, El-Sayed distinguished himself from other Democratic hopefuls early on by advocating for a government-backed, single-payer healthcare system he argues would help bring down costs. Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a news conference at the base of the Spirit of Detroit monument in Detroit, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya) He’s also taken a hardline stance on artificial intelligence, calling for public ownership and strict regulation of AI companies as well as “terms of engagement” to hold data center projects accountable if they don’t meet utility usage and environmental requirements. As a local government appointee, El-Sayed worked with a nonprofit to provide free glasses for thousands of local kids and started a free Narcan distribution system to prevent overdose deaths, programs that continue today. One of El-Sayed’s signature initiatives, a medical debt payoff program for Wayne County residents, has cleared more than $95 million in bills for more than 100,000 county residents since 2024. The totals fell well short of his $700 million goal, causing him to alter early campaign messaging that claimed he had met the target. Outside his public health roles, El-Sayed has also coauthored a book on Medicare for All, hosted a podcast and offered political commentary via columns, speaking engagements and in advisory roles. El-Sayed has never held elected office, but the 41-year-old has been on the statewide ballot before: In 2017, he resigned as Detroit’s health director to join the 2018 gubernatorial race, losing in the primary to current Gov. Gretchen Whitmer by more than 20 points. Progressive favorite with populist pitch El-Sayed wasn’t shy about touting his progressive credentials, campaigning with movement favorites US Sen. Bernie Sanders and US Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. But in the general election cycle, he worked to unite the Democratic base while making overtures to voters not historically inclined toward his party: people who supported President Donald Trump in past elections but still feel left behind by the government he had promised to change. “Our coalition is going to be anybody who has felt locked out by their politics and wants those politics to be unlocked for them,” El-Sayed said in October. El-Sayed’s strategy involved spending considerable time in rural and northern Michigan, not typically considered Democratic strongholds. Ethan Harbin, a 21-year-old Eaton County voter, voted for Trump in his first election two years ago. This time around, he chose El-Sayed and other Democrats in top offices, but selected Republicans in some local offices, such as the school board. U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), left, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, center, and U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) wave to a cheering audience during a rally for El-Sayed at the Lansing Convention Center in Lansing, Michigan on Sunday, July 19, 2026. (Ella Miller/Bridge Michigan) “We were supposed to be out of forever wars and up in the economy,” he said, noting Trump made “a lot of promises.” “I’m a fool-me-once kind of guy,” Harbin said. “You had your shot. You know, I give you the benefit of the doubt, but yeah, I feel burned.” El-Sayed also rallied frequently in Detroit, at various points enjoying support from key officials like former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris. During a Detroit rally last month, Obama compared El-Sayed’s trajectory to his own and said El-Sayed would “finish the job we started” with the Affordable Care Act and “guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every American.” El-Sayed, a former public health official and longtime proponent of a “Medicare for All” single-payer healthcare system, called that stamp of approval an honor. Blake Dembski, a 19-year-old restaurant worker in Lansing, said he supported El-Sayed and other Democrats because he aligned closely with their policies: money out of politics, healthcare for all, reining in artificial intelligence and “making things more accessible to people who are underrepresented.” “I think that El-Sayed is somebody who’s very qualified to talk about that given that he has a medical degree,” he said. “I think that that’s what we should see more in politics, is more people with real world qualifications to talk about certain issues.” Overcoming challenges El-Sayed’s biggest challenge on the campaign trail was convincing independents and other persuadable voters, including those who supported Stevens, to back him in the general election. Rogers’ campaign and other conservative groups relentlessly attacked El-Sayed, arguing his progressive views on law enforcement, healthcare and other issues were too extreme for Michigan while exploiting divisions within the Democratic Party. Even before Stevens defected to endorse Rogers, the Republican candidate had set up a “Democrats for Rogers” coalition and worked to appeal to Black and Jewish Democrats in metro Detroit. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., left, her fiance Jason Turkish, right, stand with Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, second left, and his wife Kristi Rogers during a church service at Perfecting Church, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Jose Juarez) During the primary cycle, the common refrain by Stevens and high-profile supporters came down to general election electability, arguing that nominating El-Sayed could cost Democrats the Senate seat and a chance at flipping the chamber’s majority. El-Sayed has also faced unrelenting attacks from Trump, Rogers and other conservatives over what they claim are connections to the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational Islamic organization that advocates for political systems entwined with Islamic law. Austin Haynes of Mason said he voted straight-ticket Republican, motivated by his Christian religious views, opposition to policies supporting transgender youth in schools, skepticism about Muslim people in elected office and support for Republican immigration policies. “We believe in a small government, limited. They work for us. They serve us, and then they get the hell out of our way,” Haynes said. But the rhetoric made many prominent Arab American leaders uncomfortable, even some who supported Trump in his winning 2024 campaign, and ate into Republican support among a group that took out their frustrations with the Biden administration’s handling of the war in Gaza at the ballot box in 2024. A national focus El-Sayed’s win was welcome news for Democrats, though the party ultimately didn’t need full results from Michigan’s most competitive races to win outright control of Congress. National Democrats were hoping to take advantage of favorable headwinds and flip enough Republican seats for a majority. Associated Press projections show that Democratic candidates around the country did so, flipping at least seven seats. Peters’ decision not to seek re-election opened a competitive Democratic primary for his replacement, and Republicans saw a rare opportunity for a flip this cycle in Rogers, who ran and only narrowly lost to now-US Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024. Voters’ TV screens, phones and mailboxes have been flooded with campaign ads on the race, funded by record spending from candidates and outside groups alike. The race is far-and-away the most expensive election in Michigan’s history, with more than $270 million in disclosed spending as of last month, not counting additional undisclosed “dark money” spending. That’s up from $217 million in disclosed spending in Rogers’ 2024 race against Slotkin.

articles.title: Jocelyn Benson beats John James in Michigan governor’s race
articles.description: Democrat Jocelyn Benson wins Michigan governor's race and will replace term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.
articles.content: Democrat Jocelyn Benson beats Republican John James in Michigan governor’s race Benson, currently the secretary of state, will replace term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, also a Democrat She will inherit a state with some significant challenges, including struggling schools, sluggish population and economic growth LANSING — Jocelyn Benson is poised to become Michigan’s 50th governor after soundly defeating Republican John James amid a surge of support for Democrats throughout Michigan. Benson won by nearly 11 percentage points in a wave election that saw Democrats also win full control of the Michigan Legislature. “In this election, from the western reaches of the Upper Peninsula to downtown Detroit, voters sent a clear message: they want leaders who will fight for them, fight to lower costs, fight to grow our economy, fight the corruption that too often protects the powerful and hurts the people,” Benson said in a victory speech in Detroit “We showed the nation that in our democracy, the power of the people will always rule the day.” See the vote tally here: Benson will replace term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in January. She bucked history to become the first candidate to succeed a governor from the same political party since Michigan implemented term limits in 1992. “That means we can expand on the historic progress we’ve made over the last eight years,” Whitmer said in a statement, citing senior tax cuts, free school meals and other policies she’s implemented as governor. But Benson will inherit significant challenges, too, including struggling schools, stagnant population growth and an economy outpaced by neighboring states. Related: Abdul El-Sayed beats Mike Rogers in US Senate race: ‘Michigan, we did it Voters OK Proposal 2 to get ‘money out of politics’ More Michigan election results Benson, who tapped state Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks as her running mate, called their election a “win for our young girls who tonight can look up and for the first time in our state’s history. see two women leading this state as governor and lieutenant governor.”Donate She and Brinks will “work together every day to ensure that young girls and women always have access to the health care they need and the rights and freedoms they deserve,” Benson added. James, who would have become Michigan’s first Black governor, could not overcome national trends and the unpopularity of President Donald Trump, who had endorsed him. In a message posted to social media Wednesday, James said he had congratulated Benson in a phone call and thanked his supporters, saying “my heart is full” from his experiences in the campaign. “The potential we have (in Michigan) is amazing,” James said. “I look forward to getting back to my first and most important title, and that is husband and dad.” Both candidates pitched a vision of how they’d like to reshape Lansing, from a new funding model for schools to tax cuts and an overhaul of the state’s regulatory apparatus. Benson built her campaign around healthcare and affordability, leaning on her record as secretary as evidence she can make government more efficient and responsive to taxpayers. “The heart of our campaign … is costs down, wages up, and fighting for the people of Michigan and ending corruption,” Benson told supporters during a campaign-closing bus tour. “As governor, I will work for you — not the highest bidder, not Donald Trump — you and the people of this state.” Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson is touting her record as she runs for Michigan governor. (Emily Rose Bennett for Bridge Michigan) The defeat was the third statewide loss for James, who twice lost US Senate races before winning election to Congress in 2022. He ran for governor instead of seeking re-election in his Macomb County district. James had cast his candidacy as an opportunity for change in Lansing, arguing eight years of Democratic leadership is to blame for Michigan’s trajectory. “Don’t let anybody tell you that affordability alone is what you should strive for, but prosperity is what you should strive for. Right now, we have people dumbing it down, saying that we should just accept just getting by,” James said in an October speech to supporters. “We’re not going to accept getting by because the American dream is our birthright, and greatness is in our DNA. We just need leadership who believes in you as much as I do.” The gubernatorial candidates have had to campaign in the shadow of a behemoth nationally-watched US Senate race that’s seen vastly more spending and complicated their efforts to reach voters. Benson’s counterpart in the Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed, ran a substantially more progressive campaign, while Trump — who faces nearly 60% disapproval in Michigan — repeatedly inserted himself into state politics and told Michiganders to vote “like I’m on the ballot.” The president’s presence made James’ tightrope all the more tenuous. He rallied with Trump and courted his support while trying to turn voters’ attention back to Michigan-specific issues. “We’re losing our kids, and y’all are focusing on some dude in Washington, D.C. that’s going to be done in two years? We are smarter than that,” James told reporters after the second gubernatorial debate. Bridge Michigan chronicled both candidates’ proposals to address pressing policy questions on education, healthcare, the environment, economy and democracy. What voters said Traverse City voter Elaine Hatch told Bridge Michigan she voted for Benson on Tuesday because “she is a female, for one,” but also because “I think she has done a great job as Secretary of State.” Hatch, a 61-year-old logistics manager for an import/expert company, called herself a lifelong Democrat who was especially motivated to vote this year to protest Trump. In Monroe County’s Lambertville, Timothy and Consuelo Cousino described themselves as former Trump voters who this year backed Benson and all other Democrats on the ballot. “I thought maybe he could help (the country) financially,” said Consuelo Cousino, 45, a stay-at-home mom of five children. But that didn’t happen, they said. Prices have surged. Worse, “there’s so much hate in the country right now,” said Timothy Cousino, 43, a city worker and member of the 180th National Guard in Toledo. Trump may not have been on the ballot, but he drove their votes solidly blue this year, Timothy Cousino said: “I went blue down the line; that’s how irritated I am.” Amid slumping financial support, Republican gubernatorial nominee James held a press conference on transgender children in school sports, telling reporters he’d use a ‘grassroots approach’ to spread his campaign message. (Simon Schuster/Bridge Michigan) But Mike Haines of Warren, a 57-year-old business owner, said he voted for James after backing Democrats in some past elections. “John James is more upfront, straight-shooting,” Haines said. “I have an appreciation for his approach, from all the way back to COVID situations as compared to how Benson and the administration was dealing with it.” Jesus Villa, a 34-year-old architect who lived in Traverse City and voted in his first general election as a US citizen on Tuesday, said he split his ticket to vote for James and Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “My thinking is that the government has to be managed or controlled as a business,” Villa said, explaining his support for James, who helped run his family business in Detroit after serving in the US Army. An almost unprecedented election The contest to succeed Whitmer began with a shock: a month after the 2024 presidential election, Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan announced he would leave the Democratic Party to run for governor as an independent, betting voters would back a problem-solving pragmatist who eschewed partisan labels. Duggan raised millions and rose quickly in polls, seemingly setting the stage for a competitive three-way gubernatorial race unprecedented in modern Michigan politics. But by May 2026, the national political climate had shifted, as anger toward the Trump administration translated into increased support for Democratic candidates. As his fundraising began to falter, and without the institutional support of a major party, Duggan determined his path to victory had closed and withdrew from the race. “I never ran to be a spoiler,” Duggan said in his announcement. “I was trying to change politics.” Republicans and Democrats alike scrambled to pick up his supporters in the ensuing weeks. The road to November James won a contested primary but faced significant attacks in the process. The GOP field at one point swelled to eight candidates, though by the time of the August primary had contracted to a two-man contest between James and businessman Perry Johnson, a self-funded candidate who put more than $30 million of his personal fortune into his campaign. Johnson used a flurry of advertising to promise he’d slash Michigan taxes, but James won Trump’s endorsement and went on to win the primary by about 15 percentage points. Benson, meanwhile, enjoyed a more cordial primary against Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson, whom she easily bested by more than 66 points. Benson took and maintained a fundraising advantage in the general election race. At one point in early October, it seems James had been left to “twist in the wind,” as one GOP strategist put it, after the Republican Governors Association pulled its ad reservations, leaving Benson with a roughly 12-to-1 spending advantage in the final month of the race. That abruptly changed in the last two weeks, however, after the Michigan Republican Party began spending millions to support James and other statewide candidates, thanks to big donations from DeVos family members, Elon Musk and outside super PACs. The late support seemingly ran afoul of Michigan campaign finance law, which caps coordinated spending between the party and candidates, prompting a complaint from the Michigan Democratic Party that has not been resolved. James argued the spending was legal because a recent US Supreme Court decision had nullified similar spending limits in federal races. Ad tracking firm AdImpact reported nearly $41 million has been spent on broadcast ads in the gubernatorial general election, with 56% of that designed to benefit Benson. Counting primary spending by Johnson, total spending in the race neared $74 million.

articles.title: Bergman defeats Barr once more, winning 6th term representing Michigan’s 1st Congressional District
articles.description: Defying Democrats’ efforts to rally support in northern Michigan, U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Watersmeet) has won reelection in the state’s 1st Congressional District, defeating Traverse City attorney Callie Barr. When the Associated Press called the race at 1:09 a.m., unofficial results showed Bergman had won 53.2% of the vote while Barr received 44.7%. Bergman will […]
articles.content: Rep. Jack Bergman (L) and Callie Barr (R) | Office/courtesy photosDefying Democrats’ efforts to rally support in northern Michigan, U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Watersmeet) has won reelection in the state’s 1st Congressional District, defeating Traverse City attorney Callie Barr. When the Associated Press called the race at 1:09 a.m., unofficial results showed Bergman had won 53.2% of the vote while Barr received 44.7%. Bergman will serve his sixth term as Representative for Michigan’s 1st Congressional district, which includes the entirety of the state’s upper peninsula, and the northern portion of the lower peninsula. Bergman and Barr previously faced off in 2024. Bergman prevailed, leading Barr by more than 20% of the vote. In the lead-up to election night Bergman faced repeated criticisms for his participation in a taxpayer-funded program reimbursing representatives’ housing and meal expenses and was the subject of a Detroit News investigation which found he was living in a Washington, D.C. home sold to his daughter by campaign supporters, though Bergman’s campaign maintains he paid fair market value for his rent on the home “and is in full compliance with House Ethics.” However, the negative press and attacks from his opponents were not enough to flip the northern Michigan district. In a statement shared to Facebook, Bergman thanked residents of the 1st Congressional for placing their trust in him once again. “While tonight was a tough night for Republicans, there is no shortage of work ahead of us to get our Nation back on track,” Bergman said. “Americans are rightly frustrated with inflation, reckless government spending, and the direction of our Nation. They deserve leaders who will listen, stand firm, and deliver results.”

articles.title: Eli Savit wins attorney general election, keeping state’s top law enforcement role with Democrats
articles.description: DETROIT – Democratic nominee and Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit has won the race for Michigan Attorney General, defeating Republican nominee Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd by a margin of 51.8% to 45.5% as of 2:28 a.m. Wednesday, the time at which the Associated Press called the race. “This campaign started 18 months ago, fueled […]
articles.content: Eli Savit shares a victory speech, declaring his win for Michigan Attorney General at the Michigan Democratic Party's election night event in the early hours of Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)DETROIT – Democratic nominee and Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit has won the race for Michigan Attorney General, defeating Republican nominee Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd by a margin of 51.8% to 45.5% as of 2:28 a.m. Wednesday, the time at which the Associated Press called the race. “This campaign started 18 months ago, fueled by conversations on college campuses and with young people who were concerned about their future and who wanted an attorney general who would represent the people and not the powerful, and that is what we are going to get to work on doing from day one. to stand,” Savit said in a speech while declaring victory. According to unofficial results, third-party candidates Jason Dye of the Libertarian Party, John Ludtke of the U.S. Taxpayers Party, Jeff Polonowski of the Green Party and Doug Dern of the Natural Law Party received 1.3%, 0.7%, 0.5% and 0.3% of the vote respectively. Savit declared victory around 2 a.m. on Wednesday at the election watch party hosted by the state Democratic Party. He will succeed current Attorney General Dana Nessel, who is term-limited. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Late October polling showed Savit with around a 5-point lead over Lloyd, but also showed about 15% of those polled were undecided. With neither candidate benefiting from significantly more name recognition than his opponent, Savit benefited from an overall good environment for Democratic candidates in 2026. Savit, a progressive candidate, was nominated by the Michigan Democratic Party at their April convention, defeating a more moderate candidate in Oakland County Prosecutor Karen McDonald. He will succeed the term-limited current attorney general, Dana Nessel, who endorsed Savit. Lloyd conceded in a statement on social media around 9:30 a.m. on Wednesday, congratulating Savit on his victory. “This is not the result we wanted but I am proud of the campaign we ran,” he wrote. “I still have the best job I’ve ever had as Eaton County Prosecutor and I will be back at work serving my community.” Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel congratulated Savit on the win. “At a time when Michiganders are facing threats to their freedoms and economic security, we need an Attorney General who will use every tool available to fight back. Eli has the courage, conviction, and record to do just that. I know he’ll stand up for Michigan—and I feel safer with him as our next Attorney General,” Hertel said. Also commenting was Planned Parenthood Advocates of Michigan President and CEO Paula Thornton Greear. “Eli Savit has been a staunch defender of reproductive rights in Michigan, including abortion access, and we congratulate him on this victory. A state attorney general plays an essential role in protecting those rights and people’s ability to get the care they need. With Eli in office, we know we’ll have a trusted partner who will show up for Michiganders no matter what obstacles anti-abortion politicians throw our way. We look forward to working by his side to protect and expand access to sexual and reproductive health care,” Greear said. Savit’s win completes the Democratic sweep of Michigan’s executive offices, following wins by Jocelyn Benson for governor and Garlin Gilchrist for secretary of state. The Democratic Party has maintained a hold on those offices since 2018. It also follows a declaration of victory by Democrats in the Michigan House and Senate, setting up another trifecta similar to what the party enjoyed after the 2022 election, but before Republicans won the House in 2024. 10:11 amThis story was updated to include a concession statement from Doug Lloyd.

articles.title: Opinion | Abdul El-Sayed’s Historic Win in Michigan Answers Several Questions
Michigan elects Abdul El-Sayed in hard-fought US Senate race -- here’s what he promised on the campaign trail
Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim elected to US Senate
Progressive Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race to become first Muslim US senator | US midterm elections 2026
articles.content: Democrat defeats Mike Rogers in race marked by Islamophobic attacks from Trump and Republican allies Tell us: what do you want to know about the midterm election results? Abdul El-Sayed, the doctor and progressive insurgent, has made history in winning the closely watched US Senate race in Michigan, defeating the Republican Mike Rogers to become the country’s first Muslim senator. El-Sayed’s victory adds to a decisive Democratic majority in the Senate after the party wrested control of the upper chamber on Tuesday with shock victories in Texas, Kansas and South Carolina. El-Sayed, 42, declared victory in Michigan’s US Senate race early on Wednesday at the state Democrats’ headquarters in Detroit. “You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed told the crowd in his election night speech. “You welcomed me in your homes, your churches, your synagogues.” He credited a movement built over a year and a half of campaigning in Michigan’s biggest cities and smallest towns, and said voters gave him strength in his lowest moments. His opponent and detractors, including Donald Trump and his vice-president, JD Vance, led a largely Islamophobic campaign against him, often pointing to his name and faith, including the president alleging he was a “jihadist” and that he would need to walk through a metal detector to get into the Senate. El-Sayed said his denigrators chose to be divisive rather than address the cost of gas and groceries because they didn’t have an answer to the problems he said they created. “They want an America that is too small for some of us,” El-Sayed said. “We know that America is big enough for all of us.” Addressing Vance, he noted: “JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in January.” Rogers, a former congressman who was endorsed by Trump and ran as his close ally, previously lost the 2024 Senate race to Elissa Slotkin by roughly 0.3 percentage points. This time he ran against El-Sayed, a former Wayne county health director who upset the Democratic establishment favourite Haley Stevens in the primary earlier this year. He advocated for the Medicare for All proposal for universal healthcare and called for an end to US military aid for Israel. Both candidates were running to succeed Gary Peters, an outgoing Democratic senator who has held the seat since 2015. Republicans cast the general election as a referendum on the Democratic left, and El-Sayed’s nomination prompted Trump to call him a “communist”, and to slander him as a “jihadist” and member of the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood. The race was seen as a test of whether a progressive insurgent could win a swing state. The pro-Israel lobby Aipac, through its Super Pac United Democracy Project, spent about $30m in the primary trying to stop El-Sayed, a record for a single race. More than $220m in total ad spending had been poured into the general election by mid-October by both parties, according to AdImpact. In his victory speech, he said: “We want our taxes spent here, for schools here, and healthcare here, and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid, or genocide, or war.” Rogers had backed Trump’s aggressive tariff policy and war with Iran, before breaking with the president on both in the closing weeks of the campaign, calling for an end to the US-Canada trade war and for swift conclusion to the Iran conflict. He has previously opposed the Affordable Care Act, defended the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement, and has repeated Trump’s false claims about the 2020 election. Republicans had sought to portray El-Sayed as too far left for a swing state. A Fox News poll in August found 54% of Michigan voters thought his positions were too extreme, though 51% also said Rogers was too close to Trump.

Garlin Gilchrist wins secretary of state election, maintaining Democratic control of office
articles.description: Democratic nominee and Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II has won the race for Michigan Secretary of State, defeating Republican nominee and Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini by a margin of nearly eight percentage points as of 2:00 a.m., the time at which the Associated Press called the race. “The biggest difference between us and them, […]
articles.content: Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II shares a victory speech in his win for Michigan Secretary of State with the Michigan Democratic Party's election night event in the early hours of Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Democratic nominee and Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II has won the race for Michigan Secretary of State, defeating Republican nominee and Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini by a margin of nearly eight percentage points as of 2:00 a.m., the time at which the Associated Press called the race. “The biggest difference between us and them, the biggest difference between Michigan and the rest of the country, the biggest difference between Democrats and those who vote against Democrats, is we have a place for everyone,” Gilchrist said in a victory speech. “Our vision is big enough to include everyone. Their vision is so small, so narrow, so weak that everybody can’t live. But Michigan, my arms are wide enough. I’m tall enough to bring everybody in the big picture.” Unofficial election results show Gilchrist received 52.1% of the vote, while Forlini pulled in 44.4%. Third-party candidates Scott Aughney of the U.S. Taxpayers Party, Eric Borregard of the Green Party and Christine Sloan of the Libertarian Party received 0.6%, 0.4% and 1.7% of the vote respectively. Two late October polls showed Gilchrist with a distinct lead over Forlini — he held a nine-point lead in one poll and an eleven-point lead in the other, both outside their respective margins of error. As a current statewide executive, Gilchrist benefited from broader name recognition than Forlini, as well as an overall positive environment for Democratic candidates in 2026. Forlini conceded the race in a statement just before 2:30 a.m. “Tonight, the people of Michigan made their decision. While this is not the outcome we hoped for, I respect the voters’ choice and congratulate Garlin Gilchrist on his victory as Michigan’s next Secretary of State,” he wrote. “I am encouraged by the Republicans, Independents, and Democrats who came together to support me. We demonstrated that people do not have to agree on every issue — or belong to the same political party — to recognize the value of experience, integrity and common sense leadership.” Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson won the gubernatorial election and Washtenaw County Clerk Eli Savit won the Michigan attorney general race, maintaining Democratic control in the three main elected statewide executive positions — a boost to the Democratic agenda with single-party control. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available. 3:08 amThis story was updated to include a concession statement from Anthony Forlini.

North Korea launches missiles toward the sea as Pyongyang protests against US claims on Binance hack
articles.description: North Korea launches missiles toward the sea as Pyongyang protests against US claims on Binance hack AP News North Korea fires multiple missiles in fourth weapons launch in a month, Seoul says NBC News Soft Reveal of New North Korean Stealth Strategic UAV 38 North North Korea says it tested air-defence missile, staged cruise missile drill Reuters North Korea launches unidentified projectile toward the sea, South Kore
articles.content: SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korea launched multiple missiles toward the sea on Wednesday, South Korea’s military said, hours after Pyongyang said it saw no need to resume diplomacy with Washington in protest of accusations that North Korean hackers were behind the recent cryptocurrency heist at Binance. Observers say North Korea was likely pressuring the U.S. to drop what it calls its hostility against the North and offer concessions if it wants to restore ties between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launches of several missiles fired toward North Korea’s eastern waters. It said South Korean and U.S. authorities were analyzing details of the launches. It said South Korea maintains a readiness to repel any potential provocations by North Korea. Earlier Wednesday, Kim’s sister, senior official Kim Yo Jong, again disputed an FBI announcement that North Korean hackers were responsible for the hack at Binance, calling it “an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward” Pyongyang. “It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons,” she said. “The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.” In a Tuesday statement, she described the FBI announcement as “a trite provocation.” Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The FBI later said the theft was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year. In recent months, North Korea has accelerated its weapons tests in a likely bid to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un. The news of the latest launches came amid vote counting in the U.S. midterm elections. Also Wednesday, North Korea’s state KCNA news agency released a photo showing parts of a warship under construction that would likely be its biggest naval vessel. KCNA said Kim Jong Un expressed satisfaction this week during a visit to the Nampho Shipyard over the warship that it said “is incomparably huge” relative to its 5,000-ton destroyers. Kim previously said North Korea planned to build a 10,000-ton strategic guided missile cruiser. Tensions between the two Koreas have also deepened since mine blasts at their border in September wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the border and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked. North Korea later threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.
